title: Tree stump saves Aroostook woman’s home in 2-vehicle crash
text:
A two-vehicle crash in Frenchville left the drivers uninjured but took out a resident’s mailbox and damaged her front porch. Thanks to a tall tree stump, her home remains intact.
Nancy Dellagrotta is grateful she decided to leave the nearly 6-foot trunk in front of her living room window after utility crews cut most of its branches.
“They had cut so much I told them to just take it down, but leave the trunk that height,” she said Wednesday, adding she thought it might offer protection since her house is close to the roadway. “The tree I grieved saved my life.”
Dellagrotta was startled last Tuesday morning by a loud crash and the sound of breaking glass when a pickup slammed into the tree — which stopped it from plowing into the couch on which she was sitting.
Improper passing caused the Oct. 20 crash, Aroostook County Sheriff’s Office Lt. Isaac Ward said Friday.
No one was seriously injured and neither vehicle was speeding, Ward said.
That morning at about 6:45 a.m., driver Michael Dumond of Madawaska was traveling north on Route 1, just north of Starbarn Road, in a 2019 Ford pickup. He overcorrected while trying to pass a 2020 Western Star work truck driven by Lance Michaud, also of Madawaska, according to a crash report the Bangor Daily News obtained Friday from the Maine Department of Public Safety.
Deputy Dustin Charette investigated.
Dumond struck the front of Michaud’s truck and swerved into Dellagrotta’s yard, damaging her mailbox, porch and front lawn, the report stated.
The collision damaged the center passenger side of Dumond’s pickup, which was towed. There were no adverse weather conditions and both drivers wore seat belts, according to the report.
No charges were specified.
Dellagrotta showed a reporter the damage, which included a leaning front porch pillar, broken ironwork and about a 2-foot-long marred spot on the tree trunk.
She showed a photograph depicting the felled mailbox, which had included a large arm and a post set in cement.
It isn’t the first time vehicles have left souvenirs, she said. Many trucks speed along the 45 mph stretch so fast things fly out of the beds. She’s collected cinder blocks, tires and more.
Her insurance company is working to resolve property repairs, she said.

title: Teacher who fought gunman during deadly Oregon school shooting releases first statement
text:
BEND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A teacher who fought with the gunman during a deadly school shooting earlier this month in Oregon has released her first statement since that tragic day.
On Friday, Bend-La Pine Schools released a statement from Cassidy Schutz, who is a certified learning specialist at the elementary school.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said Schutz threw her cellphone at the shooter that day and wrestled him for the shotgun he had at Silver Rail Elementary School.
Her actions have been praised for helping save lives and assisting students’ father Kaylub Giamanco in taking down the armed teen.
Schutz’s statement in full:
“There are no words to describe the depth of sadness I am feeling following the events of October 15th. This is not a story. This is a horrific and heartbreaking tragedy, and it is our real lives.
My thoughts are with those who were lost, their families, those who were hurt, and those who were there that day. My heart is with you.
It all happened so fast, and I wish with everything in me that we had more time. The pain of this loss I will carry with me forever.
There are no words for this unimaginable reality we are facing. My focus is on these families, our team, our school, and my own healing.
As I continue to navigate this, I ask that you please give me the time, space, and privacy I need to heal. I will not be making any additional public statements at this time.”
The shooting occurred on Oct. 15 when police say a 16-year-old former student went into Silver Rail Elementary and shot into a special needs classroom.
Teacher Megan Lambert, 25, was killed along with students Rhoam Summer, 5, and two other children, ages 8 and 11. The shooter was also killed.
Another teacher, Becky Drury, and a 7-year-old girl were shot and survived the shooting.

title: 17 theme park workers among 281 arrested during undercover operation
text:
POLK COUNTY, Fla. (WWSB/Gray News) — Florida law enforcement officials said a seven-day undercover operation resulted in 281 arrests and 488 new charges, including 198 felonies.
About the operation
The operation, called “Polk Around & Find Out II,” included simultaneous investigations focused on people accused of traveling to meet children for unlawful sexual activity and commercial sex activity, according to the Polk County Sheriff’s Office.
“Those who came to Polk County expecting to sexually abuse a child, found cuffs instead,” Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said during Friday’s news conference.
Authorities said those arrested had a combined 798 prior criminal charges. Officials also said 24 suspects had firearms and 32 people were charged with drug possession.
Theme park employees
The sheriff’s office said 17 people arrested during the operation worked at theme parks.
Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said Disney told investigators it had fired employees connected to the arrests.
Judd said he had not received an update from Universal about the employment status of its workers who were arrested.
Where suspects lived
Officials said 40 of those arrested lived in Polk County. Others came from elsewhere in Florida, 20 other states and 18 countries.
Immigration status
The sheriff’s office said 32 people arrested during the operation were in the country unlawfully, and 16 had been transferred to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
An ICE official at the news conference said the agency interviewed more than 65 foreign-born people and placed more than 30 detainers on people it identified as removable under immigration law.
Nonprofit outreach
One More Child, a nonprofit that worked with law enforcement during the operation, said it engaged with 93 people and that 18 agreed to receive services. The organization said officials identified 11 people they believe were victims of human trafficking.
“We know that accepting help takes trust, and people may be afraid, unsure, or not ready to take that step,” Sine Dressler, One More Child’s senior director of anti-trafficking operations, said during the news conference.
Investigation continues
Judd said investigators are also reviewing whether additional children may have been victimized in connection with one of the people arrested, a youth football coach.
The investigation is ongoing.

title: County Soccer Teams Advance as Cross Country State Titles Go on the Line
text:
County Teams Reach Soccer Regional Finals, More Soccer and Cross Country State Championships Take Center Stage Saturday
It was another big Friday for Aroostook County high school sports, and there's still plenty more to come before the weekend is over.
Fort Kent's girls, both Wisdom soccer teams, Madawaska and Fort Fairfield's boys all earned trips to the Northern Maine regional championships Friday. There were convincing shutouts, a dramatic penalty-kick finish, and another chapter added to a familiar Class D rivalry.
And Saturday won't be any quieter.
Both Presque Isle soccer teams are still fighting for spots in the regional finals, three County girls teams have Class D semifinal games, and Fort Kent's boys are heading to George Stevens Academy.
Meanwhile, some of the County's best distance runners are in Augusta for the Class B and Class C State Cross Country Championships, with Houlton/GHCA looking to defend its Class C boys state title.
Here's a look at Friday's results and everything coming up Saturday.
Friday's Girls Soccer Semifinals
Class C North: Fort Kent Breaks Open Scoreless Game Against Houlton
(1) Fort Kent 5, (4) Houlton 0
For the first 50 minutes Friday, there wasn't much separating Fort Kent and Houlton.
The two County teams battled through a scoreless first half, and the game remained tied until Reece Doucette stepped up for a penalty kick in the 50th minute.
Doucette converted to give the top-seeded Lady Warriors the lead, and from there, Fort Kent took control.
Doucette finished with two goals, Hannah Plourde added two more, and Avery Werntgen also found the back of the net.
The 5-0 victory sends Fort Kent back to the Class C North regional championship.
The Lady Warriors will face second-seeded Orono, which advanced past sixth-seeded Winslow in a penalty-kick decision following a scoreless game.
It's a matchup between the top two seeds in Class C North, with a trip to the state championship on the line.
Eight-Person Girls: Wisdom Hands Sumner Its First Loss
(2) Wisdom 5, (3) Sumner 0
Wisdom's girls are headed back to the eight-person North regional championship after a convincing 5-0 win over previously unbeaten Sumner.
The Lady Pioneers put together another impressive offensive performance, with Ellie Cyr leading the way with two goals.
Madi Cyr, Libby Cote and Hannah Martin each added a goal.
Wisdom has now scored 11 goals in its two tournament games while allowing just one.
The Lady Pioneers will face top-seeded Dexter in the Northern Maine championship after Dexter shut out Shead 2-0 in its semifinal.
Friday's Boys Soccer Semifinals
Class D North: Madawaska Returns to the Regional Championship
(1) Madawaska 2, (4) Hodgdon 0
Madawaska's boys are headed back to the Class D North championship after shutting out Hodgdon 2-0 Friday evening.
Owen Gagnon and Aiden Gagnon provided the scoring for the top-seeded Owls.
The victory sends Madawaska into the regional championship for another meeting with a very familiar opponent.
For the third consecutive season, the Owls will face Fort Fairfield with the Class D North title on the line.
Class D North: Fort Fairfield Earns Another Shot at Madawaska
(3) Fort Fairfield 3, (2) Central Aroostook 1
Fort Fairfield made sure the Tigers would get another opportunity to face Madawaska, defeating second-seeded Central Aroostook 3-1 in Friday's semifinal.
The third-seeded Tigers went on the road and earned the victory, advancing to the Class D North regional championship for the third straight meeting with the Owls.
It's become one of the area's most familiar postseason matchups, and this year's championship will once again feature two County teams competing for the Northern Maine title.
Eight-Person Boys: Wisdom Survives Dramatic Finish at Calais
(3) Wisdom 2, (2) Calais 1 (Penalty Kicks)
Wisdom's boys are also headed to a regional championship after a dramatic semifinal against Calais.
James Desjardins scored the Pioneers' goal in regulation, and the game eventually went to penalty kicks to determine who would advance.
Preston Lavoie, Sam Paradis, Zeek Cyr and Cayden Hargrove were among Wisdom's successful penalty-kick takers.
Goalkeeper Bentley Nadeau delivered the decisive moment, stopping Calais' final attempt to secure the victory.
The third-seeded Pioneers will now face fourth-seeded Penobscot Christian in the eight-person North championship.
Penobscot Christian advanced with a 3-0 victory over ninth-seeded Houlton, ending the Shires' memorable postseason run after their overtime upset of top-seeded Mattanawcook earlier in the week.
Saturday's State Cross Country Championships: County Runners Head to Augusta
While soccer teams continue their postseason runs across Northern Maine, Saturday is championship day for the state's top distance runners.
The Maine State Cross Country Championships are taking place at Cony High School in Augusta, with Aroostook County athletes competing in both Class B and Class C.
There are team championships to chase, individual titles on the line, and some County runners looking to finish outstanding seasons with one more strong performance.
Class B: Presque Isle and Caribou Bring Strong Girls Teams to States
Presque Isle and Caribou both enter the Class B state meet after strong performances at the Northern Maine regional championships.
Presque Isle finished second in the girls regional team standings, while Caribou placed third.
Caribou's Emma Graves will be one of the County runners to watch after winning the Northern Maine Class B individual championship.
Presque Isle's Lillian Johnson and Aleah Rideout have also turned in strong performances this season and will look to help the Wildcats against the best Class B competition in Maine.
The state meet gives both programs another opportunity to see how they stack up against teams from across Maine.
The Class B boys race gets underway at 11 a.m., followed by the girls at 11:40 a.m.
Class C: Houlton/GHCA Boys Look to Defend State Championship
One of the biggest County storylines in Augusta belongs to the Houlton/GHCA boys.
The Shires are the defending Class C state champions, and they're heading into Saturday with plenty of momentum after winning their second consecutive Northern Maine regional title.
Houlton/GHCA scored just 30 points at regionals, with four runners finishing among the top five.
Malachi Witmer, Brayden Drake, Wyatt Quint and Logan Witmer helped lead the way, giving Houlton another opportunity to compete for a state championship.
But Saturday brings a different challenge, with the top teams from both Northern and Southern Maine competing for the title.
The Shires will be looking to put together another strong team performance and bring another championship back to Houlton.
Class C Girls: County Individuals Earn Their Spots at States
Aroostook County will also have several runners competing individually in the Class C girls state championship.
Charlotte Estabrook and Isabella McCarthy of Houlton both qualified with strong regional performances.
Eleanora Streeter of Washburn and Sadie Wigmore of MSSM also earned places at the state meet.
Although Houlton's girls did not qualify as a team, these runners will have an opportunity to represent their schools individually against the top Class C competition.
The Class C boys race begins at 12:20 p.m., followed by the girls at 1 p.m.
Saturday's State Cross Country Schedule
Cony High School, Augusta
- 11 a.m. — Class B Boys
- 11:40 a.m. — Class B Girls
- 12:20 p.m. — Class C Boys
- 1 p.m. — Class C Girls
All times are subject to change.
Saturday's County Soccer Semifinals
There's still plenty of soccer left to play, too, with several County teams looking to join Friday's winners in the regional championship games.
Girls Soccer
Class B North
(7) Cony at (3) Presque Isle — 1 p.m.
Presque Isle is coming off a 3-1 quarterfinal victory over Skowhegan, with Peyton Boinske scoring twice and Carrlyn Buck adding another.
The Lady Wildcats will host seventh-seeded Cony, which upset second-seeded Gardiner 2-1 to advance.
Class D North
(3) Central Aroostook at (2) Fort Fairfield — Noon
Another all-County matchup will decide a regional championship berth.
Fort Fairfield advanced with a 4-0 shutout of Washburn, while Central Aroostook held off Van Buren 3-2.
(5) Madawaska at (1) Penobscot Valley — 1 p.m.
Madawaska will try to keep its postseason run going after defeating Ashland 2-1 in overtime Wednesday.
The fifth-seeded Owls now face top-seeded Penobscot Valley on the road.
Boys Soccer
Class B North
(4) Presque Isle at (1) John Bapst — Noon
Presque Isle's boys are one victory away from the Class B North championship after defeating Erskine Academy 4-1 in the quarterfinals.
The Wildcats head to top-seeded John Bapst, which survived a close 2-1 quarterfinal against Caribou.
Class C North
(3) Fort Kent at (2) George Stevens Academy — 2 p.m.
Fort Kent's boys will try to join the girls team in the regional championships.
The Warriors advanced with a 2-0 victory over Washington Academy, with Dom Cyr and Finn Marquis scoring.
Now Fort Kent travels to George Stevens Academy for a semifinal matchup in Blue Hill.

title: If Maine has a Halloween bird, it’s the raven. And there’s more to it than meets the eye.
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Halloween is a good time to celebrate one of Maine’s spookiest birds, the common raven. They’re not only spooky-looking, they’re spooky-smart. They have one of the largest brains in the avian world. Ravens are so intelligent, they may be the next species to take over the world after the AI apocalypse.
As everyone knows, the collective name for a group of crows is “a murder of crows.” For ravens, the collective name is “an unkindness of ravens” or sometimes a “conspiracy of ravens.” These nicknames have been around for at least 500 years. Ravens have a well-earned reputation.
Biologists have been testing raven intelligence for decades, trying to determine how smart they really are. Typically, the ravens beat the tests. When challenged to solve a puzzle or think creatively, ravens win the food reward. They do the same thing in the wild. Ravens have come to associate gunshots with finding a carcass. If so, they may call in other ravens for the feast, so that their gang can overwhelm other scavengers drawn to the meal, including coyotes and eagles.
That gunshot study was done in Wyoming. I don’t know if Maine ravens do it, but I’ll bet that some of our local hunters would know. The curious thing is, the ravens could distinguish gunshots from other loud human noises, ignoring the slam of a car door, for instance.
Ravens don’t mind having coyotes around. Their bills are not designed to open the carcass of a dead animal. If they are the first to find one in the woods, they may attract the attention of fanged scavengers to help open the hide. Let’s see AI do that.
Ravens cache food, helping them survive arctic winters. Researchers in Fairbanks, Alaska, have watched ravens endure 100 degrees below zero. They have specialized feathers covering their nostrils to prevent heat and moisture loss. They tuck their bare legs close to the body to conserve warmth.
Ravens are crafty. They watch each other hide food and remember where they can steal it later. Other ravens know this, of course, and go to great lengths to fool their friends. They will even pretend to cache food, then stash it elsewhere.
Ravens play. They’ve been witnessed sliding on snow, teasing other animals, and somersaulting through the air. There are accounts of ravens flying upside down for over half a mile. Juvenile ravens are particularly playful, and all ravens are fascinated by shiny things. Over time, adult ravens become suspicious of anything new and unexpected.
Ravens are the most widespread members of the corvid family. Their North American cousins include crows, jays and magpies. Other corvid species abound throughout Eurasia. All are comfortable around humans, which partially accounts for their widespread success. All can eat grains, berries, insects and animals. They can eat the byproducts of human activity, such as roadkill and undigested seeds found in manure. They eat garbage. Sometimes, all it takes to encourage a visit to your yard is to tip over a trash can.
Common ravens are not as sociable as crows. It’s unusual to see more than a single family unit together. However, Chihuahuan ravens — a separate species in the desert southwest — are more gregarious. If I’m anywhere from Texas to southern Colorado and see a flock of ravens, that’s often how I identify them.
In groups of unrelated birds, common ravens become quite argumentative. They aggressively defend nesting territories. About the only time I see Maine ravens socializing in a group is when they are sharing a feast in the woods.
Ravens have a big vocabulary. They make a wide variety of sounds, and can mimic many others. Yes, ravens have been taught to imitate human speech. They can even utter multisyllabic words such as “Nevermore.” Biologists have documented up to thirty different vocalizations in the wild. Youngsters especially have a Halloween-worthy screech that sounds like a murder in progress. I’ve got a local pair of nesting ravens that I hear year-round. The fledglings can be heard screeching from half a mile away, starting in late May.
Many birders find it difficult to tell ravens and crows apart. Here are a few clues. Ravens are much larger. They have huge bills and diamond-shaped tails, while crows have fan-shaped tails. Ravens soar, crows don’t. Ravens croak, crows caw. All winter, you may see no more than two ravens together. Meanwhile, our crows are already starting to gather by the thousands in urban areas, just in time for a spookier Halloween.

title: Houdini's centennial spotlight: A newly published essay and a fresh fight over when and how he died
text:
Houdini's centennial spotlight: A newly published essay and a fresh fight over when and how he died
His mysterious death on Halloween 1926 remains debated
Houdini's centennial spotlight: A newly published essay and a fresh fight over when and how he died
His mysterious death on Halloween 1926 remains debated
A century after his death, Harry Houdini remains a man we're still trying to learn more about.
A rare essay by the iconic escape artist about magicians of the past has just been published for the first time, while a recent book revisits longtime questions about the cause and date of his death at Detroit's Grace Hospital. Other centennial publications include a Houdini coloring book and an overview of his vast personal library.
Related video above: Cliff diver becomes the world's first known woman to dive off an iceberg
His legacy will be debated at numerous Houdini events taking place this weekend, from a "Grand Houdini Centenarium" in his hometown of Budapest to an auction of memorabilia in Hollywood, California, to seances in cities he visited such as Chicago and Frederick, Maryland. His burial site, at Machpelah Cemetery in New York City, has long been a Halloween gathering place.
"I'm not sure many of the people who know the name 'Houdini' could pick him out of a lineup, specify when he lived, or say what he actually did in his performances. But they know that 'Houdini' is synonymous with magic, an ability to do the impossible, or get out of a tight spot," said Matthew Solomon, a film history professor at the University of Michigan and author of "Disappearing Tricks: Silent Film, Houdini, and the New Magic of the Twentieth Century," which came out in 2010.
"For those who know a little more, he's the epitome of the self-made man and immigrant success story. The fact that he (reportedly) died on Halloween certainly enhanced his mystique," Solomon added.
Houdini thought a lot about the past
Houdini's "An Interesting Scrapbook" appears in the new issue of The Strand Magazine, which has published rare works by Mark Twain and Edith Wharton among others. Houdini offers tribute to some magicians who preceded him and laments that more wasn't known about them. He was inspired by playbills shared with him by cartoonist Kin Hubbard for appearances by such popular 19th-century entertainers as Robert Heller and H.J. Sargent.
"The following information was presented to my gaze, and I herewith present it, so that we can eventually form a list of the early American magicians," Houdini writes. "American magicians never were thought of enough to be placed in books or chronicle lists so that the future generation could read of the various old-timers; no, magicians were in a class by themselves, and it is only of late years, when Vaudeville had to make use of them as headliners and drawing cards, that magicians became prominent enough to be listed as real acts."
Eric Colleary, whose "Houdini's Library" came out in September, says that Houdini had a deep interest in other magicians, to the point of visiting their graves and even personally paying to have the graves maintained. The magicians' families would in turn give him scrapbooks, playbills and other items "so that he could keep their memories alive," says Colleary, the curator of Theatre and Performing Arts at the Harry Ransom Center at The University of Texas at Austin.
Houdini was born Erik Weisz in 1874, a rabbi's son whose family emigrated to the U.S. in part to escape the antisemitism of what was then Austria-Hungary. By his teens, he was a professional magician and by age 30 an international celebrity known for his astounding ability to break out of handcuffs, shackles and other restraints. He was also an author, a movie actor and a spoken-word recording artist whose audio archive was purchased by magician David Copperfield.
Questions linger over his death
According to contemporary media accounts, Houdini died Oct. 31, 1926, from diffuse peritonitis after being hospitalized with appendicitis, possibly aggravated days earlier when a college student in Montreal tested his legendary strength by punching him in the stomach. His demise on Halloween fit well — too well, some allege — with his mysterious, even supernatural aura.
Aided in part by no autopsy being performed, alternate theories have thrived ever since, including that he was poisoned by a cabal of circus performers. In "Houdini: The Man Who Died Twice," author Larrian Gillespie draws upon medical records, his death certificate and other materials to challenge the official diagnosis and to contend that he actually died Oct. 30.
The real cause of death, she writes, was intestinal blockage, caused by a doctor's fatal decision to allow Houdini to eat a bowl of vegetables and sour cream while he was recovering from surgery. She also cites conflicting records of his date of death: a doctor's affidavit among other documents lists it as Oct. 30, while the state death certificate — which she found highly flawed — has him dying on the 31st.
Houdini's inner circle wanted his death to be on Halloween "so he would always be remembered," says Gillespie, a forensic medical researcher who has also written books on menopause, dieting and cystitis.
"Houdini: The Man Who Died Twice" received a starred review from the book industry publication Kirkus, which called it an "absorbing, argument-starting account." Houdini's great- nephew, George Hardeen, told The Associated Press that he found the book "convincing and persuasive" and had "zero doubts" about Gillespie's findings.
Some Houdini followers differ
Others were skeptical, including two experts Gillespie cites in her book as among "the most respected and knowledgeable men in the Houdini world."
Bruce Averbook told the AP he doubted that the date was altered so it could land on Halloween.
"The family was in significant grief and not thinking about legacy," he said. Averbook, a Houdini scholar, added that writings from Houdini's personal assistant list his death as Oct. 31.
"He had no reason to lie about this," Averbook said.
Another man praised in her book, John Cox, told the AP that while the "book does have some very good new information" about his career, a "second opinion" was still needed about his death. Cox, a Houdini blogger and founder of the Houdini publishing imprint Wild About Harry Press, acknowledged there was "confusion about his death and a desire for clarity."
"But I think his death is a very small part of the story," he said. "Houdini's fame, and why he's remembered today, comes from his remarkable life."

title: Comfortable weather continues through at least Tuesday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - It will get chilly overnight into Sunday with lows dropping to the mid 20s. Sunday will be yet another very pleasant fall day with highs near or into the 50s and light winds. Overall about as good a weekend as you could ask for this time of year.
Saturday night: A cold and clear night
Temps will drop off quickly on Saturday night with clear skies so if you’ve got any late night Halloween events make sure to grab your jacket because it’ll get chilly fast. Temps will drop into the mid to low 20s for a large portion of the state and winds will be light. And don’t forget to reset your clocks!
Sunday: A slightly warmer day with clear skies
It will be a few degrees warmer than Saturday and clear skies. Most places get to the middle 50s with some colder areas still stuck in the 40s. It will feel comfortable though with full sun for most. Winds will be light.
Sunday night: Near freezing for most
It will be chilly once again but probably not as cold as the previous night. Most places will be clear and drop to only the middle 30s or so with some spots into the 20s.
Monday and beyond: Placid weather continues
Monday into Election Day on Tuesday will be calm and quiet with no major weather events on the horizon. A few showers may be possible late Tuesday night into Wednesday but they look light and scattered in nature. Late next week may bring a storm but it’s a long way off and details are still hard to pin down.
Saturday: Cooler but sunny. Highs near 50. Winds NW at 10-15 mph
Saturday night: Cold with lows in the middle 20s. Winds light.
Sunday: Warmer with highs in the 50s. Winds light.
Sunday night: Clear with lows in the middle 30s. Winds light.
Monday: Mainly sunny with highs in the 50s and 60s. Light wind.

title: Make no bones about it, the giant skeleton has become an American Halloween fixture
text:
(AP) - It reared its bony head in 2020, during that first, chaotic pandemic year that was rife with grief and fear but also toilet paper hoarding and questionable lockdown-inspired purchases. Behold Skelly, the 12-foot, 90-pound skeleton with glowing LCD eyeballs, on sale for $299 from Home Depot, just in time for Halloween — at least, if you can get your hands on one.
Many did, because this is America. And when we get sad, stressed or bored, we shop, drowning our collective anxieties in things that we definitely don’t need but most certainly want.
So, beginning in 2020, Skelly showed up on suburban lawns from California to New Jersey and on brownstone stoops in Brooklyn, naked or dressed in a costume, towering over jack-o’-lanterns and plastic gravestones with spooky puns like “Rest In Pieces.” It didn’t take long for people to realize that keeping Skelly out year-round meant new opportunities to dress him for every season: Christmas, Fourth of July, or even just a bikini for summer.
In 2024, Skelly got a chest lightning attachment. And in 2026, a Bluetooth connection lets you record sounds or speak into it live, entertaining (or unsettling) your whole block. He also has a dog, a cat, and a smaller, 6½-foot version for those who can’t quite commit to a giant. It has sold out before Halloween every year.
“It is the ultimate American decoration,” says Aubrey Horowitz, merchant of Decorative Holiday at Home Depot. “We really love this sense of nostalgia and having some form of connection with our communities and the people that live around us. And frankly, you know, a lot of times bigger is better.”
I did not celebrate Halloween until I arrived in the U.S. from Eastern Europe at age 13. I was shocked by the sheer size of everything: giant cars, highways with all those lanes, enormous gallons of milk instead of our polite liters, skyscrapers so tall they were licking the clouds.
We also weren’t used to whimsy. Gaudy yard decor, whether for Halloween or Christmas, was as foreign a concept as warehouse shopping or smiling at strangers.
Skelly would have certainly stopped us in our tracks. It still does. The uniquely American delight it brings to me, an immigrant still often in awe of Americans’ seasonal joy and over-the-top ornamentations, is contagious.
The U.S. did not invent Halloween. But Halloween excess, with its pillowcases full of candy, elaborate costumes for everyone from babies to adults to dogs (and a few unlucky cats), could not be more American.
And why have a 5′8″ skeleton when you can have a 12-foot one?
___
Part of a recurring series, “American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. For more American objects, click here. For more stories on the anniversary, click here.

In 2024, Skelly got a chest lightning attachment. And in 2026, a Bluetooth connection lets you record sounds or speak into it live, entertaining (or unsettling) your whole block. He also has a dog, a cat, and a smaller, 6½-foot version for those who can’t quite commit to a giant. It has sold out before Halloween every year.
“It is the ultimate American decoration,” says Aubrey Horowitz, merchant of Decorative Holiday at Home Depot. “We really love this sense of nostalgia and having some form of connection with our communities and the people that live around us. And frankly, you know, a lot of times bigger is better.”
I did not celebrate Halloween until I arrived in the U.S. from Eastern Europe at age 13. I was shocked by the sheer size of everything: giant cars, highways with all those lanes, enormous gallons of milk instead of our polite liters, skyscrapers so tall they were licking the clouds.
We also weren’t used to whimsy. Gaudy yard decor, whether for Halloween or Christmas, was as foreign a concept as warehouse shopping or smiling at strangers.
Skelly would have certainly stopped us in our tracks. It still does. The uniquely American delight it brings to me, an immigrant still often in awe of Americans’ seasonal joy and over-the-top ornamentations, is contagious.
The U.S. did not invent Halloween. But Halloween excess, with its pillowcases full of candy, elaborate costumes for everyone from babies to adults to dogs (and a few unlucky cats), could not be more American.
And why have a 5′8″ skeleton when you can have a 12-foot one?
___

title: 'General Hospital' wins outstanding drama series for a record 19th time overall
text:
'General Hospital' wins outstanding drama series for a record 19th time overall
Scott Clifton of “The Bold and the Beautiful” and Tamara Tunie of “Beyond the Gates” won lead acting honors at the 53rd annual Daytime Emmys on Friday night, with “General Hospital” honored as outstanding drama series for a record 19th time overall and sixth in a row.
Video above: Anthony Geary, 'General Hospital' star, dies at 78
Clifton plays Liam Spencer on the CBS show. It's his second lead actor trophy, having won in 2017, to go with previous wins as younger actor and supporting actor that made him the first male actor to sweep all three categories.
He beat out a heavyweight field of veterans Eric Braeden, Steve Burton, Thorsten Kaye and Christian Jules LeBlanc.
“I’m speechless,” Clifton said. “This means so much to me, not the thing, the atta boy from my peers. I think of few things that bring me more joy than that.”
Tunie plays strong-willed matriarch Anita Dupree on “Beyond the Gates,” which debuted on CBS last year featuring the first primarily Black cast since “Generations” in the 1990s and the first new network soap since 1999.
Tunie made her daytime debut in 1987 on “As the World Turns,” leaving in 2009, a year before the CBS show ended.
“My heart is so full right now," Tunie said. “This is the best welcome back to daytime ever. There is a host of Black actresses who paved the way for me, and I feel them as I stand here.”
Along with its outstanding drama series award, ABC’s “General Hospital” also earned trophies for writing and guest performance in a daytime drama for Jeff Kober.
Roger Howarth and Beth Maitland of “The Young and the Restless” swept the supporting acting categories, with both winning decades after their first triumphs.
Howarth currently plays Matt Clark on the CBS soap. He first won in 1994 in the younger actor category for his breakout role as Todd Manning on “One Life to Live.”
Maitland was honored for playing Traci Abbott, a role she originated in 1982 — the year of her first supporting actress win — and has played off and on ever since.
“Every one of you a winner, every one of you a part of the contribution daytime makes in a world gone mad, offering just a few minutes of relief — to laugh, to cry and to celebrate," she said in tribute to her peers.
Genie Francis, who began her role on “General Hospital” at age 14 in 1977, received the Lifetime Achievement Award, presented by her actor-director husband, Jonathan Frakes. She was teary-eyed watching a video of career highlights before taking the stage, supported by her two children because she's recovering from a broken right ankle.
“I know 50 years sounds like an awfully long time, but it doesn’t feel like it to me,” Francis said. “As they say, if you love what you do you don’t work a day in your life. I wouldn’t go that far because doing a party scene in high heels is hard work.”
Francis said she's worked with “all the greats,” ticking off such names as Anthony Geary, Erika Slezak, David Canary, Maurice Bernard, Michael Knight and Eric Braeden.
“I have had the most amazing ride and I am so grateful,” she said. “I would do it all over again if I could.”
Tracee Ellis Ross won in the travel and adventure category for her Roku show “Solo Traveling with Tracee Ellis Ross.”
“Wow, how fun is this?” Ross said, while thanking the countries of Morocco, Mexico and Spain.
Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, lost in the lifestyle program category. She was nominated for her Netflix show “With Love, Meghan” that ran for two seasons, but the Prime Video documentary series “A Different Breed” about competitive canine sports prevailed in that category.
Ambyr Michelle of CBS' “Beyond the Gates” won for emerging talent in a daytime drama, the second year the award was handed out.
Directing honors went to Peacock’s “Days of Our Lives.”
Two talk shows no longer in production scored victories. Sherri Shepherd won as daytime talk series host for “Sherri,” which ended its four-season run on Fox in May. Kelly Clarkson won for daytime talk series, having wrapped her eponymous NBC show in August after seven seasons. Neither was on hand to accept.
Giada De Laurentiis won as non-daily daytime personality for “Giada in the Kitchen.” The trophy for daytime personality daily went to Star Jones and Corey Jovan for Fox's “Divorce Court.”
Ina Garten was a two-time winner for culinary host and culinary instructional series for “Be My Guest” on Food Network.
The ceremony held at the Hollywood Palladium was streamed live for the second straight year after airing on CBS for five consecutive years.

title: Collins, Jackson campaign three days ahead of midterms
text:
Collins, Jackson campaign three days ahead of midterms
Three days away from the election, both Maine candidates for the U.S. Senate spent their Halloween campaigning.
Democratic candidate Troy Jackson joined the Maine Democratic Party for a canvassing event in Bangor before traveling to Portland to trick-or-treat.
He was dressed as a cord of wood, pointing toward a recent pro-Susan Collins advertisement that stated, "We're not talking about buying a cord of wood here. We're sending someone to the U.S. Senate."
Following the candy collection, Jackson was asked about his final message to voters.
"I think the closing message is: do people like the government that they have right now? I mean, up and down the state, I hear people that are being crushed by health care, by high fuel costs, prescription drugs, child care, tariffs and all those things," Jackson said.
Collins began her Halloween Saturday at a hunter's breakfast in Old Town to celebrate the beginning of hunting season, according to her campaign.
Then, she traveled to Bangor's Cross Point Church for a trunk-or-treat.
“Bangor’s strong sense of community was on full display at this year’s trunk-or-treat celebration at Cross Point Church,” Collins said in a statement from her campaign. “It was a pleasure to spend the morning with so many local families. Stay warm, be safe, and Happy Halloween!”

title: Semiannual time changes are bad for our health
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Katie Saunders is from Hampden. She has over 10 years of experience as a family nurse practitioner in family medicine.
It’s that time of year again where we all ask ourselves “Why do we keep changing the clocks back and forth?” I’ve heard more than one person say, “I thought Congress fixed that,” or “I thought we weren’t doing that anymore.” Many more people oppose changing the clocks twice a year than those that support continuing it (47% versus 12%).
In case you don’t follow federal legislation (or perhaps you’ve been too busy with other, more pressing issues like the war in Iran, the ever-rising cost to fill up your tank, your grocery cart, and cover your health care expenses, and the mid-term elections), I’ll remind you of where things stand on an issue that is so important, but often not at the top of mind — our sleep.
There are two opposing bills working their way through Congress, both of which would stop the biannual clock change, but with opposite effects. I’d like to argue that the differences are not just a matter of personal preference for more morning or evening sunlight, but an important matter impacting our physical and mental health, safety, performance, mood, and more. When we look at the science, research, and our own history, I believe it becomes clear which option is the best, common-sense choice.
The Sunshine Protection Act, which has passed the U.S. House and has been referred to a Senate committee, would move to a permanent daylight saving time (DST) model, making it darker in the morning, and lighter in the evening. The Sunshine for Our Kids Act has been referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and would make standard time, the time based on natural sunlight, permanent.
As a health care clinician and someone that frequently helps patients with their sleep, allow me to explain the stark difference between the two, and why scores of organizations that care about our health support permanent standard time.
Humans’ sleep and wakefulness cycle is linked to a circadian rhythm (biological clock), which is ruled by the sun. Permanent DST would delay sunrise in most states past 8 a.m. for more than three months, and close to 9 a.m. for a week.
Our bodies need exposure to morning sunlight. In fact, not only does delayed morning light affect our sleep but it affects many other health variables including metabolic disorders, depression, cardiovascular disease, obesity, and even an increased risk of cancers. Setting a permanent standard time has been shown to decrease traffic deaths, lower crime, reduce chronic illnesses and improve performance at school, sports and work.
Science and history both show that permanent DST is even worse than switching the clocks twice a year.
These are all reasons why permanent DST lasted less than one year back in the 1970s. It was quickly repealed due to safety concerns (including deaths), public outcry, and significant decline in support after its first winter (79% to 49%).
As Heather Turgeon and Julie Wright pointed out in an Atlantic article in 2022, daylight saving time is a trap and a lie — what most people actually like is summer, when the days are naturally longer. Changing the clocks cannot add hours of sunlight to the day, all it does is wreak havoc on our biological, natural clocks.
Industry support for permanent daylight saving time is mainly from golf groups and those who would benefit from people shopping after work, which is actually quite American — putting consumerism and money making over health. What also seems to be American these days is the individualist sentiment that if I prefer evening light, then it’s the best way.
I believe if we took a step back and considered the most vulnerable in our society (children, teenagers, shift workers) and how they would be impacted, we could accept that early morning light is best for everyone’s health. I personally try to embrace the natural rhythm of the seasons — winter is a time to rest, reflect, and reset, while the longer days of summer are a time to be more active and busy.
I urge you to call your elected officials and encourage them to support legislation that makes standard time permanent.
Here’s to your healthy sleep!

title: On Halloween, front lawns play host to the most popular public art
text:
The nail in the coffin was a small plastic tombstone sticking out of a neighbor’s lawn which reads: “LET ME OUT” punctuated by a bat-like demon gargoyle. One is dying to know more about the speaker with his assorted ins and outs.
This piece, along with the classic hands reaching up from the grave, creaky hinges, fluttering ghosts and acrobatic skeletons – some nearly as big as a house – gives us an image of the non-living as quite active, opinionated, alert, and very much on the move. Death ducked once again.
Lawns near and far now become temporary sculpture gardens devoted to the riddle of being dead, and plastic tombstones are not cheap: this year, Americans were on target to spend upwards of $4.3 billion (!) on exterior Halloween decorations, up significantly from last year despite heaps of mournful economic news. This amount is a bit less than we spend on costumes, but a bit more than we spend on candy. By comparison, the total spending for art projects in this country by federal, state, local and non-profit sources totaled just $1.7 billion for all of 2025, less than half our Halloween budget.
This makes Halloween by far this nation’s single biggest, best investment in the plastic arts, and all in service of a single night. For this reason alone it is surely good and right to examine what all the money and effort are trying to say, and to whom.
The backstory is largely familiar, always linked to the time of year when crops are harvested, nights get longer, and humans feel a bit more vulnerable. A Roman festival (Lemuria, which shooed away pesky household spirits with black beans) gave way to a Celtic ritual (Samhain, which used bonfires to urge misguided ancestors, spirits, and fairies to go home), which in turn lent its atmosphere to a Catholic holiday (All Saints’ Day, which lights candles for the souls of Christian martyrs is and preceded by vespers on All Hallows’ Eve)
…which was (though alive and well in many countries) ultimately eclipsed in Protestant America by the much more recent, rather un-Christian, sugar-blasted evening celebration we know so well.
Since Protestants in Ireland, Scotland, and England (and later in North America) did not wish to promote the Catholic saints, they decided to reverse the night’s polarity. The souls floating around on their Oct. 31st did not belong to the hallowed ones wending their way heavenward, it was said, but belonged rather to those lost, dangerous, and thirsty ghosts who got trapped somewhere between Earth and the nether regions.
Though all these symbolic substitutions were a late amendment to an old holiday, they tap into deep roots. As far back as 2,000 BCE, art history records the use of scary objects – special geometries, deformed faces, gorgons’ heads – to ward off evil spirits, fighting fire with fire in the realm of appearance and behavior. This is an ongoing negotiation between the living and dead, the light and the dark, the constructive and the destructive forces of the world. Like most negotiations, bargaining and extortion are part of the process.
The ancient, inherited idea is that these spirits are sneaky and treacherous and resentful of we the living. On Halloween the boundaries thin and tremble. Masks are used to both blend in with them and scare them away.
One night, and one night only, rings a bell and opens a door to special kinds of blending, generosity and mischief. When else do Americans open their doors to strangers at night, with a smile no less? When else do we peer into each others’ living rooms, accepting every visitor?
Historically, this is the night to tempt fate, to invite human pranksters in close then bribe them into submission with fruit, nuts, cakes (before) and candy (now). Trick or treat? What will it cost to make the evil spirits leave us alone? A big bowl of Snickers seems like a small price to pay.
Yet naturally it is not so simple, psychologically speaking. We Americans seem pretty half-hearted in our efforts to expel the evil spirits. We seem to enjoy their company. Like many of our celebrities, they have some core qualities we firmly admire: bravado, irreverence, strength, confidence, recklessness, and various kinds of immunity from the usual humiliations of normal human frailty. We are in no great hurry, in the end, to see them disappear, and we enjoy the annual get-together with enthusiasm.
The result is a bit bewildering. Each Halloween, a great basket of hopelessly tangled and intertwined pop cultural quotations is dumped unceremoniously out onto the lawns and streets of American suburbia. Dying, death and decay mixes freely with vitality, vigor and valor. A strange and morbid pantheon!
Whistling past the graveyards, American cheer and Batman meet a miniature Grim Reaper in service of Halloween commerce pulling in billions annually.
Pumpkins (harvest, nature, growth) glare at Deadpool (Hollywood, fantasy, immortality). Spiderman (savior) chats warmly with a serial killer (villain) about how much loot is in a pillow case. A Minecraft character (c. 2011) stumbles into Frankenstein’s monster (c. 1818) because it missed the steps and is helped up by a mother dressed up like a lethal, sarcastic psychiatrist (Harley Quinn, c. 2016) on loan from the Italian commedia dell’arte theater’s stock character Harlequin (c. 1585). Sugar is sprinkled on cemeteries.
In this way, each year at this time we take the temperature of the national mood. We carve out a core sample from the collective consciousness and get a nice, clean, spontaneous reading of what Americans wish to be. This year the blender whirs away with ever-increasing speed and franticness. So much for fencing out the evil spirits and protecting the harvest! Siphoning every creepy thing that captures our imagination, or clicks, we invoke the undead from video games, movies, television, and animation (high-budget media dominate, pushing real-life characters to the margins).
We gleefully churn together superheroes, ghouls, monsters, creeps, murderers, immortals, the strong, the famous, the extreme, the non-human, the inhuman, and the inhumane. Regarding these kinds of intimately familiar evil spirits, it is notoriously difficult to tell whether we want them to stay or to go.
Some of this season’s most popular costumes may look playful and charming, but many are associated with an extreme case of psychosis, trauma, or bloodshed. Nikki from the hit horror movie “Obsession,” for instance. Or Buddy the Unicorn, the terrifying orange mascot character and main antagonist of the dark comedy-horror film “Buddy.”
For those readers, like myself, born well before the year 2000, you will probably have to look them up. Even Agamemnon, whom I thought I recognized, is not really so much Agamemnon, brother-in-law of Helen, but rather a hunky cosplay character particular to the recent Christopher Nolan film, which departed shamelessly and often from Homer’s famous book.
If blending in seamlessly with the hungry ghosts is an intentional part of getting rid of them, we are doing an artful job of it this October. If this night is, and has always been, about giving some free play to the souls of the lost, then we seem to be honoring that tradition too.
Regarding the privately curated public art exhibitions which suddenly blossom in zillions of Maine front yards every year, it is easy to become confused and a little snarky. Why so big? Why the pumpkin head? Why is it up and stalking, when horror of death is usually tied to a fear of the stoppage of motion? Should one feel afraid or thrilled?
An alternate reading is better, however. Also pictured above is a friendly, inviting living room and an illuminated vestibule. The sculpture, lights and decorations were pulled together with no small effort and expense for no reason other than human amusement and pleasure. This is art to be freely enjoyed by everyone in the community for its surprise, weirdness, and excitement. It conveys the useful message to passing children that some rules are momentarily suspended, that it is safe to approach, that the bell will ring, the door will open, and good things will follow.
If only every night were like this. The dead and the dark may be, after all, the least of our worries.
Jon Calame holds a master’s degree in historic preservation of architecture and is a Fellow of the American Academy in Rome. He currently teaches art history at the University of Southern Maine. This column is free to access through support by The Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation.

title: There's new guidance on menopause symptoms like hot flashes. What women need to know
text:
There's new guidance on menopause symptoms like hot flashes. What women need to know
For the first time in a dozen years, a leading OB-GYN group has updated its guidance on managing hot flashes, night sweats, sleep changes and other disruptive symptoms that often come with menopause.
Doctors stressed the importance of hormone therapies, which many women are considering again after the removal of federal safety warnings. On Friday, federal officials said the Food and Drug Administration has been taking steps to ensure there's an adequate supply.
Doctors also described various nonhormonal options in the new advice released this month by the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, or ACOG.
“We would love our patients to go to their OB-GYNs regarding questions about menopause and really advocate for getting the treatment that they need,” said Dr. Camille Clare, the group’s president.
Menopause occurs when a woman has gone 12 consecutive months without a menstrual period. In the U.S., it usually happens around age 50. The time leading up to it is called perimenopause, during which the body’s production of the hormones estrogen and progesterone declines sharply.
Problems commonly arise. More than half of women in menopause report having “vasomotor” issues such as hot flashes and night sweats, said ACOG. As many as two-thirds report menopause-related sleep disruption. And more than a third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal women worldwide report depressive symptoms.
In the past, doctors said, many women quietly suffered.
There's growing consensus that "these symptoms should be treated,” said Dr. JoAnn Manson, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School. “This should help to empower women to discuss their symptoms with their healthcare provider.”
Hormone therapy supported as a good option for many
Manson said ACOG’s new guidelines are similar to those put out by other medical organizations.
"Moderate to severe or bothersome menopausal symptoms should be treated with hormone therapy as the first line of treatment,” she said. While it's not appropriate for all women, she added, it’s a good option for many.
But some have been wary.
In 2002, a landmark study in women taking a pill-based combination of estrogen and progestin was stopped early because of links to breast cancer, blood clots and other serious issues. Concerns lingered even though later studies showed the benefits of today’s hormone therapies outweigh the risks for many women. For more than 22 years, all hormone-based menopause treatments carried a government warning, which Manson said discouraged patients and doctors from using them.
But last year, the FDA announced it would remove the boxed warning from more than 20 pills, patches and creams containing the hormones estrogen and progestin. On Friday, the FDA approved updated labeling for three additional estrogen-based patches.
Removing the boxed warning has helped revive interest in and demand for the treatments.
Since the FDA labeling change, some women have reported difficulty obtaining estrogen patches in certain doses and formulations.
FDA officials said Friday that despite such reports, they are unaware of “an imminent risk of a nationwide shortage.” Officials also noted that drug manufacturers have doubled their output of the products over the last year by adding extra manufacturing shifts and production capacity.
Dr. Stephanie Faubion, medical director at The Menopause Society, said she’s glad to see ACOG’s guidelines stress the importance of these treatments. “It’s undisputed that hormone therapy is the first line and most effective therapy for hot flashes,” she said.
ACOG reviews the latest evidence on hormone therapy and includes detailed information about the various types. Whole-body therapies, which come in pills, patches, sprays, gels and a vaginal ring, deliver doses of hormones into the bloodstream at levels high enough to have significant effects on symptoms like hot flashes. Low-dose vaginal estrogen therapy is applied directly with very little circulating in the blood. It’s often prescribed to women whose biggest complaint is vaginal dryness.
ACOG recommends that decisions about hormone therapy should be made jointly by doctors and patients, and take into account the benefits and risks given a patient's age and medical history. If it’s appropriate, the group advises starting it before age 60, or within 10 years of menopause.
Hormones aren't the only treatments
Some patients choose not to take full-body hormonal medications or are advised by their doctors to avoid them because of their medical histories or conditions.
For them, doctors pointed to different medicines. One is fezolinetant, which works in the area of the brain that controls body temperature and blocks a source of hot flashes and night sweats. Another is elinzanetant, which works similarly.
Doctors also said certain antidepressants can help manage symptoms like hot flashes and depression in patients with either or both of these problems.
There’s also evidence supporting some non-drug treatments for hot flashes, night sweats and sleep or mood problems, ACOG said. These include cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness, exercise, clinical hypnosis and acupuncture. Such approaches can be used alone or alongside medications.
Clare said women may see misinformation and disinformation about menopause treatments online, and urged patients to come to their doctors with any questions. ACOG offers advice on sorting out truth from false claims as well as overall information on menopause.
“Women have options. They have lots of options, hormonal and nonhormonal,” Faubion said. “They shouldn’t be told that nothing can be done about their symptoms. Because again, we have evidence for many different things that can help.”

title: National healthcare caravan passes through 17 states, pushing for reforms
text:
The “Care Force One” tour bus traveled nearly 8,000 miles in October from coast to coast, to protest funding cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act and to demand the restoration of enhanced ACA tax credits. (Protect Our Care) By Mark Richardson Oct 30, 2026 Listen to this story HERE. A national bus tour demanding lower healthcare costs wraps […]
The “Care Force One” tour bus traveled nearly 8,000 miles in October from coast to coast, to protest funding cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act and to demand the restoration of enhanced ACA tax credits. (Protect Our Care)
By Mark Richardson
Oct 30, 2026
Listen to this story HERE.
A national bus tour demanding lower healthcare costs wraps up Friday after trekking across the country.
Protect Our Care’s “Sick of It! Fix Health Care Now” tour made October stops in Scranton and Bethlehem, putting Pennsylvania families’ struggles with insurance bills and access to care in the spotlight.
The advocacy group Protect Our Care spent four weeks gathering stories from patients, providers and families. Organizers said rising premiums, coverage losses and prescription costs mean difficult choices.
April Niver, a self-employed consultant from Easton, Penn., said coverage gaps often leave patients gambling on how much care they need.
“We’re left with trade-offs. We make trade-offs for a plan that might not offer us as much coverage for certain things, because we’re rolling the dice here,” Niver said.
The “Care Force One” tour bus traveled to more than 36 stops in 15 states to protest cuts to Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act.
The group wants lawmakers to restore Affordable Care Act premium tax credits and reverse Medicaid cuts. It also wants Medicare to negotiate prices for more prescription drugs and extend those savings to people with private insurance.
Cesar Nieves, a Pittsburgh-based medical technologist who cites 25 years of healthcare experience, attended the rally in Lebanon, Penn. Nieves said high healthcare costs are forcing his family to make hard choices.
“We’re going to be hurting,” Nieves remarked. “Right now, my insurance is $1,800 that I have to pay upfront, every time, before I get covered. I tell my wife, ‘You can’t go to the doctor till after mid-April.'”
The group’s other demands include penalties for drug makers that raise prices faster than inflation. Advocates also want a $2,000 annual prescription spending cap and $35 insulin copays for people with private coverage.
The tour’s final events take place Friday in Arizona, following stops in California.

title: Troy Jackson rallies Bangor canvassers in final push before Election Day
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - With just three days to go until Election Day, political groups are rallying canvass volunteers together for one last push toward the finish line.
And all eyes remain on the controversial U.S. Senate race between former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson and incumbent Sen. Susan Collins.
Jackson joined the Maine Democratic Party in Bangor on Saturday morning for its “Get out the Vote” event, designed to train volunteers to get out in their local neighborhoods to speak to voters ahead of the election.
In his speech, Jackson thanked volunteers and reiterated his campaign promises of prioritizing working-class Mainers above corporate interests.
Party leaders emphasized that face-to-face conversations remain the most effective tool in the campaign’s final hours.
“Here in the state of Maine, we know we’re all like one big little community. And where you might hear or see news articles and get reports secondhand, when you can talk to somebody that you know and you already trust, that’s a better way to get information sometimes. And you get to share opinions in a safe space. And I think that that’s really what makes door knocking and canvassing one of the most essential parts of any good campaign,” said Imke Schessler, vice chair of the Maine Democratic Party.
“It’s really not about me at all and that’s okay. I don’t care, because what I want is what I’ve wanted for 30 more years. I want a government that fights for us, works for us. I want a government that does Medicare for all. I want a government that’s staying up for everyday people instead of the billionaire class that we have right now,” said Jackson.
Voters are encouraged to make their plan to vote ahead of Election Day: while early voting in Maine has ended, same-day voter registration is available at polling locations on Tuesday. Absentee ballots must be received by local municipal clerks by 8 p.m. on Nov. 3.

title: Ghost hunters declare Freeport fudge shop as haunted after a night of investigating
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ghost hunters declare Freeport fudge shop as haunted after a night of investigating
The owners of "What the Actual Fudge?" reported hearing strange sounds in their building that they couldn't explain, so they called some local paranormal experts.
Ghost hunters declare Freeport fudge shop as haunted after a night of investigating
The owners of "What the Actual Fudge?" reported hearing strange sounds in their building that they couldn't explain, so they called some local paranormal experts.
When owners Kathy and Jim Welles opened their second "What the Actual Fudge?" location in Freeport, they didn't expect to get a haunting.
Located at 7 Mill Street, on the outside of Freeport Village Station, the Welles set up shop inside the E.B. Mallet Office building, which was built in 1888. The couple makes small batches of handmade fudge.
When you walk inside and up the stairs of their Freeport shop, you'll immediately smell different flavors of fudge. Various candy lines the shelves of the store. Nothing out of the ordinary, but the Welles say it's what you can't see that is much more sinister.
"From the time we moved in, we've heard things," Kathy said. Nonexistent doors make opening sounds, banging from the attic.
"Footsteps on the stairs when nobody was there," she said.
It's scariest, Kathy says, when they are in the store alone. One morning, Jim was getting ready to open up the store when parchment paper started flying off racks on their own.
"I hear something, and I turned around, and they were all just cascading down. I was like, 'Knock it off!' And as I said that, it stopped, and I was like, 'Oh,'" Jim said.
They both said there wouldn't have been any draft moving through the store to cause the parchment to fall.
One of their employees, fascinated by the paranormal, wanted to see if they could prove whether or not ghosts were causing the commotion. So, she called the Ghost Hunters and Occult Study Team, which goes by the acronym G.H.O.S.T.
G.H.O.S.T. sent about half a dozen of their team to go investigate the strange occurrences at "What the Actual Fudge?"
They offered their services for free and spent the night in the empty store.
"When we first got here, there wasn't a whole lot going on. Then, it just started kind of trickling," said Matt Greenleaf, one of the lead investigators.
Throughout the night, the ghost hunting team captured sounds both in the shop and in the attic above. Footsteps, pipes banging, and at some point even hearing words like "get out."
Greenleaf said they start by trying to prove that there isn't a ghost.
"When we come across stuff that we can't prove, then we go into the investigation and see if we can find a paranormal reason for it," he said.
At the end of the night, they had several pieces of evidence to present to Kathy and Jim. They have been led to believe there is a ghost that is in the attic that wants to be left alone. Another ghost remains downstairs that they believe is a little girl.
Kathy and Jim got to listen to the sounds and watch the video the ghost hunters captured. They said it's very similar to the sounds they have been hearing since they moved in.
"The sounds are very real," Kathy said.
G.H.O.S.T. said that the building "What the Actual Fudge" resides in is haunted. The team hopes that more businesses take them up on their services so they can eventually make a "ghost passport" so visitors can stop by all of the haunted locations in town.
Was it enough to make Kathy and Jim believe in the occult?
"Believe, who knows? But it's always been fun," Kathy said.
"I never did not, not believe in ghosts. But now, I'm pretty sure I'm pretty sure that they exist," Jim said.
"What the Actual Fudge?" also has a location in the Maine Mall, but Kathy and Kim say they don't believe any ghosts live there.

title: Midcoast algae bloom is gone, but impacts on clammers and farmers could last for years
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
September’s algae bloom has faded from the waters around Harpswell, but harvesters and growers are still taking stock of the damage.
Some of the most vulnerable species, like worms and soft-shell clams, appear to have been wiped out in certain areas, while hard clams and oysters mostly survived. But with the bloom happening just before winter, growers and harvesters say they will have to wait for spring to know if the stress and lack of nutrients will lead to more losses.
Clam diggers and others started seeing signs of the bloom around Sept. 8 and 9. Dead and dying shellfish and worms were found on mudflats at the head of Middle Bay, in Long Cove, and in other areas, while some places in Harpswell saw no impacts at all. Maine’s Department of Marine Resources and other authorities soon confirmed that the bloom was spreading from Casco Bay as far south as New Hampshire and Massachusetts.
Tests revealed that the bloom contained the plankton Karenia mikimotoi, which is toxic to shellfish but not dangerous to humans. In addition to the plankton’s toxicity, any large algae bloom uses up oxygen, suffocating marine life. Those decomposing animals further deplete oxygen, both in the water and the mud, and can increase acidity.
The near-shore bloom seemed to peak around the middle of September. There were fears that a large storm that moved up the East Coast in the last week of September might push offshore algae back into Maine’s bays, but the storm ultimately tracked away from land and had minimal impact on Harpswell.
On Oct. 9, Harpswell Harbormaster Darcie Couture reported on Facebook that there were no more visible signs of the bloom, even offshore.
Harpswell clam digger David Wilson, who chairs the town’s Marine Resources Committee, said that in Long Cove and Middle Bay, he and other harvesters have found that larger quahogs, also known as hard clams, survived the event, while younger clams and seed clams did not. Wilson said it could take as many as seven years for populations to rebuild. And he worries that even the clams that did survive the bloom might not make it through the winter if they haven’t built up their fat stores sufficiently.
Bloom’s impact extends to sea farms
Harpswell has more than 100 aquaculture leases, with oysters as the main crop, and farmers reported mixed experiences of the bloom.
Kat Lipp, general manager of Mere Point Oyster Company, on Middle Bay in Brunswick, estimated that the farm lost about 20% of its oysters from the bloom. The farm discovered the harm early on, before the bloom was fully evident. When the extent of the threat became clear, Lipp said, staff stopped handling the oysters to reduce stress on them and give them the best chance of survival.
Like Wilson, she said it remains to be seen how many of the oysters will survive the winter.
Snow Island Oysters, which farms oysters on Harpswell Sound near the north end of Orr’s Island, has not seen an unusual die-off, according to Tait Nygaard, farm manager. The farm has been cautious about handling oysters, he said. He speculated that its location closer to the open ocean may have been a safer spot than farther up in the bays.
Another oyster farmer, Seth White, said his shellfish near Little Birch Island in Middle Bay seem to be doing OK. But his other crop, urchins, was hit hard. White said that when he pulled them up in the middle of September, he found many dead urchins. Some of the live ones didn’t look so good either.
White said he only knows of one other urchin farm, in Portland, and he heard that it survived the bloom. He said it may be a few years before he can try to grow urchins again, because their seed can cost 40 times as much as oyster seed.
He got his urchin seed from the University of Maine through a grant. This was his first time trying to grow them, and he had hoped they would be ready to sell next season. Now he’ll have to wait years to see if urchins can be an economically viable crop.
A more immediate concern for many in the aquaculture and harvesting industries is the immediate loss of income. White said that when oyster farms decided to take a break from their usual schedule of harvesting and handling oysters to give the shellfish a better chance of surviving the bloom, farm workers saw their hours cut. He knew of a dozen or more people at the end of September who hadn’t had any work to do.
At Mere Point Oyster Company, Lipp had a similar message. “The folks out there really being affected by this are the diggers, the farmers, the wild harvesters — the individuals, not the companies,” she said. It will likely be months more before the full effects on workers is known.

title: Judge puts off decision in Comey case as prosecutors pursue new indictment against ex-FBI head
text:
Judge puts off decision in Comey case as prosecutors pursue new indictment against ex-FBI head
A federal judge put off a decision Friday on whether to dismiss a placeholder criminal case filed against former FBI Director James Comey, giving the Justice Department an opportunity to pursue an indictment over allegations of a decade-old news media leak.
U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden acknowledged, though, that despite the Justice Department's hopes, an indictment was no sure thing in the nation's capital where grand juries have repeatedly rejected prosecutors' requests for charges in politically delicate cases. And he said that in the meantime, he would be "extremely frustrated if there's some sort of dawn raid" to arrest Comey before he can be indicted, a concern defense attorneys raised.
"That's not going to happen," prosecutor Dustin Farahnak said.
Related video above: Former FBI Director James Comey indicted over alleged ‘threat’ against Trump
Lawyers for Comey urged McFadden to immediately block the Justice Department from pursuing its third criminal case against the outspoken critic of President Donald Trump and frequent target of the Republican's retribution campaign. They said the Justice Department had failed to secure an indictment within the 10-year statute of limitations and that the charging document they filed instead, known as a waiverless criminal information, was legally invalid and inoperable.
“The criminal information in this case is time-barred and must be dismissed,” said Ephraim McDowell, one of Comey’s attorneys.
A closed-door court fight came into focus this week
The existence of the criminal information was revealed in court documents unsealed Monday that show the Justice Department is pursuing a case against Comey over allegations of a previously investigated news media leak from 2016. An information is a document that is typically filed when a defendant has waived his right to a grand jury indictment and intends to plead guilty, but Comey did not waive that right and his lawyers have made clear that they are contesting the charges.
The Justice Department defended the maneuver as an effort to extend the statute of limitations for seeking a grand jury indictment. The complaint was filed just as the statute of limitations was set to expire, and a prosecutor said in court Friday that the Justice Department was currently presenting evidence before a grand jury in pursuit of an indictment.
But Comey’s lawyers say the law required the Justice Department to secure an indictment, not an information, within the 10-year period and that it was unfair to Comey to leave the matter open.
“Letting this hang out there pending is a very unfair and unjust result,” McDowell said, later adding that Comey would essentially “be sitting here” in limbo under the threat of indictment even though the statute of limitations has run.
McFadden, a Trump appointee, said he understood the point but quipped that ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days. That remark referenced the oft-quoted colloquialism that indictments are so easy to obtain that even a ham sandwich can be indicted.
Farahnak, the prosecutor, told the judge it was premature to rule now while the grand jury investigation is still in progress. He hinted that evidence being presented to the grand jury would concern activities from after October 2016 and thus fall within the statute of limitations.
“They may indict, they may not indict,” Farahnak said of the grand jury.
McFadden agreed to hold off on an immediate ruling.
The case is the latest one against Comey
The effort to prosecute Comey, who says he is innocent of the allegations, is part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week’s midterm elections.
Comey was fired by Trump in May 2017 as he oversaw an investigation into whether Trump's presidential campaign conspired with Russia to tip the 2016 election in his favor over Democrat Hillary Clinton. The two men have been bitterly at odds ever since, with Comey likening Trump to a mafia don in a book he wrote and the president accusing him of treason and calling for his imprisonment.
The first criminal case against Comey accused him of lying to Congress in 2020 but was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor had been illegally appointed.
A separate pending indictment charges Comey with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of “86 47" — 86 is slang meaning “to throw out,” “to get rid of” or “to refuse service to,” and Trump is the 47th president. The former FBI director has sought to dismiss the case.
"Well, they’re back — again," Comey said in a video statement Monday. “It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice — one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing’s changed with me; I’m still innocent, I’m still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.”
The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing.
Prosecutors in an unsealed filing said investigators found evidence that Comey “sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before” the New York Times story was published, directed his staff to speak to a journalist at the newspaper related to accuracy concerns “and thereby illegally transferred classified information.”
Federal authorities, including prosecutor John Durham, began investigating the disclosure in early 2017. Durham, who later investigated the FBI’s conduct as it scrutinized potential ties between Russia and Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign, wrote a classified memo in 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey’s attorneys said in a court filing.
In 2019, the U.S. attorney’s office for the District of Columbia opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name “Tropical Vortex.” But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in early 2020.
