title: 17 theme park workers among 281 arrested during undercover operation
text:
POLK COUNTY, Fla. (WWSB/Gray News) — Florida law enforcement officials said a seven-day undercover operation resulted in 281 arrests and 488 new charges, including 198 felonies.
About the operation
The operation, called “Polk Around & Find Out II,” included simultaneous investigations focused on people accused of traveling to meet children for unlawful sexual activity and commercial sex activity, according to the Polk County Sheriff’s Office.
“Those who came to Polk County expecting to sexually abuse a child, found cuffs instead,” Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said during Friday’s news conference.
Authorities said those arrested had a combined 798 prior criminal charges. Officials also said 24 suspects had firearms and 32 people were charged with drug possession.
Theme park employees
The sheriff’s office said 17 people arrested during the operation worked at theme parks.
Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said Disney told investigators it had fired employees connected to the arrests.
Judd said he had not received an update from Universal about the employment status of its workers who were arrested.
Where suspects lived
Officials said 40 of those arrested lived in Polk County. Others came from elsewhere in Florida, 20 other states and 18 countries.
Immigration status
The sheriff’s office said 32 people arrested during the operation were in the country unlawfully, and 16 had been transferred to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
An ICE official at the news conference said the agency interviewed more than 65 foreign-born people and placed more than 30 detainers on people it identified as removable under immigration law.
Nonprofit outreach
One More Child, a nonprofit that worked with law enforcement during the operation, said it engaged with 93 people and that 18 agreed to receive services. The organization said officials identified 11 people they believe were victims of human trafficking.
“We know that accepting help takes trust, and people may be afraid, unsure, or not ready to take that step,” Sine Dressler, One More Child’s senior director of anti-trafficking operations, said during the news conference.
Investigation continues
Judd said investigators are also reviewing whether additional children may have been victimized in connection with one of the people arrested, a youth football coach.
The investigation is ongoing.

title: UNE football rolls to win over Nichols
text:
The University of New England had three players rush for more than 100 yards and cruised to a 62-14 win over Nichols in a Conference of New England football game Saturday in Dudley, Massachusetts.
The Nor’easters (3-5, 3-2 CNE) charged out to a 27-point lead by halftime. Gavin Martin’s 10-yard pass to Alex Yeaton and a 4-yard run by Nathan Delgado opened a 13-0 lead after one quarter. A 1-yard run by Damien Jones, an interception return by Will Migliaccio and Chris Lang’s 15-yard scoring pass to Jones extended the edge to 34-7.
In the third quarter, Delgado added a 12-yard rushing touchdown before Lang connected with Dante Howard for a 17-yard score. UNE added rushing touchdowns in the fourth quarter from Javin Willis (46 yards) and Delgado (25 yards)
Jones finished with 143 yards on 15 carries, while Willis racked up 140 yards on 10 carries. Delgado had 108 yards on 18 carries.
HUSSON 17, CURRY 7: Brody Gibson completed 10 of 16 passes for 103 yards, Daniel Ruiz Cantu rushed for 77 yards, and Anthony Santacroce rushed for 69 yards and a touchdown as the Eagles (3-5, 3-2 CNE) beat Curry (4-4, 3-2) in Bangor.
Husson opened a 14-0 lead by halftime on a 1-yard touchdown run by Santacroce and a 4-yard pass from Gibson to Dominic Trott.
After a scoreless third quarter, a 20-yard field goal by Ricardo Schulz made it 17-0 before Curry got on the scoreboard, with Ronin McNamara throwing an 18-yard pass to Wesley Williams.
ENDICOTT 83, MAINE MARITIME 7: Shea Lynch was 14 of 16 for 238 yards and five touchdowns as the Gulls (8-0, 5-0 CNE) rolled to a win over the Mariners (0-7, 0-4) in Castine.
Auston Harris scored for MMA on a 2-yard run in the third quarter.
COLBY 21, BATES 19: Jagger Matera threw two touchdown passes to Jack Nye in the first half, and the Mules (1-6) held off a Bates comeback bid in the second quarter to earn their first win of the season, beating the Bobcats (0-7) in Waterville.
Bates erased most of a 21-3 deficit, but Colby stopped a 2-point conversion attempt after Bryce Carberry caught a 5-yard touchdown pass from Jack Gilmore with 4:45 remaining.
Colby led 14-3 at halftime and extended its lead late in the third quarter when Antone Moreis scored on a 1-yard run.
The Bobcats began their comeback with a six-play, 75-yard drive that ended with a 10-yard pass from Gilmore to Jeff Vidou. Marcos Ruiz kicked his second field goal of the game — from 39 yards — in the fourth quarter.
WESLEYAN 28, BOWDOIN 0: Sean Cannon rushed for 72 yards and a score as the Cardinal (6-1, 6-1 NESCAC) rolled past the Polar Bears (0-7, 0-7) in Brunswick.
Matt Fitzsimons threw a 10-yard touchdown pass to Blake Newcomb with 3:40 left in the first quarter to give Wesleyan the lead, which stood through halftime. Matt Diaz extended the margin with a 61-yard run in the third quarter. In the fourth, Fitzsimons connected with Sean Cannon for a 30-yard score and Angelo LaRose added a 50-yard TD run.

title: More than 40% of names on DOJ list of alleged noncitizens not on California's voter rolls: analysis
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — More than 4 in 10 names flagged as possible noncitizen voters in California by the Trump administration cannot even be found on the state’s voter rolls, according to a legal filing Saturday by an immigrant rights group. It’s the first outside analysis of a list that the Department of Justice has used to threaten prosecution of election officials.
The analysis also found that thousands of U.S. citizens appear to be flagged as ineligible to vote on the government’s list.
The contention was made in a filing by two UCLA data scientists who analyzed the 20,930 names that the department demanded that California election officials treat as possible illegal voters by separating their ballots during the vote count on Election Day. Multiple judges have rejected the demand as unconstitutional and a threat to democracy, and local and state officials have said the list appears riddled with errors.
The breadth of its problems was outlined in Saturday’s filing. It describes an analysis by two members of the UCLA’s Voting Rights Project, who filed a lawsuit challenging it with the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights. The research found that 8,880 of the names, representing 42% of the entire list, do not correspond to anyone on California’s current voter file. It also found at least 22 are U.S. citizens and many more may correspond to those of confirmed citizens.
“This review proves, at least as a preponderance of the evidence, that demands of election officials under criminal and civil threats, endangers the voting rights of plaintiff CHIRLA’s members and clients,” said the filing, which was co-signed by Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for California governor and an adviser to the UCLA Voting Rights Project.
The Trump administration had objected to sharing the list, calling it a “fishing expedition” and noting it included sensitive information.

title: ‘Grasping at straws’: Judge dismisses Trump’s $10B lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
text:
(AP) - Saying the president was “grasping at straws,” a federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to Jeffrey Epstein.
U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law. The ruling said the lawsuit had attempted to “manufacture” flaws in the Journal’s investigative reporting.
When a case is thrown out “with prejudice,” it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.
The dismissal is a blow to Trump and his administration, which have both pursued adversarial relationships with news organizations during his second term. In addition to the Journal, he is embroiled in lawsuits involving the BBC, The Associated Press and — most recently — CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which are suing him for restored access after he banished them from the White House in mid-September.
Trump has denounced media outlets that write things to which he objects and frequently calls them “fake news” and insults their journalists.
Trump called the reporting ‘malicious’
The lawsuit against the Journal was over a story it published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the paper said bore Trump’s name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein’s 50th birthday.
The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Trump.
The letter bearing Trump’s name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, “Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret,” according to the newspaper.
Trump denied writing it and called the story “false, malicious, and defamatory.”
The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami, accused the paper and its reporters of having “knowingly and recklessly” published “numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements,” which, it alleged, caused “overwhelming financial and reputational harm” to the president.
Epstein died by suicide in a New York jail cell in August 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges.
The lawsuit was dismissed once, then refiled
Gayles previously dismissed the suit in April, saying Trump had failed to make the argument that the article was published with the intent to be malicious. But he gave the president a chance to file an amended complaint, which he did in May.
In Saturday’s ruling, the judge cited the Supreme Court’s landmark 1964 ruling in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. That decision made it harder for public figures to win libel lawsuits because it requires proof that a media outlet knowingly published something false or showed a reckless disregard for the truth.
“The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice,” Gayles wrote. “Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false.”
The judge also noted that the Journal’s story did not ignore or minimize Trump’s denial, “Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it.”
Gayles also said several other allegations in the lawsuit did not have merit.

title: Maine secretary of state addresses DOJ plans to send Election Day monitors
text:
Maine secretary of state addresses DOJ plans to send Election Day monitors
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows discussed federal election observers, voter intimidation allegations, and absentee ballot updates ahead of Election Day.
Maine secretary of state addresses DOJ plans to send Election Day monitors
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows discussed federal election observers, voter intimidation allegations, and absentee ballot updates ahead of Election Day.
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows is addressing the U.S. Justice Department’s plan to send election observers to Portland, South Portland, and Lewiston on Election Day next Tuesday.
In an interview for Sunday’s “Total Maine,” Bellows said voters should not expect any disruptions.
“They can observe what is happening, but they cannot speak with voters. They cannot handle ballots. They cannot handle equipment,” Bellows said.
The move is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to deploy 1,000 poll watchers across all 50 states.
“We've met with the Department of Justice to make sure that they understand what the laws and rules are here in Maine,” Bellows added.
Bellows also addressed recent complaints of voter intimidation in Lewiston, where she said a “political operative” was harassing voters with unwanted questions.
“We take those allegations very seriously and we are going to do everything in our power to protect a safe, comfortable voting experience for every voter,” Bellows said.
Additionally, Bellows responded to claims made by Janet Beaudoin, a Republican candidate for House District 94, who alleged that an interpreter at a polling location asked her inappropriate questions and made concerning statements.
Beaudoin alleged the interpreter was breaking election laws by telling a voter who to vote for but admitted she did not report the incident to the Secretary of State's Office.
“We checked in with the Lewiston city clerk, who is very experienced, one of the state's best. They were providing instructions to the interpreters and they were really confident in the integrity of that program and so I am skeptical,” Bellows said.
As of Friday, the Secretary of State’s Office reported that more than 313,000 voters in Maine had requested absentee ballots, with over 275,000 of those ballots already returned.

title: Few know about this trail in Acadia National Park
text:
This story was originally published in October 2023.
Acorns rolled and crunched beneath my boots as I followed Breakneck Road deeper into the wilderness of Acadia National Park.
Boarded by towering oaks and sugar maples, the old roadway serves as a little-known walking path, with wintergreen and sweet ferns encroaching on its gravel base.
It measures about 2.5 miles long, spanning from Route 3, near Acadia’s Hulls Cove Visitor Center, to Eagle Lake Road, near park headquarters.
Threading through the woods, it passes a small waterfall, crosses Breakneck Brook and passes between two bodies of water that are together known as Breakneck Ponds.
So what’s with the name “Breakneck”? Sounds a bit ominous.
Back in the 19th century, the road was open to carriages headed to Northeast Harbor. It earned its dark name from several carriage accidents that took place on the steep hill that the road descends before crossing Breakneck Brook, according to information posted online by the Davistown Museum.
The road was built in 1777, but it has served as simply a recreational walking path since the early 1900s, according to the 2006 publication “Pathmakers: Cultural Landscape Report for the Historic Hiking Trail System of Mount Desert Island” by Margie Coffin Brown and Jim Vekasi.
In 1923, a natural spring along the road was excavated and lined with stones so that walkers would have access to fresh water.
Nowadays, the trail travels right through Acadia National Park. It isn’t marked with signs, cairns or blazes like the park’s many hiking trails, yet it’s easy to follow because of its width and rocky base.
It’s also marked as a trail on the park trail map created by Maine-based Map Adventures.
Over the years, I’d heard a few locals mention the route as a nice walking path, away from the crowds. But in all my explorations of Acadia, I hadn’t walked Breakneck Road until recently.
With my dog Juno leading the way, I walked the entire thing, out and back.
When preparing for the hike, I originally put on sneakers, but at the last minute, I switched them for waterproof boots — and I’m glad I did. Recent rain had flooded a few areas of the path.
Plus, there’s no bridge where the road crosses Breakneck Brook. The brook was shallow, but in order to cross without flooding my boots, I had to hop from rock to rock.
A short part of Breakneck Road is open to vehicles. In fact, that’s where you’ll find Davistown Museum, an eclectic tool, art and history museum.
It’s also home to Breakneck Hollow Historic Site, where an educational display offers information about the area’s past.
A small parking area for the hike — large enough to fit two or three vehicles — is located at the end of the auto portion of Breakneck Road. From there, I walked past a gate to begin my adventure with Juno.
The walk ended up being the perfect way to embrace the lingering colors of late autumn. Oaks, I’ve noticed, tend to hold onto their leaves later than most other trees. There were plenty of oaks in that forest, their leaves shades of gold and orange.
Some maple trees still had bright foliage as well. I paused to admire one with leaves ranging from yellow to peach. Another maple displayed leaves of bright crimson.
Less than half a mile into the hike, the old road passed a small waterfall pouring down a cleft in a cliff. At the base of the waterfall was a jumble of rocks that continued across the trail and beyond.
The rockslide occurred in July 2021, when a huge beaver dam collapsed upstream, dislodging rocks on both sides of the waterfall, according to a story in the Mount Desert Islander.
After crossing Breakneck Brook, the old road traveled uphill. The forest quickly transitioned from mostly hardwood to mostly softwood, with tall pine and spruce trees shading the path.
Sheep laurel and sweet ferns lined the trail, along with blueberry and huckleberry bushes. And in small clearings, small red dragonflies roamed over beds of crunchy reindeer lichen.
At Breakneck Ponds, I let Juno wade into the water as I basked in the sun. I had visited the ponds before. Nearby carriage roads lead to their shores.
But it was nice to see them from a different perspective. They’re a great place to spot wildlife, such as ducks or beavers, though I didn’t see any animals that morning.
Continuing past the ponds, the old road became a bit rough and washed out in places. Still, I followed it to its end on Eagle Lake Road, then turned around to retrace my steps.
As we walked back, I noticed the sounds of the forest — the sweet chirping of chickadees mixed with the sharp calls of blue jays and crows. With Halloween just around the corner, I was hoping for Breakneck Road to be a bit spooky. But the route was nothing but peaceful and lovely, with sunlight filtering through a canopy of golden leaves.

title: Solar moratorium a necessary step for Jay
text:
Jay voters should support the proposed solar moratorium because our town deserves time
to establish clear protections before major development changes our landscape for decades.
Forests, fields, wildlife habitat and neighboring homes deserve careful consideration. So
do taxpayers, who deserve a clear accounting of projected revenue, public costs and any
promised savings.
A temporary pause would give residents and town officials an opportunity to examine setbacks, screening, stormwater management and financial guarantees for removing equipment when a project ends. These questions should be answered before commitments become permanent.
Renewable energy can have a place in Jay. Residents should help determine where it belongs, how large projects should be, and what safeguards developers must provide. Our community should set thoughtful standards for its future. Please support the moratorium and give Jay time to do this work carefully, openly and with meaningful public participation throughout the entire process.
Clinton Brooks
Jay

title: A flurry of last-minute legal developments could impact midterm elections
text:
A flurry of last-minute legal developments could impact midterm elections
A criminal probe involving one of the closest Senate races of the year is underway, while several legal battles continue over ballots from suspected non-citizens
A flurry of last-minute legal developments could impact midterm elections
A criminal probe involving one of the closest Senate races of the year is underway, while several legal battles continue over ballots from suspected non-citizens
As candidates make their final pitches to voters in the last weekend before Election Day, a flurry of legal developments could also shape the battle for control of Congress.
A criminal probe in Alaska
One of the closest Senate races of the year is now at the center of a criminal investigation looking into how two candidates with the same name ended up on the ballot in Alaska.
On Friday, the state's top federal prosecutor, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman, said that the months-long probe received a surge of law enforcement resources after a report from The New York Times that was published earlier this week.
The report said that Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign appears to have helped recruit a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan to run for Senate, to divert votes from the two-term Republican incumbent who is also named Dan Sullivan.
Heyman would not say on Friday what potential crimes authorities are looking into or who the probe is targeting.
Peltola has denied any involvement in the alleged scheme, and Dan J. Sullivan has denied claims that he was planted by Democrats as a spoiler candidate, though such campaign tricks have been used in American politics for decades.
Alaskan officials have already taken some steps to distinguish between the two Sullivans on the ballot, which uses a ranked-choice system.
However, as part of a lawsuit, the Justice Department is seeking to separate ballots that rank the retired teacher in case an investigation into whether voter confusion impacted the results should be needed.
Setbacks on campaign against suspected non-citizens
A federal appeals court shot down the Justice Department’s demand that California set aside ballots from 20,000 suspected non-citizens until their immigration status can be verified.  
In Friday's 2-1 decision, the majority sided with state officials, who have argued the DOJ’s demand isn’t doable this late in the process and risks disenfranchising eligible US citizens.
The dissenting judge argued that California’s unwillingness to separate the ballots encourages the violation of federal law.
The DOJ has previously said that it would appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.
Past audits have found non-citizen voting is very rare and is unlikely to impact election results.
In a separate decision on Friday, a panel of judges ruled that federal investigations into the issue will remain on hold in nine states until after Election Day. Those states include California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.
Judge bars intimidation of election workers
In another legal development out of California, a federal judge barred the Justice Department from threatening election officials or coercing them not to count disputed ballots.
The lawsuit was filed, in part, by a coalition of unions representing election workers whom the Trump administration has threatened to potentially prosecute.
After urging California to separate disputed ballots, the DOJ warned that workers who knowingly process ballots from non-citizens could be in legal jeopardy. The Associated Press obtained grand jury subpoenas issued to some election officials in Los Angeles County earlier this week.
Separately, the DOJ reportedly sent letters to election officials in all 50 states this week reminding them of federal requirements to preserve election records and warning of possible prison time if they don’t comply.
The DOJ says it relies on those records to investigate potential voter fraud, but critics view the outreach as the latest intimidation tactic from the Trump administration leading up to Election Day.

title: Late for class: 8th grader says bus ride to school routinely takes up to 3 hours
text:
NEW YORK (Spectrum News NY1) — A New York City eighth grader is routinely late for school because his bus ride takes about three hours.
The bus also picks up children who attend a different school.
Michael Mileto gets up at 5:30 a.m. and catches the school bus at 6:20 a.m. He has been late to school on a regular basis, arriving after the first bell at 8:15 a.m.
“It’s ridiculous,” Michael said.
Commute longer than last year
Michael has a speech-language disability. He attends a private school on the Upper East Side at the city’s expense because his needs could not be met in a local public school.
The city’s Education Department is responsible for busing him from his home in Brighton Beach.
This year, the ride has routinely taken two and a half or three hours. Once, Michael did not arrive until 10 a.m.
Last year, Michael was picked up around 6:45 a.m. and arrived at school on time at 8:15 a.m.
This year, his bus also carries children who attend a different school in Manhattan. That has required Michael to be picked up earlier and dropped off later.
“Now, all of a sudden, they just decide to make my school late,” Michael said.
Missed class time
Michael’s mother, Annie Mileto, said he is missing class time.
“He’s missing math, literacy, main subjects, things, and I’m worried. Of course, school makes up for it, sits with him and makes sure he gets it right, but he’s not doing it with his other students. You’re missing out on all of that,” Annie Mileto said.
Michael said the late arrivals affect his lessons.
“I miss lessons, and then I had to rush and get catched up,” he said.
The ride home has also run long. Michael said there was one day he did not arrive home until 6 p.m.
“I always feel tired and drowsy. I just want to go to bed, but I have to do my homework,” Michael said.
Other students affected
At the start of the school year, around 2,000 children on 300 bus routes did not have a driver. The city provided students with prepaid rideshare options, bought new buses and worked to get more drivers online at bus companies that have contracts with the city.
Randi Levine, policy director at Advocates for Children, said her organization is hearing from families who still do not have bus service. She said the organization is also hearing from families, like Michael’s, whose buses are more crowded and arriving later.
“There are times when it is most efficient to have children on the same bus, going to two different nearby schools, and we’ve seen that in past years. But what we’re seeing this year, in some cases, is that routes that were probably meant to be separate are being combined,” Levine said.
City reviewing route
A spokeswoman for the city’s public schools said the department takes concerns about long routes seriously. She said the department is reviewing Michael’s route, including GPS data and any delays that may have been caused by stops along the way, to see what happened and whether it can be improved.
Michael said he hopes something changes soon.
“I know its not their fault, but I think they should do better,” he said.

title: Wildfire jumps fire lines, burns nearly 20 acres in Casco
text:
A wildfire ignited Saturday morning and burned through nearly 20 acres in Casco before crews were able to contain it.
The fire near Coffee Pond was first reported just before 5 a.m., according to first responder alerts. Windy conditions and dry weather caused the fire to quickly swell in size and jump over fire lines crews had established to contain it.
Roughly a dozen fire departments from southern Maine responded to the blaze. Aerial crews were dispatched as well, with videos shared by North Yarmouth Fire Rescue showing a helicopter scooping water from a nearby lake and dumping it over the fire.
Photos and videos from the scene showed the fire sweeping through underbrush in the woods beside Coffee Pond.
Most of Maine was at high risk of fires on Saturday, according to the state forest service.
The blaze was about 90% contained by 9 a.m., according to Casco Fire Rescue. Its cause remains unclear.
Officials warned residents and hunters to avoid the area Saturday as firefighters are expected to remain on site through most of the day to fully extinguish the fire.

title: Deer crashes through window, jumps onto machines at laundromat
text:
Deer hits woman, crashes through window at laundromat | Caught on video
A deer caused quite a scene at a North Carolina laundromat, shocking customers as it crashed through a window and jumped onto laundry machines.
Click the player above to watch the video.
Security footage from The Wishy Washy Laundry on South Main Street in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, showed the deer running through the parking lot and running into a woman who had just left the business. It then crashed through a window and climbed onto the machines before escaping through the broken window.
Corey Pendergrass, owner of The Wishy Washy Laundry, said nothing like this has ever happened to him before.
"Like a deer coming through the business, what in the world?" Pendergrass said. "Who has to deal with this?"
And while he wasn't present when the deer ran amok, he was shocked when watching the security footage.
"One in a million chance of something like this," Pendergrass said. "You don't expect this to happen."
But he said he's grateful nobody was seriously injured.
"It was nonsense, and it was just a miracle that no one got hurt," Pendergrass said. "So we're very thankful for that."
Pfaff's Glass repaired the broken window just a couple of hours after the deer smashed into it.
"And so, I only had to fix one window, thankfully," Pendergrass said.
Pendergrass also said the woman hit by the deer drove away shortly after it happened.

title: Woman says protest was free speech after arrest for allegedly blocking robot’s path
text:
PHILADELPHIA (WPVI) — A Philadelphia woman was arrested after allegedly blocking the path of a delivery robot.
Police said witnesses called to report a disturbance earlier this month between Carolyn Marvin and an Uber delivery robot in Philadelphia.
“I have been protesting them whenever I saw them by standing in front of them and preventing them from going forward,” Marvin said.
Police said Marvin was arrested for disorderly conduct after she ignored officer commands to move out of the robot’s path.
Marvin said she was there “to publicly demonstrate on a public sidewalk my protest against delivery robots.”
Marvin said she believes her actions are protected free speech and plans to keep protesting the robots.

title: 7 people shot, 1 fatally, at Spirit Halloween store, police say
text:
FAIRFIELD, Calif. (AP) - A targeted shooting inside a Spirit Halloween store in Northern California left a pregnant woman dead and six other people wounded, police said.
Gunfire rang out at about 8:30 p.m. Friday inside the store, which sells Halloween costumes and decor, at the Solano Town Center in Fairfield, the city police department said Saturday in a statement on Facebook.
The shooting “stemmed from a targeted incident involving one suspect,” police said.
The woman who died was identified by police as Constance Hages, 31, and family members told authorities she was pregnant.
Three male victims ages 16, 19 and 32 were in critical condition, and a 23-year-old man was hospitalized in critical but stable condition.
Two other men, ages 19 and 43, were treated for gunshot wounds and released from the hospital.
No arrests have been made. Authorities said they were reviewing video and other evidence “to identify the individual responsible for this heinous act of violence.”
The department said no additional information would be released at this time.
“We recognize the concern and uncertainty this incident has created throughout our community, particularly with the many Halloween events and celebrations planned for today,” the department said. “We understand that an incident of this nature is frightening and deeply unsettling. We encourage everyone to remain vigilant, look out for one another, and report any suspicious activity.”
Solano Town Center, which has 130 stores and restaurants, remained open but said it was canceling its planned trick-or-treating event scheduled for later in the day “in light of last night’s event.”
“We appreciate your patience and understanding during this time,” the mall said in a statement.
The FBI’s Sacramento office said it was assisting Fairfield police in the investigation.
Fairfield, a city of some 120,000 residents, is about 37 miles (60 kilometers) southwest of Sacramento and halfway between there and San Francisco.

title: Crews respond to 19-acre fire off Coffee Pond in Casco
text:
Nearly 20-acre fire contained in Casco
Officials say the fire is contained but ask residents to avoid the area
Nearly 20-acre fire contained in Casco
Officials say the fire is contained but ask residents to avoid the area
Officials in Casco are asking residents to avoid the Coffee Pond area for the next week after a large woods fire burned nearly 20 acres.
Casco Fire and Rescue says the fire is contained, but crews are still monitoring several hot spots that have burned down to the roots.
The fire broke out early Saturday morning, prompting a response from Casco firefighters and several mutual aid departments.
Officials estimate 19.4 acres were involved in the fire.
Earlier Saturday, fire officials asked the community to stay away from the area while crews worked to contain the flames. They said they encountered several hunters in the area and wanted to keep everyone safe.
Casco Fire and Rescue says crews will work with the Maine Forest Service along Coffee Pond Road throughout the coming week to clean up the area.
The department is thanking everyone who assisted with the response and asking residents to continue avoiding the area while that work is underway.

title: Jefferson Food Pantry to Expand With Move to New Space
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After operating out of St. Giles’ Episcopal Church for over a decade, the Jefferson Area Community Food Pantry is preparing to move to the United Baptist Church of South Jefferson this spring.
“Here we have space to grow,” pantry Executive Director Allison Brooks said.
The pantry will operate out of a vestry built in 1913 and the former Grange hall that sit behind the church, at 495 South Clary Road. Brooks and her husband, Scott Brooks, are currently working to renovate and update the historic space for use.
Allison Brooks anticipates the pantry will open at its new location in March. It will operate out of St. Giles’, at 72 Gardiner Road, until then.
“St. Giles has been a wonderful home for 10 years,” Brooks said. “We grew out of a little cupboard.”
Since its start in 2015, Brooks said that the growth of the pantry began to encroach on the church’s regular operations. St. Giles’ Senior Warden Charles Dow said the church and pantry were sharing a limited space, from which issues arose.
Additionally, pantry volunteers, who are mostly seniors, sometimes had trouble with the stairs used to reach the pantry space, Brooks said.
Dow added the church will assist the pantry’s transition, if possible.
“We wish them continued success,” Dow said. “We’ve been glad to be a part of it for so long.”
Candy Hilton, head deacon at United Baptist and treasurer for the food pantry, said she brought up the relatively unused buildings behind her church to Brooks in September. The move was announced on pantry social media pages in mid-October.
“We just kind of did it by the seat of our pants because we have faith it will work out,” Brooks said.
The Grange hall and vestry will be free to use for the pantry, as long as it remains an organization that serves the community. The vestry and its kitchen will be shared with the church for events.
“Our missions are very aligned,” Hilton said about the food pantry and United Baptist church. She called the arrangement a “win-win.”
Alongside an expanded and mostly stairless space, the property also has parking space that can’t be seen from the road for patron privacy. Brooks also said the pantry will expand its hours to open at 2 p.m., instead of its current opening at 4 p.m., and close at 5:30 p.m.
“We’re (going to) be spoiled,” Brooks said.
With about 30 regular volunteers, the pantry serves primarily Jefferson and Somerville, but also patrons from across Lincoln County and beyond. It stocks produce, dairy, meats, canned goods, dry goods, diapers, pet food, and more. Brooks hopes to expand to clothes, books, and other personal items in its new space.
The pantry occasionally makes home deliveries and does not check identification or proof of receiving government benefits, such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, Brooks said. The team also supplies food to Jefferson Village School staff and keeps a “help-yourself” pantry at the Somerville town office.
“You just never know when you’re one tragedy away from using this service,” Brooks said. “We just give without judgment.”
Brooks, who has been executive director of the pantry since 2019, has recently applied for half a dozen grants that she hopes will support the pantry’s expansion.
“We’re really praying for a lot of grant money to come in,” Hilton said.
While Brooks said she utilizes social media for fundraising, she also thinks community has been lost to the digital world, and that community and interaction is the true heart of the pantry.
“Come and save some money, have a conversation,” Brooks said. “We’re missing something in society where we’re not caring for the people that are next door to us.”
The pantry is also supported by food and monetary donors. Food can be dropped off at the beginning of pantry hours, and donations can be sent via PayPal or mailed to the pantry at P.O. Box 208, Jefferson, ME, 04348.
Prospective donors, patrons, and volunteers can find more information and the pantry schedule on the Jefferson Area Community Food Pantry on Facebook. For more information, call 315-1134 or email [email protected].

title: ME State Senator Joe Baldacci Tapped as Maine State Chair for U.S. Term Limits
text:
October 31, 2027 BANGOR, ME, October 30, 2026 /24-7PressRelease/ — Today, U.S. Term Limits announced that former Maine State Senator and Bangor Mayor Joe Baldacci has agreed to serve as Maine State Chair for U.S. Term Limits. Baldacci brings decades of public service, community leadership, and firsthand experience with state and local government to the effort to enact congressional term […]
October 31, 2027
BANGOR, ME, October 30, 2026 /24-7PressRelease/ — Today, U.S. Term Limits announced that former Maine State Senator and Bangor Mayor Joe Baldacci has agreed to serve as Maine State Chair for U.S. Term Limits. Baldacci brings decades of public service, community leadership, and firsthand experience with state and local government to the effort to enact congressional term limits and bring greater accountability to Washington, D.C.
A longtime supporter of congressional term limits as part of broader political reform, Baldacci believes limiting the amount of time members of Congress can remain in office is an important step toward protecting representative government and ensuring elected officials remain accountable to the people they serve.
“I am honored to serve as Maine State Chair for U.S. Term Limits and to help advance congressional term limits,” said Baldacci. “Public service should be about serving your neighbors and your community—not building a lifetime career in Washington. Term limits can help bring new voices, fresh ideas, and greater accountability to Congress.”
“Throughout my career in local and state government, I have seen the importance of elected officials staying connected to the people they represent,” continued Baldacci. “Maine people expect their government to work for them, not for powerful special interests or entrenched political insiders. Congressional term limits are an important part of restoring that balance.”
“People across the political spectrum recognize that Washington needs reform,” concluded Baldacci. “Congressional term limits are a commonsense reform that can help restore trust in government and ensure that public office remains a public service. I look forward to working with Mainers across our state to build support for this effort.”
Whether in his law practice or serving as a Bangor City Councilor, Mayor, or State Senator, Baldacci has dedicated much of his life to serving his community and helping his neighbors.
Born and raised in Bangor, Baldacci grew up working in his family’s restaurant, Momma Baldacci’s, alongside his seven siblings. He spent countless days washing dishes, making the restaurant’s signature sauce, and talking with customers about their lives. His parents instilled in their children a simple principle: everybody pitches in, and you look out for each other. Baldacci has carried that philosophy throughout his professional career and public service.
After graduating from Bangor public schools, Baldacci attended the University of Maine and later the University of Maine School of Law. He returned to Bangor and established a general law practice in the early 1990s, representing Mainers in a wide variety of cases and often helping clients through some of the most difficult periods of their lives. That experience gave him firsthand insight into the challenges facing Maine families, workers, and small businesses.
Baldacci was elected four times to the Bangor City Council and served two terms as Mayor. During his time in municipal government, he focused on economic development and protecting essential services, including school funding, public health, law enforcement, and infrastructure. He also opposed efforts to locate a private prison in a residential Bangor neighborhood without meaningful local input or involvement.
In 2020, Baldacci was elected to the Maine State Senate and was reelected in 2022 and 2024 to represent Bangor and Hermon. In the Senate, he focused on issues affecting seniors and health care, teachers and public schools, property taxpayers, working families, and Maine communities. His work included efforts to restore Medicare subsidies and lower property taxes to help Mainers remain in their homes. He was recognized as a Legislator of the Year by the Maine Council on Aging and earned a 100 percent rating from the Maine Education Association four years in a row.
During the 132nd Legislature, Baldacci served on the Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services Committee and chaired both the State and Local Government Committee and the Inland Fisheries and Wildlife Committee. He has also served on and chaired the Health and Human Services Committee.
Throughout his public service, Baldacci has focused on strengthening local economies, standing up for working families, and making government deliver results for the people it serves.
“We are honored to have Joe Baldacci leading our efforts in Maine,” said Philip Blumel, President of U.S. Term Limits. “Joe brings extensive experience at both the local and state levels of government and a deep understanding of what genuine public service means. His commitment to accountability and citizen government makes him a strong advocate for congressional term limits. We are confident his leadership will help build tremendous momentum for term limits reform throughout Maine.”
Baldacci lives in Bangor with his wife of more than 30 years, Beth. They are the proud parents of two adult daughters, Caroline and Olivia.
U.S. Term Limits is the nation’s largest grassroots advocacy organization dedicated to establishing term limits at all levels of government, particularly for the U.S. Congress. The organization works with citizens and lawmakers across the country to advance constitutional reforms that increase accountability, encourage citizen legislators, and restore trust in government.

title: Man posing as Amazon delivery driver accused of stealing multiple packages from neighborhood
text:
LAKE OSWEGO, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A Portland man has been arrested after police say he stole packages while posing as an Amazon delivery driver.
According to the Lake Oswego Police Department, 51-year-old Ramiro Despaigne Rodriguez was arrested on Oct. 21 after packages were reported stolen from at least eight homes in the Lake Oswego area.
Police said the suspect was caught on surveillance video driving a car marked with a “delivery driver” sticker and wearing an Amazon vest.
Rodriguez was arrested and booked into the Clackamas County Jail, where he faces first-degree theft charges.
Investigators believe there may be more victims connected to this case.

title: Democratic congressional candidate served with felony warrant at campaign event
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A Democratic candidate running for North Carolina’s Congressional District 14 was served with a felony warrant at a campaign event earlier this month.
According to the Polk County Sheriff’s Office, deputies served 49-year-old Lakesha Womack with a felony warrant on Oct. 11.
Authorities said the warrant was from 2020, charging her with failure to return a hired motor vehicle valued at more than $4,000.
The arrest warrant stated that Womack rented a 2019 Toyota Corolla from Budget Car Rental in October 2019 and did not return it by the agreed-upon date.
The car was reportedly worth $20,000.
The criminal summons was originally issued in January 2020 but was not served until this month. It was not immediately clear why the warrant was not served earlier.
Womack is running for Congressional District 14, which includes Gastonia, Shelby, Morgantown, and parts of far south Charlotte. She is challenging Republican incumbent Rep. Tim Moore.
Womack’s campaign did not directly address the felony warrant when asked about the situation, but did address the alleged attack ads from Moore’s campaign.
“Over the past few weeks, allegations involving me have drawn significant media attention and attack ads from Friends of Tim Moore. Candidates for public office should be held accountable and voters deserve transparency,” a statement read in part.
“Throughout this campaign, I have emphasized accountability and affordability. I believe every candidate and elected official should be evaluated by consistent standards, including their record of public service, their decisions in office, and their responsiveness to the people they represent,” the statement continued.
The midterm general election will be held on Nov. 3.

title: Kingfield, Strong to vote on withdrawing from school district in upcoming election
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Kingfield, Strong to vote on withdrawing from school district in upcoming election
On Nov. 3, Kingfield will decide to withdraw from M.S.A.D. 58 and create its own S.A.U.
The school district consists of four schools: Mt. Abram High School, Day Mountain Regional Middle School, Phillips Elementary School and Kingfield Elementary School.
Currently, Pre-K through fourth-grade Kingfield students attend the town's elementary school before traveling to Day Mountain for middle school and Mt. Abram for high school.
If the ballot question passed, Kingfield students in Pre-K through eighth grade would all go to school at what is currently the town's elementary school before having the option of the area's high schools. Supporters have said that the preferred option would continue to be Mt. Abram.
Proponents of the proposal include Kathy Houston and Kim Jordan, both members of the Kingfield Withdrawal Committee.
They said the committee was created after a school budget meeting presented the idea of closing the town's school.
"It's heartbreaking to walk into that school," Jordan said. "Now we know only half of the school is being used. You still have all the same operational costs all year long. We need to bring our fifth- to eighth-grade kids back to Kingfield."
The town's school hosted students up to eighth grade until a change was made in 2022. The pair said that with that change came a loss of energy in the town. They pointed to a lack of sporting events and generally fewer kids around the town.
They also say withdrawal will hold financial benefits for Kingfield residents.
Houston said that Kingfield taxpayers contribute 42% of the school district's budget with 17% of the total student population, while holding a limited voice in decision-making.
"We have limited voice on the school board," Houston said. "The school board, they have their vote. So they have a weighted voting system, and Kingfield has 27% of that weight."
According to the committee, the change would save the town $500,000, as they currently pay $2.3 million toward the school budget. If passed, they said that number wouldn't change, but the state would contribute $700,000.
Opponents think the change could have drastic impacts for the rest of the district.
"It would dramatically reduce the funding that's coming into the district. If they leave, then we lose the facilities cost for maintaining their school and also all their employees. Right off the bat, it's going to be a big financial hit for the district," Adam Masterman said.
Masterman works for Mt. Abram. He and his kids graduated from Mt. Abram. But he can't vote on the ballot question as he lives in an unorganized territory within the district.
Strong, one of the four towns in the district, is also voting to separate from the district to create its own S.A.U.
Masterman thinks if both questions pass, it could lead to the closure of schools.
"Two of our smaller towns would be responsible for maintaining the high school," Masterman said. "It's very hard to predict, but the Kingfield withdrawal would be an immediate budgetary challenge."
Closure would require students to have to travel to a different high school, which Masterman believes could bring safety concerns.
Maine law requires the question to have approval from two-thirds of voters in order to be passed.
If passed, it would go into effect in the fall of 2027.

title: Greely volleyball completes storybook season with Class B title
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SOUTH PORTLAND — There was no championship-or-bust mission for the Greely volleyball team going into this season. There were no grandiose dreams, no Gold Ball expectations.
Which is why, when the season did end with a championship, the Rangers were as surprised as anyone.
No. 1 seed Greely won its first volleyball title in 10 years on Saturday, sweeping second-seeded and two-time defending champion Washington Academy in the Class B final at Southern Maine Community College.
“I don’t think any of us really believed that we would be here in this moment,” said senior hitter Annabelle Talley, who totaled eight kills and six aces in the 25-16, 25-16, 25-23 victory. “If you had told me in the beginning of the season that we would be state champs this year, I don’t think anyone on the team would have believed it. It’s honestly an insane feeling.”
That wasn’t just one player’s feeling.
“I didn’t expect us to be in the championship this year,” said junior middle hitter and co-captain Maddie Huntington. “But I think after our last (regular) season game, we really saw the possibility. People worked really hard, and I think it showed.”
Greely (16-1) reached the semifinals last year, falling to Washington, but graduated nine seniors and went into the year with freshmen and sophomores scattered throughout the lineup. The goal was to win as many matches as possible. Not a championship.
A regular-season win over Washington (15-2) got the Rangers thinking bigger, however. On Saturday, that newfound belief was rewarded.
“That told us ‘This is a top team. We can take this team, we can do it again,'” Greely coach Autumn Vargo said. “And then when we beat York at the end of the season, that gave us really good momentum going into the playoffs.”
The first step was starting strong, something the Rangers didn’t do in the previous round against Messalonskee. But that box was checked Saturday; Greely never trailed in the first set, and a string of three straight aces by Talley gave the Rangers a 9-6 lead in the second that they never surrendered.
“They just played calm, they played composed,” Vargo said. “They went out there telling themselves maybe we don’t necessarily deserve it over this team, but we have earned the spot here. We’re going to come out and show them that we can play with the best of them.”
Greely again took a big lead in the third set, going up 22-16 and prompting chants of “It’s all over!” from the student section. But the reigning champs didn’t go down quietly. Jaylyn Warren and Marlee Carver had kills as the Raiders won the next five points.
A block kill by Huntington stopped the bleeding, however. An ace from Alena Tierney (one of Greely’s two sophomore setters, along with Avery Enos) followed, and Talley set up sophomore Reagan Dailey two points later for a hit that Washington couldn’t return, starting the celebration.
“Obviously it’s disappointing, but it is what it is. I think it’s a privilege to have the opportunity to play in this game, because not everyone does,” first-year Raiders coach Kalyn Stevens said. “Greely played phenomenal. Their defense was frustrating for us, they were getting to all sorts of balls. (Talley) did fantastic, she’s a great player.”
Greely was consistently able to find an answer for Washington hitters Warren (seven kills), Aubrey Faukingham (six) and Carver (five), with libero Ellie Desorbo and Maple Bouchard-Simpson — both sophomores — delivering one clutch dig after another.
“They are just steady, consistent players in our lineup,” Huntington said, “and they did an amazing job tonight.”

title: US plans to deport Afghans back to their home country through Pakistan, documents show
text:
President Donald Trump’s administration is planning to deport Afghans detained in the U.S. back to their home country via Pakistan, according to court documents obtained by The Associated Press — a move advocacy groups say could put their lives at risk.
Immigrant rights organizations say those deported could face retaliation from the Taliban. Thousands fled persecution and feared for their lives after helping the U.S. military and aid groups in Afghanistan.
“This is absolutely unconscionable,” said Shawn VanDiver, a U.S. Navy veteran and president of the advocacy group #AfghanEvac. “It seems like there’s no end to their willingness to break the law and violate people’s human rights.”
The U.S. intends to initially deport Afghan immigrants as early as Monday on flights from Louisiana, where the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency has immigrant detention and processing facilities, to Pakistan, according to court documents.
The plan to deport Afghans to Pakistan was first reported by Bloomberg on Monday. On Friday, The New York Times reported that the immigrants were going to be sent to Afghanistan after arriving in Pakistan.
A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in an email to the AP on Saturday that ICE does not comment on future immigrant-removal operations, citing operational security and personnel safety. Officials at the Pakistani Embassy in Washington did not immediately return email messages.
Afghans caught up in Trump’s immigration crackdown
U.S. officials confirmed the Afghan deportations in sealed court documents obtained by the AP.
In a document filed in federal court in Virginia on Friday, a senior ICE official acknowledged that an Afghan immigrant had been scheduled to be on an upcoming charter flight from Alexandria, Louisiana, to Pakistan, “with further transport onward to Afghanistan.” The document was filed in the case of an immigrant who is not in custody and is challenging efforts to deport him.
In another federal court case in Oklahoma, federal prosecutors filed a document on Monday disclosing that another Afghan immigrant was scheduled to be deported to Afghanistan sometime next week.
The Trump administration has deported thousands of immigrants to countries other than their own. It has done this in some instances when it is unable to send them to their own countries because the US does not have formal relations, like with the Taliban government in Afghanistan. In other instances, it has been used as a deterrent.
In many cases, a U.S. immigration judge has determined their lives would be in jeopardy if sent to their home countries. It was not immediately clear if any designated for return to Afghanistan have protective orders against being sent there.
Immigrant groups and Democrats decry deportation plan
Human Rights First, an advocacy group for refugees and asylum seekers that tracks U.S. deportation flights, said Saturday that it had confirmed a scheduled flight from Louisiana to Pakistan on Tuesday carrying Afghan immigrants.
“It is beyond egregious that this administration plans to carry out an unprecedented mass deportation flight of Afghans, forcibly sending them through Pakistan and into the hands of the Taliban,” Savitri Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights for Human Rights First, said in an email to the AP.
“This follows previous unconscionable deportation flights we have tracked under this administration, including Iranian Christian converts and political dissidents removed via Qatar and Kuwait to Iran, as well as a Russian political dissident removed via Egypt to Russia,” Arvey said.
Some Democratic members of Congress took to social media to criticize the Afghan deportations after seeing the Times story on Friday.
“It is reprehensible that the Trump Administration plans to deport hundreds of Afghans, including women, children and those who supported U.S. forces, to Pakistan — who then risk being sent back into the hands of the Taliban. Congress must stand against this,” Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire posted on X.
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut added in his own X post, “We made a promise to our Afghan allies — that after aiding & protecting our troops during the conflict in Afghanistan, America would not abandon them. This Administration is betraying that promise, deporting them to potential torture & death.”
Thousands fled war and persecution in Afghanistan
In September, Trump’s administration finalized a last-minute reprieve to avoid the closure of a camp in Qatar that houses more than 1,000 Afghans who assisted America’s war effort or are the relatives of U.S. service members. The administration extended for nine months the life of Camp As Sayliyah, which had been due to close Sept. 30 at the end of the U.S. budget year.
Upon entering his second term, Trump, a Republican, paused his Democratic predecessor’s Afghan resettlement program as part of a series of executive orders cracking down on immigration, including dramatically altering refugee admissions to focus on white South Africans.
The refugee changes left thousands of people who fled war and persecution — and had gone through yearslong vetting processes to start new lives in America — stranded at places worldwide, including the base in Qatar.

title: 20-year-old man dressed as zombie accused of stabbing 2 people at a coffee shop, police say
text:
AUSTIN, Texas (KEYE) - A man dressed in zombie makeup and clothing that looked like a Halloween costume is accused of stabbing two people Wednesday night at a coffee shop in southeast Austin, according to police.
The stabbing happened at Buzz Mill Coffee around 9 p.m. Wednesday.
According to the Austin Police Department, 20-year-old Shanor Temple Grace then left in a pickup truck. APD said he hit an unoccupied Tesla Cybercab.
Officers arrested Grace a short time later as he walked on a nearby trail, APD said. He is facing two counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.
Both victims were taken to a hospital. One had life-threatening injuries, and the other had non-life-threatening injuries. Both are now in stable condition.
Detectives are working to determine whether Grace knew the victims. Police have not said what led to the disturbance.
The stabbing comes as APD is urging people to take precautions around Halloween.
Asked whether police see criminals use Halloween costumes to commit crimes, Cmdr. Christopher Juusola of Austin police said:
“No, that’s not something that we normally observe downtown. And again, I think that one’s just related to it’s Halloween time. People are going to costume parties, and that’s what caused that to occur.”

title: Veazie mobile home park joins pilot to replace oil furnaces with heat pumps
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
VEAZIE, Maine (WABI) - Dawn Bisson, a nine-year resident of Greystone Mobile Home Cooperative, invited neighbors to her mobile home deck Saturday to share their struggles with affordability as heating costs rise while temperatures fall.
“I worry about my coworkers, my children, my grandchildren, and the people who live in this park,” Bisson said.
Greystone is the third park to join a pilot program run by Efficiency Maine aimed at lowering heating bills for mobile homes. It joins Arundel’s Shady Oaks and Lewiston’s Fox Run mobile home parks in the program.
Sen. Mike Tipping, D-Penobscot, said prices and housing conditions are creating a crisis this winter.
“We have the highest prices ever, we have the oldest housing stock in the country, and it is creating a crisis this winter,” Tipping described. “But what we’re hearing right now is really concerning. People are looking at kerosene that is over $7 a gallon, oil that’s over $6.”
Since mobile homes often do not have the same insulation as houses and usually heat with the more expensive kerosene, Tipping said “it’s often the people that can least afford it that are facing some of the highest costs right now.”
Residents expressed frustration Saturday over running out of fuel and having to choose between paying for lot rent, medicine or heating their homes.
If fuel runs too low, residents risk frozen pipes, which stops all water flow and plumbing.
Bisson said she has applied to Efficiency Maine’s Mobile Home Initiative after seeing her neighbor benefit from the program. The Maine Labor Climate Council has helped with outreach and installation efforts for the program.
“Part of what we do is introduce Efficiency Maine’s Mobile Home Initiative, which replaces the oil furnace in a mobile home with a ducted heat pump system,” Jake Norris, coordinator of external organizing for the Maine Labor Climate Council, said. “When we think about heat pumps, we quite often think of a mini split where you have the head on the wall and heats one room. This initiative, it heats the whole entire house and it uses duct work to heat the home.”
Norris said eligible residents must be low income, and their mobile homes must pass an energy audit to be considered. Those who receive MaineCare, HEAP, TANF and SNAP are also eligible.
Through Dec. 31, installation costs are offset by a $13,900 rebate, leaving homeowners with a $1,000 copay.
Norris added that Efficiency Maine’s Green Bank can help finance the copay at 0% APR.
“While your electricity bill does rise, you’re not paying for any oil,” Norris said. “With the price of electricity, it is relatively stable when we talk about compared to oil and gas.”
Bisson said the gathering Saturday was meant to remind neighbors that they are not alone and that resources to support them this winter are available.
“A lot of people in this park have no hope and you have to provide hope if they don’t have it,” Bisson said.
To learn more about the Mobile Home Initiative, visit Efficiency Maine’s website or Maine Labor Climate Council’s website.
Veazie’s Greystone Mobile Home Cooperative joins Arundel’s Shady Oaks and Lewiston’s Fox Run mobile home parks in the pilot program.
If you are in need of heating support this upcoming winter, Tipping advised to reach out to your local Community Action Program for resources.

title: Pro-Israel groups are spending big on Maine’s Senate race. Will it matter to voters?
text:
At a crucial moment for U.S.-Israeli relations, a major pro-Israel lobbying group has dropped millions on Maine’s U.S. Senate race, according to campaign finance data — throwing its support behind Sen. Susan Collins’ reelection bid.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, is a group that endorses and puts money behind pro-Israel candidates. It is far and away the largest donor to Collins’ campaign and leadership PAC this year, Federal Election Commission data shows.
The group has contributed about $2.8 million so far — more than her next 20 top donors combined, according to data compiled by OpenSecrets, a nonprofit campaign finance tracking organization.
While her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, made a point to disavow AIPAC donations at the start of his Senate campaign, he has in recent months accepted some $250,000 from J Street, a left-leaning Zionist group that has endorsed his campaign and listed the race as a “priority” to win.
Zionist groups are broadly defined as those that support establishing and in some cases expanding a Jewish state in the Middle East.
The spending is especially noteworthy given that Israel has not been a major discussion point in Maine’s crucial Senate race. Only 5% of Maine voters ranked foreign policy and affairs as their most important issue, according to a September poll conducted by The New York Times, the Portland Press Herald and the Siena Research Institute.
But while it may not be voters’ top issue, the next senator’s stance on Israel clearly matters a great deal to America’s closest ally in the Middle East.
The wider pro-Israel lobby has been a powerful force in American politics for decades. But its presence has become increasingly fraught since Israel launched its offensive in Gaza following Hamas’ attack on Oct. 7, 2023.
The Israeli bombing campaign in Gaza has been deemed a genocide against the Palestinian people by an independent United Nations commission, though the Israeli government and many pro-Israel groups dispute that label.
In that time, backlash against the pro-Israel lobby has grown on both the left and the right.
AIPAC did not respond to emailed questions about its support for Collins. J Street’s national political director, Lexi Goldwyn, said the group is backing Jackson because it believes he “will be a champion of peace for Israelis and Palestinians alike.”
“Troy Jackson’s moral clarity on issues surrounding Israel-Palestine stands in sharp contrast to Susan Collins, who has co-signed blank-check support for Netanyahu’s extremist policies for decades,” Goldwyn said in a statement.
Though both AIPAC and J Street are pro-Israel, the latter is generally more critical of the Israeli government and military. The group describes itself as “pro-Israel, pro-peace, pro-democracy,” and has accused AIPAC of backing “deeply unqualified, antisemitic and anti-democracy candidates.”
The amounts given to both Collins’ and Jackson’s campaigns constitute relatively small portions of their respective war chests, which each contain upward of $20 million. The totals also don’t include donations to outside super PACs supporting the candidates, which have cumulatively raised hundreds of millions of dollars — largely to back Collins.
Much of AIPAC’s support for Collins came in the form of individual contributions routed through the committee, as did J Street’s contributions to Jackson.
Many large ideological groups have developed extensive fundraising networks that galvanize individual donors to contribute millions of dollars to preferred candidates, raising far more money than the groups themselves and their associated PACs could contribute directly.
A LONGTIME ALLY VS. A FRESH, UNCERTAIN FACE
Collins and Jackson have taken markedly different stances on Israel.
Collins has been a staunch supporter for much of her 30-year congressional tenure. She has consistently voted to send billions of dollars in military aid to Israel, and has helped defeat resolutions to block such funding — though she has opposed President Donald Trump’s proposals to annex and redevelop Gaza.
“I will always stand with the Jewish community and with Israel, our closest ally and the one true democracy in the Middle East,” Collins said in a video this month.
A spokesperson for Collins’ campaign said Maine’s senior senator has always been an ally of Israel. She noted that Jackson’s predecessor in the race, Graham Platner, had been dogged by allegations of antisemitism for having a Nazi-linked tattoo and cited Jackson’s controversial comments regarding the term “genocide” as reasons pro-Israel groups are backing Collins.
“Given Graham’s and Troy’s strident comments about Jewish groups and the tattoo and Holocaust blunder, it should surprise no one that Jewish Americans are strongly supporting Susan Collins,” Collins’ communications director Blake Kernen wrote in an email.
Jackson drew the ire of some Jewish community groups last month after saying that Maine Jews don’t like to use the term genocide to describe Israel’s actions in Gaza “only because they’re Jewish” — a comment he subsequently apologized for.
The Democrat has opposed funding Israel’s military. Many of his backers, including Maine-born children’s entertainer Ms. Rachel, have cited that stance as a core tenet of their support.
Jackson’s stance on the conflict in Gaza has shifted slightly over the campaign. Jackson posted to X in July that he would flatly oppose all military support for Israel. But at a campaign event in September, Jackson said he only opposes U.S. funding for “offensive weapons” in Israel. He reiterated that at a debate this month.
Jackson’s campaign said he has been consistent in describing the Israeli government’s military actions as a genocide and that he will work to fight antisemitism and bring “lasting peace, freedom, and security for Palestinians and Israelis.”
“Troy rejects AIPAC’s money because he opposes giving Netanyahu a blank check to wage war in Gaza,” spokesperson Maggie Amjad wrote in an email. “Susan Collins, meanwhile, is bankrolled by AIPAC and has repeatedly voted to keep billions in military aid flowing to Netanyahu despite warnings from human rights organizations and the United Nations.”
AN UNPOPULAR WAR
Israel and its military actions in Palestine have become increasingly unpopular as the war has marched on. A Gallup poll earlier this year found that more Americans sympathize with Palestinians in the Middle East than Israelis for the first time in the firm’s decades of polling on the issue.
That sentiment has presented itself in Maine, too. Though few Mainers say it’s their top concern, a survey by the University of Massachusetts Lowell and YouGov earlier this year found a majority, 66%, oppose sending additional military aid to Israel. Just under half said America’s close relationship with Israel hurts U.S. interests.
At the same time, the number of anti-Jewish hate crimes spiked immediately following the Oct. 7, 2023, terror attacks and has modestly risen in the time since, according to FBI data.
In March, a man drove a car into a Michigan synagogue and lit the building on fire. In June 2025, a man threw Molotov cocktails at a group of pro-Israel demonstrators in Colorado. Weeks prior, two Israeli diplomats were shot and killed on the streets of Washington, D.C.
But many critics of Israel’s government and its military actions have drawn a sharp distinction between opposing the ongoing conflict and being antisemitic. It’s not inherently hateful, they’ve said, to criticize a government accused of such atrocities as Israel’s.
“I promise I will always listen and work to approach these conversations with the care and respect they deserve,” Jackson said in a statement late last month. “In the U.S. Senate, I’ll fight antisemitism and work for lasting peace and security for Palestinians and Israelis.”
While the Senate has repeatedly rejected measures to block arms sales to Israel, the margin has grown thinner with each new vote. An April resolution to halt some military aid to Israel was ultimately defeated, but it received 40 votes in favor — more than any that came before it.
As opposition to Israel’s government and its actions in Palestine grows, it’s likely that more similar proposals will be made in the future. And in a closely divided body, whether Maine’s next senator supports or opposes such measures may prove crucial in determining if the U.S. continues to support Israel’s war in Gaza.

title: First Parish offers ‘Election Eve Vigil’
text:
All are welcome to this non-partisan, media-free hour of music, word and sacred silence
PORTLAND – First Parish Unitarian Universalist in Portland will open its doors for an Election Eve Vigil from 5 to 6 p.m. on Monday, Nov. 2 to offer the public a non-partisan, media-free, worshipful space where they can rest in the midst of a tense election cycle. Visitors are invited to come and go as they please, to light a candle, say a prayer and enjoy intervals of readings and music. Musical interludes will be provided by pianist Sara Sturdivant and vocal quartet Una Voce.
Rev. Norman Allen commented, “We hope that people of all political persuasions – and none – will join us during this quiet, contemplative time. It’s a chance to escape the media coverage, campaign ads, and political pundits and to remember everything that connects us. Our beautiful old Meeting House is the perfect place to experience the truth that we’re all in this together, that we’ve come through tough times in the past, and that we’ll come through them again.”
First Parish has a long tradition of serving the greater public. Among its many social justice endeavors, it hosted the city’s emergency warming shelter for two years and currently works with community partners to distribute meals to the unhoused twice a week, while also offering a monthly community dinner. The congregation is a proud participant in the Greater Portland Multi-Faith Organizing Group and the Unitarian Universalist Association. It practices a liberal faith that affirms the “inherent dignity and worthiness” of all people and advocates for a “free and responsible search for truth and meaning.” Worship services are offered every Sunday at 10 a.m., with vespers held on second Wednesdays at 6:30 p.m., October through May. For more information, visit www.firstparishportland.org or call 207-773-5747.

title: Letter: We can reduce money in politics
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
We are living through what is projected to be the most expensive midterm election ever. According to opensecrets.org, more than $71 million has been spent on Maine’s congressional elections so far, shattering the previous record for midterm spending. And nearly 83% of those contributions came from out of state.
All that money is paying for months of nonstop political ads, mailers, and negative messages, leaving many of us feeling more divided than ever.
But here’s some good news: Americans are united in our concern about unlimited spending in election campaigns. In a May Pew Research Centre survey, voters across parties ranked the role of money in politics as the biggest problem the survey tested — above health care costs, inflation, crime, immigration, and the federal deficit.
Citizens did not choose the system we have today. Decades of federal court decisions created it by sharply limiting what lawmakers can do about election spending.
There is a solution, and it’s gaining momentum. A proposed constitutional amendment would restore the authority of voters and our elected representatives to set reasonable rules for money in elections. H.J. Res. 191 has been introduced in Congress with Republican and Democratic support, and Maine has called on Congress to support this amendment, joining 24 other states across the country.
Don’t let another election season leave our voices drowned out by elite out-of-state donors. Learn more about the proposed amendment and urge your elected representatives to take action.
Rebecca Buyers
Sweden

title: Teacher who fought gunman during deadly Oregon school shooting releases first statement
text:
BEND, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A teacher who fought with the gunman during a deadly school shooting earlier this month in Oregon has released her first statement since that tragic day.
On Friday, Bend-La Pine Schools released a statement from Cassidy Schutz, who is a certified learning specialist at the elementary school.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said Schutz threw her cellphone at the shooter that day and wrestled him for the shotgun he had at Silver Rail Elementary School.
Her actions have been praised for helping save lives and assisting students’ father Kaylub Giamanco in taking down the armed teen.
Schutz’s statement in full:
“There are no words to describe the depth of sadness I am feeling following the events of October 15th. This is not a story. This is a horrific and heartbreaking tragedy, and it is our real lives.
My thoughts are with those who were lost, their families, those who were hurt, and those who were there that day. My heart is with you.
It all happened so fast, and I wish with everything in me that we had more time. The pain of this loss I will carry with me forever.
There are no words for this unimaginable reality we are facing. My focus is on these families, our team, our school, and my own healing.
As I continue to navigate this, I ask that you please give me the time, space, and privacy I need to heal. I will not be making any additional public statements at this time.”
The shooting occurred on Oct. 15 when police say a 16-year-old former student went into Silver Rail Elementary and shot into a special needs classroom.
Teacher Megan Lambert, 25, was killed along with students Rhoam Summer, 5, and two other children, ages 8 and 11. The shooter was also killed.
Another teacher, Becky Drury, and a 7-year-old girl were shot and survived the shooting.
