title: Will federal election monitors remain neutral?
text:
Federal election monitors are coming to Maine. The DOJ has done this for decades. So, under normal circumstances it should be no cause for concern. But these are not normal times. The Trump administration has already signaled plans to contest close election losses with its suit to deny a Democratic election victory in Alaska, and demands that states use flawed lists of supposed non-citizen voters.
Will Trump’s law enforcers remain neutral if Troy Jackson wins the Senate seat? Hopefully, the monitors will do what they have done in the past, ensure elections are conducted according to existing law — not impose new interpretations of how states should conduct their elections. We’ll see.
The concern over federal monitors could prove to be a tempest in a teapot. Or it could be the beginning of the end of democracy as we have known it.
Raymond Michalowski
York

title: Elias Lindholm’s OT goal lifts Bruins pat Blackhawks
text:
BOSTON — Elias Lindholm scored in overtime as the Bruins rallied from a two-goal deficit in the third period to top the Chicago Blackhawks 5-4 and extend Boston’s home winning streak to five games.
Mason Lohrei scored to pull Boston within a goal and Morgan Geekie’s second goal of the season with 12 seconds left in the third period sent the game into overtime.
Ryan Greene and Connor Bedard scored in the third period as the Chicago Blackhawks took a 4-2 lead. Anton Frondell had his second career two-goal game for Chicago.
The Blackhawks came into the game with the worst power play in the NHL, converting on 4 of 40 opportunities and were 0 for 11 on the power play on the road. However, it took Frondell just 11 seconds to give Chicago the lead after Will Borgen was whistled for a delay-of-game penalty.
Goaltender Michael DiPietro kept Boston in the game with key saves as the Bruins were outshot 28-13 in the first two periods. He stopped a Bedard shot from the slot with 2:09 left in the first period. Geekie, who hasn’t scored in his previous nine games, hit a shot off the post late in the first period.
David Pastrnak scored on a breakaway in the first period for his 428th career goal, passing Patrice Bergeron and moving into sole possession of third place on the Bruins’ career goal-scoring list. Casey Mittelstadt and Mason Lohrei also scored for the Bruins.
Frondell redirected Tyler Bertuzzi’s wrist shot from the point past a surprised DiPietro early in the second period for his second career two-goal game. DiPietro, coming off his first career NHL shutout, kept it a one-goal game with a point-blank save of 500-goal scorer Patrick Kane midway through the second period. The Bruins tied the game when Mittelstadt took a feed from James Hagen and snapped a shot past Arvid Soderblom.
Up next
Blackhawks: Host Avalanche on Monday.
Bruins: Host Vegas on Monday.

title: Trump lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday letter is dismissed with prejudice
text:
A federal judge on Saturday threw out President Donald Trump’s multibillion-dollar lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to wealthy financier Jeffrey Epstein.
U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice.
The ruling said the lawsuit was “grasping at straws” as it attempted to “manufacture” flaws in the Journal’s investigative reporting.
When a case is thrown out “with prejudice,” it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.
The lawsuit was over a story the Journal published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter that the paper said bore Trump’s name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein’s 50th birthday.
The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Trump.
The letter bearing Trump’s name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, “Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret,” according to the newspaper.
Trump denied writing it and called the story “false, malicious, and defamatory.”
The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami, accused the paper and its reporters of having “knowingly and recklessly” published “numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements,” which, it alleged, caused “overwhelming financial and reputational harm” to the president.

title: Clear and cool Halloween
text:
Clear and cool Halloween
Clear and cool Halloween
Saturday starts on the cooler side with breezy conditions in the morning and early afternoon. Wind gusts could reach up to 25 mph, which will make temperatures in the low 50s feel like the upper 40s. Skies will stay nice and sunny until the evening, when cloud cover will begin to increase around sunset.
Trick-or-treaters should keep in mind that layers may be needed for Halloween costumes. Temperatures will be in the low 40s this evening as you are heading out to collect candy, and overnight will be chilly.
Temperatures tonight will dip into the low 30s and 20s, making for a very cold start on Sunday morning. Clocks fall back an hour tonight, so you will gain an hour of sleep and the sun will rise an hour earlier as well.
Sunday will be sunny and slightly warmer in the mid to upper 50s. Temperatures really warm up on Monday, when conditions could reach the mid to upper 60s. The warm trend will continue into the workweek, and we are watching some shower chances at the end of the week.

title: Public, private funds lock in protections for western Maine forest
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Winter snow in Maine’s Chadbourne Tree Farm helps replenish local streams and underground aquifers, which feed into the Sebago watershed and provide drinking water for more than 200,000 people in the greater Portland area. (Adobe Stock) Listen to this story HERE Oct 31, 2026 By Kathryn Carley Conservationists are celebrating the permanent protection secured for more than 27,000 acres of […]
Winter snow in Maine’s Chadbourne Tree Farm helps replenish local streams and underground aquifers, which feed into the Sebago watershed and provide drinking water for more than 200,000 people in the greater Portland area. (Adobe Stock)
Listen to this story HERE
Oct 31, 2026
By Kathryn Carley
Conservationists are celebrating the permanent protection secured for more than 27,000 acres of forest in western Maine.
The land serves as an important corridor for wildlife to northern forests and will continue to provide year-round recreational access to a connected trail network.
Tom Duffus, vice president and Northeast representative for The Conservation Fund, said various land trusts and multiple public and private funders worked for years to ensure the area remains free of development.
“Here in the state of Maine, our tradition and our culture is that we help our neighbor and we work with each other to get bigger things done, and that’s exactly what has happened here,” Duffus explained.
Year-round outdoor recreation has grown increasingly important to Maine’s economy, contributing nearly $4 billion in 2024, while supporting more than 32,000 jobs.
The project removes the boundary between the popular skiing spots of Sunday River and Mt. Abram, turning the area into a single, connected outdoor destination. The effort began in 2020 with the purchase of the 15,000-acre Chadbourne Tree Farm near Bethel, which is rich with red oak and white pine trees.
Duffus pointed out the area will remain a working forest and the land will still provide timber and pulp. He noted the work done by multiple partners and agencies shows it is possible to preserve a forest and grow a local economy.
“By securing large-scale working forests, we’re able to contribute to the long-term sustainability of some of these communities and the mills and the jobs that are provided by the land,” Duffus said.
Natural resource leaders said forests also serve as powerful water filters. The Chadbourne Tree Farm sits at the head of the Crooked River, the largest tributary to Sebago Lake, which provides drinking water for some 250,000 people in the Greater Portland region.
Duffus added the value of the efforts in the face of climate change is to support the region’s biodiversity and build resilience across the landscape.

title: Woman says protest was free speech after arrest for allegedly blocking robot’s path
text:
PHILADELPHIA (WPVI) — A Philadelphia woman was arrested after allegedly blocking the path of a delivery robot.
Police said witnesses called to report a disturbance earlier this month between Carolyn Marvin and an Uber delivery robot in Philadelphia.
“I have been protesting them whenever I saw them by standing in front of them and preventing them from going forward,” Marvin said.
Police said Marvin was arrested for disorderly conduct after she ignored officer commands to move out of the robot’s path.
Marvin said she was there “to publicly demonstrate on a public sidewalk my protest against delivery robots.”
Marvin said she believes her actions are protected free speech and plans to keep protesting the robots.

title: Maine football falls to Rhode Island in overtime, 14-13
text:
SOUTH KINGSTOWN, R.I. (WABI) - The Maine football team lost to Rhode Island, 14-13 in overtime, on Saturday.
Tyson Grimm opened the scoring by intercepting Caden Drezek and returning the pick 84 yards for a touchdown to give the Rams a 7-0 lead they held until the fourth quarter.
Rashawn Marshall scored the game-tying touchdown run from 25 yards out with 12:48 left to play in regulation.
The Black Bears and Rams played into overtime.
Nick Laughlin ran in a one-yard score to give Maine a 13-7 lead, but Patrick Conserve blocked the ensuing extra point.
Rhode Island’s Marquis Buchanan caught a 25-yard touchdown on the Rams’ overtime possession.

title: Police corporal killed in ‘freak’ motorcycle crash remembered by wife, father
text:
AUTAUGA COUNTY, Ala. (WSFA/Gray News) - An Alabama woman says she just had two and a half weeks with her husband before he was taken away from her in a motorcycle crash.
“I’m waiting for him to walk through the doors,” newlywed bride Chloe Greiner-Davis said.
Greiner-Davis’s husband, Dakota Davis, was a corporal with the Prattville Police Department.
The 25-year-old was killed after a wreck on his motorcycle, something Davis’s wife and father say was a freak accident with no one to blame.
According to loved ones, motorcycles were a hobby for Davis and something he had a passion for since he was a kid.
“I was so upset that he got a motorcycle, but I knew it was his calling,” Greiner-Davis said. “My biggest thing was you could be the best driver on this planet, but other people just don’t know how to drive.”
Davis was described as a family man who was intentional with his words and found real purpose in his job as a police officer protecting and serving the public.
“A man of few words, and he meant what he said. Deep into the heart. He didn’t say it unless he meant it,” his father, Paul Davis, said. “Very outgoing young man, but a man of few words. You know, he loved his family, loved playing sports.”
The emotions remain raw as the family prepares for a funeral on his favorite holiday: Halloween.
Paul Davis shared a heartfelt message for this son through tears:
“He is loved, and he is missed.”
For Greiner-Davis, the message to her husband is simple:
“I just want him to know that I love him. So much. I just love him so much.”
Greiner-Davis said she has been left to navigate mortgage payments and moving expenses without the love of her life, all while continuing to work toward her master’s in elementary education.
Thankfully, the community has already stepped up, raising thousands of dollars in support.

title: Mamdani says Trump agrees to grant visa to mother of Ghanian teen killed in Bronx shooting
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said on Saturday in a social media post that after talking to President Donald Trump, he has agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a 15-year-old immigrant from Ghana who was shot to death earlier this week.
The White House did not immediately respond to an email from The Associated Press confirming the administration would be issuing the visa.
The teen, Javits Frimpong, was on his way to school in a Bronx neighborhood shortly before 9:30 a.m. Thursday when he was shot in the abdomen, New York City police said. He was pronounced dead at a hospital later that day. No arrests have yet been made, and the killing remains under investigation.
“The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away,” Mamdani wrote Saturday on X. “Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately.”
“All of New York City is mourning this tragedy,” he said.
Frimpong arrived in the Bronx from Ghana a year ago to be with his father and begin a new life in the United States, according to U.S. Rep. Ritchie Torres, a Democrat from the Bronx.
Frimpong was on his way to school when he was shot, Torres wrote on X.
“Our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him,” Torres said. “Every child in the Bronx deserves to walk to school without fearing for their life, and no parent should ever have to endure what Javits’s father, Thomas, is enduring now.”
Thomas Frimpong described his son as a quiet teen who spent much of his time on his cellphone. He told reporters that several days before the shooting he learned his son was being bullied at school.
“It was the principal who told me,” Thomas Frimpong said. “He said two guys are disturbing my son so he has suspended the two guys. My son is at school. He’s innocent, so I call him. I talk with my son, he said ‘dad, I’m OK.’ ”
Foreign Minister Sam Okudzeto Ablakwa said in a post on X that Ghanaian officials in New York are coordinating with local authorities and that the foreign ministry “will work tirelessly with U.S. authorities to ensure justice is secured.”
Trump has clamped down on immigration during his second term, including suspending the processing of visas from 75 countries.

title: Susan Collins is not the rainmaker we’ve been led to believe
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A common consideration among those on the fence about Sen. Susan Collins’ candidacy is the idea that she brings home the bacon for Maine.
Let’s look at the data.
According to analysis by Federal Funds Information for States (a project of the National Governors Association and the National Conference of State Legislatures), in 2025 Maine received $3,346 in federal funds per capita, of which $2,280 was Medicaid.
That puts Maine’s rank at #21 of the states, or #22, not counting Medicaid; solidly middle of the pack, and hardly commensurate with what you might expect of the Chair of the Appropriations Committee. Susan Collins’ rainmaker status is vastly overstated.
Chris Carlson
South Portland

title: Troy Jackson supporters anxious but hopeful days before election
text:
Election 2026
Visit the BDN election page for our latest coverage of local, state and national races.
BANGOR, Maine — Troy Jackson’s campaign emphasized voter turnout Saturday in one of his last events before Election Day in a tight race against U.S. Sen. Susan Collins that has some supporters on edge.
He addressed about a dozen workers and a group of reporters at a campaign field office in the former Bangor Sandwich Company storefront that afternoon, where staffers were training and supplying volunteers to canvass. Supporters knocked 50,000 doors last weekend alone, according to the campaign.
Jackson’s short speech focused on his campaign’s central message of fighting for working people. He railed against President Donald Trump, Elon Musk and other billionaires, framing Tuesday as a “change election” that’s about more than himself as a candidate.
“We will not outspend them, but we will outwork them,” he said.
In brief comments to reporters who stopped him afterward as he departed across Hammond Street for another event, Jackson said the race is tight and Collins is a strong candidate, but he’s confident and believes the election will come down to voter turnout.
Recent polls have given him slim or single-digit leads over Collins, who is seeking reelection to a sixth term in a race that could determine control of the Senate. Jackson became the party’s nominee in July after Graham Platner dropped out of the race following a sexual assault allegation.
In the last race for the seat in 2020, Collins’ Democratic challenger, Sara Gideon, consistently polled ahead of her but lost the election.
That memory, and polling indications that this year’s race appears tighter, has some supporters nervous three days before the election. But they also said things have changed since 2020 and feel the sitting senator’s image as a moderate has continued to erode; polling has also suggested Collins faces a tougher environment this year.
Maddie Johnson, of Bangor, said as she stopped into the office for more canvassing materials that most people she’s talked to — which, this close to election, are those who haven’t made up their minds — still seem ambivalent about who they’ll vote for. Some aren’t excited about Jackson, but support other Democratic candidates down the ballot.
Remembering Collins’ surprise victory over Gideon in the last race is “nerve-wracking” for Johnson. Collins has been in office longer than Johnson has been alive, and things have only seemed to get worse, she said.
But she thinks Gideon and Jackson are much different candidates — Jackson has a tougher, everyman personality with more populist appeal, in Johnson’s view — while Collins is six years older now with six more years of “failures” under her belt.
In the final days before finding out whether that will lead to a different outcome, Johnson is focused on doing what she can do to try to bolster local turnout.
“It’s definitely a stressful election,” she said. “I know it’s going to be a tight race.”
Katy Bolduc, another canvasser from Bangor, was also worried about Tuesday.
Most of her door-knocking interactions have been positive, she said, though the attack ads Collins supporters have poured millions into are proving effective. Other people have wanted to talk to her as a listening ear about the deep, long-running anxieties over the country’s trajectory, Bolduc added.
By 2020, people were no longer seeing Collins as the moderate senator she had developed a reputation to be, Bolduc said, also citing the senator’s votes that have helped Republicans and support Trump policies, such as her vote in favor of $70 billion in ICE and Border Patrol funding earlier this year.
She also thinks this race is different from the Gideon contest, though she felt positive about that candidate’s chances at the time.
“I am a little anxious. Everyone is,” Bolduc said. “…But I’m hopeful.”

title: Federal officials investigate fire at beleaguered police department in Mississippi
text:
A fire Saturday morning damaged the building of a beleaguered police department in Mississippi that has drawn outrage from the community in recent months after an officer shot and killed a 1-year-old.
It was unclear what caused the fire at the headquarters of the Senatobia Police Department and whether it was intentionally set. The U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives and local agencies are investigating.
The Associated Press has reached out to the fire department, police department, and the Tate County Sheriff’s Office for comment.
Firefighters were dispatched to the city’s police department at 4:58 a.m. to respond to smoke in the building, the Senatobia Fire Department said in a statement, and crews were able to quickly knock out the fire. There were no details on the damage.
The Senatobia Police Department ignited anger in the community of 8,000 after an officer fired into a vehicle and killed 1-year-old Kohen Wiley in June while investigating a shoplifting call at a Walmart.
Wiley, who is Black, was in the vehicle with his mother, who was unharmed, and her friend, who was seriously injured. The two women denied having stolen anything, and no charges have been filed against them.
In September, the police chief was fired after reporting by The New York Times, Mississippi Today and Verite News alleged that he used racist slurs in private text messages. Earlier this month, the officer involved in the shooting resigned, though he was cleared of criminal wrongdoing by the Mississippi Attorney General’s office after its probe concluded his use of force had been justified.
Senatobia is about 40 miles (65 kilometers) south of Memphis.

title: Maine shipbuilders and their union brass split over Susan Collins and Troy Jackson
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Visit the BDN election page for our latest coverage of local, state and national races.
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson are closing their race with a fight over thousands of Maine shipbuilders, pitting a five-term senator many rank-and-file workers credit for keeping their shipyard busy against a career labor organizer.
The International Association of Machinists’ Maine State Council unanimously endorsed Jackson in July, aligning with many other Democratic-affiliated unions. But its Local S6, which represents more than 4,000 Bath Iron Works employees and backed Collins in 2014, has stayed out of the Senate race for the second straight cycle.
The split at BIW distills the campaign. Collins is running on seniority and the federal money she has steered to the shipyard as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, while Jackson’s politics are rooted in the labor movement, including close ties to the local’s parent union.
Days before the election, rank-and-file workers and union leaders remain at odds over the future of perhaps Maine’s most famous employer. Its roughly 6,800 workers include commuters from more conservative inland towns. Many are working-class men, a group President Donald Trump has dominated in recent years.
“The sentiment inside the shipyard does not match the endorsement from IAM,” Ray Gauthier, a Collins supporter, said Friday. “It’s appalling to me that anybody who works at the shipyard would not support her.”
Jackson has been endorsed by more than 20 unions, and Local S6 was behind his third-place gubernatorial run. Its 2014 endorsement of Collins in a race she easily won over Democrat Shenna Bellows was the first time it had backed a Republican, according to her campaign.
The IAM paid Jackson $90,000 as a consultant from March 2025 until August, after he won the Senate nomination, according to his financial disclosure. In 2019, while working for the union’s Lisbon office, then-Senate President Jackson warned BIW that lawmakers could reconsider a $45 million state tax break over its hiring practices.
The Collins campaign pointed to a September letter from more than 100 BIW workers, organized by Gauthier, crediting her with helping bring in almost $11 billion in Navy contracts since 2020. It also cited $300 million this year in wage enhancements, shared with Ingalls Shipbuilding in Mississippi, and money for training, child care and housing. The congressional delegation celebrated a federal decision this month clearing the yard for another destroyer.
Jackson, who told reporters in Brunswick on Wednesday that he would push for more ships in Maine rather than Mississippi, has called what Collins has brought the state a “pittance” compared with Trump administration cuts. Hours later at the shipyard’s South Gate, Collins pointed reporters to the workers.
“Ask a lot of workers at BIW,” Collins said.
Jackson and IAM allies argue that Collins could do more for the shipyard when she has too often voted with President Donald Trump. Dave Sullivan, who worked at the yard for nearly four decades and is now IAM’s general vice president for the Eastern Territory, told voters at a Jackson event this month that Collins is “horrible on shipbuilding.”
He pointed to how the Navy has split destroyer work between the two yards that build them. Under a 2023 multiyear deal, Ingalls is building seven destroyers to BIW’s three, after a 2018 deal gave Ingalls six of 10. Sullivan did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Gauthier countered that Ingalls, which builds a wider variety of ships, has greater capacity. Defense News reported in 2023 that the split reflected Ingalls’ faster delivery as Bath dug out of a backlog.
Jackson’s support for union workers is well known, Gauthier added. But he argued that Jackson’s progressive stances on social issues and immigration enforcement may rankle members who have long backed Collins.
The Jackson campaign says labor outreach has been central to the former logger’s bid and that he would keep pushing for more ships and funding for BIW.
“Troy is a strong supporter of BIW and the Local S6 union shipbuilders,” David Farmer, a Jackson spokesperson, said. “That won’t change, period.”
Tim Suitter, president of Local S6, did not respond to requests for comment. He recently told The New Yorker that “we have a very, very strong union ally in Troy Jackson,” but suggested Collins’ argument on seniority was on the mark.
“Is he going to go in and sit on the Appropriations Committee as a freshman?” he asked. “Nope.”

title: Cape Elizabeth boys soccer starts fast to knock off York in B South semifinal
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
YORK — Max Hayward said he began to develop his ability for long throw-ins last year. He tried it once in practice and it went pretty far. Hayward has a possible theory on why he can throw a soccer ball unusually far.
“Maybe because swinging a baseball bat is kind of like throwing and I do that a lot. I’m not really sure how I do it,” said Hayward, a Varsity Maine All-State baseball player this past spring.
However it happens, it’s a major weapon for the seventh-seeded Capers and led to their first two goals in a 3-2 Class B South boys soccer semifinal win at No. 6 seed York on Saturday. Hayward scored the Capers’ third goal on a direct kick, showing he has power in his legs, too, with a first-half blast from at least 30 yards.
Cape Elizabeth (8-6-2) will play No. 1 Yarmouth (14-1-1), the defending state champion, in the regional final Wednesday at Falmouth High. It will be Cape’s first trip to the regional final since 2023, when it lost to Yarmouth, 1-0.
OH, THOSE THROWS
York coach Julie Johnson said her team was well aware of Hayward’s ability to turn a seemingly harmless ball out of bounds into a dangerous situation. But, Johnson said, it’s also something that’s hard to prepare for in practice.
Hayward’s first long throw-in found Max Nudd’s right foot, and Nudd tapped it home for a 1-0 lead three minutes into the game.
“My teammate, Max Backman, did a good job of boxing somebody out and it kind of rolled to me and I just tapped it in,” Nudd said.
York’s Zach Tremblay tied the game minutes later when his inward-curving corner kick was mishandled by Cape goalie Cam Branch and went into the net.
Cape regained the lead on a similar play. Hayward zinged a throw across the goal mouth that went into the net. The officials ruled after a brief discussion that the throw barely glanced off York keeper Orrin Culp Dechant’s raised hand, making it a goal.
Hayward’s direct kick goal came with 17:32 left in the first half for a 3-1 lead.
York (8-6-2) cut the margin to a goal with 31:37 to play on a goal by Robert Dickson after a missed clear by the Cape defense.
“I thought scoring that second goal early would calm us down and I felt our body language and belief got better after scoring that goal, but I think the urgency kind of took over for all of us,” Johnson said.
Most of the rest of the game could be described as two similar teams charging hard for loose balls and then kicking it forward, with little sustained possession. In the waning moments, Cape midfielder Sam Turner and Nudd on the outside wing were able to win balls and keep possession to burn valuable seconds off the clock.
YARMOUTH UP NEXT
In the regular season, Yarmouth beat Cape Elizabeth, 4-1, in the season opener and 4-0 in the rematch. Yarmouth rolled to a 7-0 semifinal win Saturday against Freeport, scoring six goals in the first half.
“The second one, we played them at home and were even for the first 60 minutes, and then they kind of took over for the last 20 minutes,” said Cape coach Ben Raymond. “I think we’re a better team than we were then. That’s one of the strengths our group has. We get better as the season goes on.”

title: 60-year-old rescued from Adirondacks stood in same spot for 7 hours, rangers say
text:
KEENE, N.Y. (WCAX/Gray News) — A 60-year-old Canadian man was rescued from the Adirondacks after he stood in the same spot for seven hours, forest rangers said.
The rescue happened Oct. 21 on the Mount Colden Trap Dike.
Satellite beacon sent after loss of crampons
Forest rangers said the man sent a satellite beacon around 6:30 p.m. after he lost his crampons on an icy ledge. The loss left him stranded.
Forest rangers reached the man around 1 a.m. and began the rescue.
Ranger describes securing the man
“When I got out to him and was trying just to get him secured to me, the thought went through my mind, ‘If we both slip before I have him clipped in and on my tether, he’s dead. He’s like, gone,’” Forest Ranger Jenna Curcio said.
Trap Dike route
Forest rangers said the Trap Dike route is a fourth-class climb. Several deaths have been linked to the climb over the years.
Rangers encourage hikers to do their research and come prepared.

title: ‘I choked that dog out’: Rescue operator charged with felony animal torture
text:
BUTLER, Ind. (WPTA/Gray News) - An Indiana woman who operated an animal rescue is facing criminal charges.
Butler authorities say Kayla Dillenburg, 30, strangled a dog she pulled from an Indianapolis shelter, profited from donor pledges meant for its care, and admitted to the killing on a recorded phone call.
Dillenburg, who operated Welcome Home Canine Rescue out of her residence, has been charged with torture or mutilation of a vertebrate animal, a felony, and fraud.
Court documents stated Dillenburg pulled 21 dogs from Indianapolis Animal Care Services over a 10-day period in late April.
Investigators allege she targeted animals carrying high financial pledges raised by social media donors trying to save shelter pets from euthanasia.
According to an affidavit of probable cause filed by DeKalb County Sheriff’s Office Animal Control Officer Erika Hedge, the investigation began in May after an IACS volunteer rescue coordinator raised concerns that dogs transferred to Dillenburg had gone missing and her rescue’s social media accounts were taken offline.
Authorities said the criminal charges center on a dog named Motley. According to court documents, he was scheduled for rescue and had $925 in public pledges.
Investigators said Dillenburg picked Motley up from Indianapolis on April 28, but records showed Motley died and was dropped off for cremation that same day.
Court documents stated Dillenburg told an Indianapolis donor that Motley was alive and had an approved adoption lined up.
However, investigators concluded Dillenburg deceived the donor into paying for care after the animal was already dead.
Court documents stated Dillenburg claimed Motley died at her home of pneumonia and denied euthanizing him.
Investigators contacted a former friend of Dillenburg. That friend told deputies that Dillenburg approached her in April with a scheme to make money by pulling dogs with high pledges from Indianapolis.
Investigators obtained a recorded phone call between Dillenburg and the friend in which they say she admitted that she “choked that dog out” after claiming he went after her child.
Officer Hedge outlined the basis for the felony and misdemeanor charges:
“I believe Kayla Dillenburg has knowingly, intentionally, and recklessly tortured and/or mutilated a dog in her care because, by her own admission, as stated in a recorded conversation, she strangled Motley to death.
Kayla told the public that Motley died from pneumonia, but there was no record of Kayla providing him medical care or a diagnosis ... I believe Kayla has knowingly and intentionally committed fraud by obtaining dogs from Indianapolis Animal Care and Control for the sole purpose of making a profit off their pledges.”
While the criminal affidavit directly addresses Motley’s death, animal welfare advocates and volunteers still have questions about the other animals Dillenburg allegedly acquired.
Court records confirm that IACS received paperwork for only four of the 21 dogs.
Dillenburg told police that a mother dog and her puppies were placed with a rescue in Michigan, but investigators noted she never produced paperwork or proof to verify the claim.
Officer Hedge said she could not comment on the status of the remaining animals because the investigation remains active and ongoing.
Hedge added that she has received numerous calls from additional people coming forward with information as news of the charges continued.
Court records showed Dillenburg appeared before a judge on Friday. She entered a plea of not guilty, and a public defender was appointed to represent her.
Dillenburg was released on her own recognizance and scheduled to appear in court again in January 2027.

title: Remember: All citizens get to vote
text:
I was struck by the comment from Maine Wire’s Steve Robinson in last Sunday’s paper about people bringing “jobless Somali bums to vote” (“State monitoring complaints of voter harassment in Lewiston,” Oct. 25).
The scornful disapproval here misses something fundamental about our country. Whether one is a citizen by birth or by the hard work of earning it, every election America lives out its amazing creed: citizens get to decide how they shall be governed. Whether a citizen has a job or not, whether they were born here or not, whether they have the approval of Mr. Robinson or not, they get to vote.
It is a marvel worth celebrating every election. The proper emotion here is not scorn, Mr. Robinson. It’s gratitude that, unlike countless millions from the past and the present, we get to live in such a country.
Michael Hayashida
Auburn

South Portland should reject the proposed $88.6 million bond to relocate its police and fire departments.
For years, the city has grossly neglected existing facilities, then asked taxpayers to finance expensive replacements. Neglected athletic fields helped produce a $4.6 million bond. Meanwhile, basic services like trash collection are in jeopardy, and a $204 million Mahoney School renovation (which included police and fire) — developed without a budget and featuring a rooftop garden — has merely been postponed, not abandoned.

title: Rising health costs and coverage changes are big concerns for older adults as Election Day nears
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Barbara Weigand could not have prepared more for retirement. She stayed healthy and saved diligently for years.
This year, though, a shoulder surgery and a bladder cancer diagnosis have really tested her finances. She recently withdrew $4,000 from her retirement account to cover medical expenses associated with her cancer treatment.
“On my monthly income, I would not be able to afford my new medical expenses,” says Weigand, 83, who lives in North Canton, Ohio. She is currently on a Medicare Advantage plan and was searching for new coverage as Medicare’s open enrollment period began in October.
For older adults in the United States, the rising cost of healthcare is hitting where it hurts most — their pocketbooks. With Medicare costs, prescription drug prices and long-term care expenses weighing on household budgets, their concerns could carry significant political weight heading into Tuesday’s elections.
Weigand is part of a reliable voting bloc; 83% of voters over age 50 say they’re extremely motivated to vote in the midterms, according to an AARP poll conducted in early October. Their concerns over managing healthcare costs put the issue of affordability squarely in the spotlight.
Here are some of their biggest healthcare concerns — and how Weigand sees them.
Worry No. 1: Changes to Medicare plans
THE SITUATION: Open enrollment for Medicare plans began in mid-October, and enrollees are facing a slew of changes that will go into effect in 2027.
During the enrollment period, people are considering higher Part D out-of-pocket caps, the end of temporary federal Part D premium subsidies, and new drug price negotiations. Additionally, in some states, insurers put caps on the number of people who can enroll in Advantage plans, pulling out of markets or eliminating plans that people have come to rely on.
Juliette Cubanski, director of KFF’s program on Medicare policy, told The Associated Press that the open enrollment period offers enrollees “an opportunity to evaluate the coverage they have and see if there might be better options for them in terms of accessing the care that they need, at possibly a lower cost.”
While Weigand is grateful to have the mental acuity to do the research and the spiritual community that she relies on, she worries about other older people who are struggling to plan for the year ahead. “There are so many changes, and a lot of people my age who don’t know where to start,” she says. “What do they do?”
Worry No. 2: The affordability of prescription drugs
THE SITUATION: The Trump administration has made lowering drug prices a priority in its effort to show Americans that it is tackling soaring costs. Republican President Donald Trump has struck multiple most-favored-nation drug deals with pharmaceutical companies and has launched the discount drug website TrumpRx, among other steps.
In September, his administration said all 50 states would join in on a program set to provide most-favored-nation pricing to some drugs within the Medicaid program, bringing the net price of selected drugs down to prices paid in certain other countries.
Still, the cost of prescription drugs prevents some people from filling prescriptions. A KFF survey from March found that about 4 in 10 U.S. adults say they have not taken their medication as prescribed in the past year due to costs.
Weigand is considering rationing her drugs to save money. “I’ve been thinking — if I could just do this every other day rather than every day to make the medicine last longer,” she says. “Isn’t that sad?“
The KFF report says about 1 in 5 people surveyed had cut pills in half or skipped doses of medicine in the prior year because of the cost.
Worry No. 3: The costs of long-term support
The costs of receiving long-term care — whether from spouses, home-care aides or friends — have risen steeply for retirees.
An AARP report released Wednesday that examines out-of-pocket caregiving expenses finds that family caregivers are spending nearly 60% more supporting a family member or friend than five years ago. They spend an average of $11,508 a year supporting a family member or friend, compared with $7,242 in 2021, according to the report.
Nancy LeaMond, AARP’s executive vice president and chief advocacy officer, said “we’re already hearing from our members about healthcare affordability — its prescription drug costs, caregiver costs, co-pays, premiums,” she said. “Not only are we trying to help family caregivers with their finances, but also to get them the kind of information they need to help their loved ones.”
These worries are top of mind for older people. About one-third of Americans over 50 provide regular care to an adult relative or friend with a health issue or disability, according to a national poll on healthy aging conducted in September 2025 by the University of Michigan.
Worry No. 4: The solvency of Social Security
The Social Security Administration announced this month that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will rise by 3.6% beginning in 2027. That translates to $75 extra per month for the nearly 72 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and about 7.3 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
The agency faces an approaching bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.
The Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report from June states that Social Security’s combined trust funds, which cover old age and disability recipients, will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.
With 2034 not far away, the upcoming Congress will be on the hook to determine how to shore up the program.
Matt Hogan, a partner at the Impact Research polling firm, has this advice to candidates in the closing days of the midterm campaign: “Regardless of party, to make inroads with these voters, Social Security and Medicare should definitely be part of their messaging.”

title: Explore the unexplained at cryptozoology museum’s new Bangor home
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Spooky season is a time to venture into the unknown, and the International Cryptozoology Museum specializes in just that.
Exploring the elusive has been author Loren Coleman’s life work, leading to the museum’s opening in Portland in 2003.
Over the summer, the museum moved into a larger building on Broadway in Bangor.
Christopher Packard, the museum’s assistant director, describes cryptozoology as “the science for people who are interested in the edge of science, what might be out there.”
Housing more than 20,000 artifacts, including 250 Bigfoot prints, the museum explores the science and pop culture of creatures whose existence remains unverified.
Here, you’ll find classic cryptids such as Mothman and werewolves, alongside local Maine lore such as the Allagash alien abductions and Pamola, the traditional Wabanaki winged moose that protects Katahdin.
Cryptozoology also includes out-of-place animals and living fossils once thought extinct or entirely unreal.
“The colossal squid and the giant squid are things that were depicted in art of sailor stories and on maps. And then, of course, they were real, right? Like we actually found those scientifically,” Packard says.
Maine has had its share of misplaced animals.
The museum showcases the skin of the Westbrook River Monster, which turned out to be an anaconda, not a relative of Nessie. It also has the preserved foot of the Turner Terror, which had the whole town on edge and was found to be just a Husky mix.
“But then these [Turner Terror] sightings had been going on for years, right? So like, is that all the explanation?” Packard questions.
For museum leaders, whether these creatures are real or folklore doesn’t matter as much as the impact on the people who experience them.
“Part of cryptozoology is, for better or worse, hoaxing. Some stuff is fake, right? And that’s part of the story of cryptozoology. We have stuff about pop culture and movies, and we tell those stories,” Packard says.
“Throughout human history, people have always had these stories, and they’re similar stories. They’re stories about big, hairy, giant men in the forest. They’re stories about water serpents in lakes and rivers and oceans. They’re stories of fearsome beasts of all sorts and giant birds. And I don’t think it’s necessarily a coincidence that people, no matter where they are, have these same stories,” details Packard. “People should wonder what’s out there, what’s real, and they should go out and try and have experiences.”
You can find the International Cryptozoology Museum at 490 Broadway in Bangor.
Regular admission is $10 for adults and $5 for kids 12 and younger. The museum frequently hosts author events and more that are free to attend.

title: A papal audience before tipoff: College basketball takes over Rome
text:
A papal audience before tipoff: College basketball takes over Rome
Pope Leo XIV is set to hold a private audience on Saturday with basketball teams from his alma mater, Villanova, and fellow Catholic university Notre Dame, plus thousands of traveling American fans in town for the season opener.
A total of about 7,000 people streamed in Saturday to the Paul VI audience hall inside the Vatican after a special private Mass in St. Peter's Basilica.
Related video above | Pope Leo XIV leads Sunday prayers as he recovers from lung surgery
The audience precedes the U.S. college basketball season opener in Rome on Sunday. The Villanova and Notre Dame men’s and women’s teams will play a doubleheader at the 11,000-seat Palazzo dello Sport — which is located about a half-hour drive from the Vatican.
The event has been dubbed the Eternal City Tip-Off and was created to honor the first American pope.
Leo graduated in 1977 with a Bachelor of Science in mathematics from Villanova, the Augustinian school near Philadelphia. He was born in Chicago — not all that far from Notre Dame, which is located in South Bend, Indiana.
Like popes before him, Leo has praised the value of sport for both physical and spiritual development, calling sport a “school of fraternity” that nurtures friendship, respect and teamwork.
“May those who play, train or cheer discover in sport a universal language that brings cultures together, unites peoples and sows respect, solidarity, and personal growth,” Leo said for his June prayer intention, which was dedicated to sport.
Leo, who himself is an avid tennis player and sports fan, has also warned about how the win-at-all-cost mentality of sport has contributed to episodes of doping, match-fixing and other forms of corruption.
The Rev. Robert Dowd, president of Notre Dame, acknowledged Villanova had something of an edge considering it counts the pope as an alumnus. But in an interview Saturday, he said the occasion to bring both teams together with all their fans in Rome for a papal audience and season opener was “amazing.”
“That could be a little challenging, but I know that the pope is a pope for all of us, and so I’m grateful,” he said. “I know in a particular way the pope talks about the importance of bridge building, and I’m sure he’ll be a bridge builder when we play each other.”
Philadelphia Archbishop Nelson Perez celebrated a private Mass for traveling fans in St. Peter’s Basilica on Saturday morning, and asked the thousands of people in the pews to give a round of applause to the players. The English-language liturgy was unusual in that it had all the trappings of a papal Mass celebrated at the main altar and televised live by Vatican Media.
Asked about the upcoming games on the papal plane during a recent trip to France, Leo said, “They tell me that the people coming to the match, 90% are Villanova and 10% Notre Dame, so the voice of the people of God will be very strong on the Villanova side.”
Leo is an avid Chicago White Sox fan, and has been known to follow basketball, too.
“He will know who they (the players) are. He’s a true, blue Villanovan,” said the Rev. Rob Hagan, Villanova’s longtime team chaplain. He said Leo used to attend Villanova games at the Palestra, the Philadelphia arena known as “The Cathedral of College Basketball.”
Sunday's games coincide with All Saints' Day, a major Catholic holiday.

title: I’m ready to get to work for Portland
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ilma Lopez lives in Riverton and is a candidate for Portland City Council in District 5,
which includes North Deering, Riverton and Deering Center.
My kids are eight years apart, and in that time, Portland has changed from a city where I didn’t worry about the safety of my kids outside, to a city where I do. Part of the change comes from the actions — or inactions — of our City Council. This motivated me to run for office, so I could help be part of the solution.
I grew up in Venezuela with my mother and brother. We didn’t have enough food to eat, but my mother always made sure the kids had enough. Twenty-four years ago, when I was nearing college age, my mother sold our tiny apartment to raise the money to send me to culinary school in the U.S. (So, no, I am no fan of ICE, but that is not why I’m running.)
As a chef, I worked in some of the finest restaurants in New York, Madrid and elsewhere. I met my future husband in New York, and 15 years ago we moved to Portland, where we are raising our family. We now own two restaurants — Chaval and the Ugly Duckling — that are part of Portland’s vibrant food scene.
As a small business owner, I understand the challenges of hiring and keeping good employees, living within a budget and meeting the expectations and needs of our customers. I want to bring that same customer-service mindset to the City Council. Because I view the job first and foremost as working for the people of my district — which includes Riverton, North Deering and Deering Center.
I also want to bring to the council a mindset of living within our means, because every resident of Portland struggling with rising property taxes has to do the same. I don’t profess to have all the answers, but I will ask the right questions.
Part of what we need is more housing and more business to help spread out the property tax burden so that less falls on individual homeowners or renters, and to help rents go down. Yet, there are times when our City Council seems anti-business, as evidenced by a growing number of empty storefronts in our city.
And while our council says they want more housing, they sustain policies like inclusionary zoning that have slowed housing development. Worse, our council has adopted policies that encourage housing in the wrong places that hurt the strong neighborhoods we have. Yes, we need more housing, but we should focus on our arterials where there is public transit and where density makes sense.
But, the number one reason I am running is public safety. In September, I was in one of our restaurants in the evening with several employees when someone broke in. We called the police, but the person got away. It was scary but emblematic of a growing epidemic of homelessness and substance use disorder. Like everyone else in Portland, I am tired of stepping over needles. And I’m tired of being harassed. I’m tired for myself, my kids and all of us.
Also in September, Mayor Dion declared “enough is enough.” I agree, which is why I am so honored that Mayor Dion agreed to endorse my candidacy this month. I look forward to working with Mayor Dion to fix what seems so broken.
I am also honored to have the support of longtime public servants like former mayors Jim Cohen, Nick Mavodones and Dave Brenerman, former state senator Heather Sanborn, former councilor John Coyne, also from Riverton, current councilor Pious Ali, owners of restaurants and small businesses throughout the city and the New American Leaders Action Fund.
As I always tell my kids at night, if you see something wrong, step up. And that’s what I’m doing. I want to hear from you, and I hope to have your support for City Council, District 5.

title: UMaine men’s hockey swept by BU
text:
Tynan Lawrence’s second goal of the third period tied the game with 2:12 left in regulation, and Caleb Malhotra scored 1:35 into overtime as Boston University rallied for a 3-2 win over UMaine in a Hockey East game Saturday night in Boston.
The Black Bears (4-4, 0-2 Hockey East) were on the verge of salvaging a split of the weekend series after BU (6-2, 4-2) cruised to a 7-2 win Friday night, but they couldn’t protect a 2-0 lead in the third period.
Lawrence cut into the deficit with 13:04 remaining in regulation, drilling a one-timer from the top of the right circle past Black Bears goalie Albin Boija while the Terriers had a 4-on-3 power play.
Maine jumped in front early, starting with Rowan Calvert’s first college goal at 5:37. The freshman forward from Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan, whacked in the rebound of a Jaden Lipinski shot.
Max Scott made it 2-0 at 14:45, scoring from the slot after a pass from Lee Parks.
Maine goalie Albin Boija finished with 24 saves. BU’s Mikhail Yegorov stopped 34 shots.

title: Letter: Penobscot should adopt rules before allowing a pub
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I believe the question before Penobscot is not whether to modernize a supposedly backward town. It is whether to authorize a new commercial use with no rules to govern it.
Jamie MacNair says her proposed pub would be small, with limited hours. She also says she is open to expanding it. Good intentions are no substitute for enforceable limits, and the upcoming vote wouldn’t set hours, control noise or stop future expansion.
Blue Hill offers a cautionary tale. As the Bangor Daily News has reported, that town fought all summer with a bar called Blaze over outdoor expansion and noise, eventually suing over land-use violations. But Blue Hill had regulations to invoke. Penobscot does not. Its own comprehensive plan acknowledges that the town lacks commercial-development regulations and needs commercial site-plan review.
I believe there is also a safety concern. Southbound drivers on Southern Bay Road reach the market on a difficult turn, with limited visibility and excessive speed. A bar would add more cars, and the possibility of drivers who have been drinking, to this corner.
Residents can reasonably ask the town to pause new commercial development while it adopts these rules. This is not opposition to business. It is common-sense planning.
Before changing its liquor laws, Penobscot residents should ask: Is the town ready to manage the consequences?
John Zeaman
Penobscot

title: Mother of 2 dies after falling through 30-inch gap in bridge median
text:
KANSAS CITY, Kan. (KSHB) — A Kansas mother of two died after falling 40 feet from a raised trafficway bridge.
Police said surveillance video shows Monica Rivera, 24, walking across the lanes of traffic early in the morning Oct. 23 after exiting a car.
Police: No foul play involved
Rivera was seemingly unaware of a 30-inch gap in the median that allowed her to fall. Police said no foul play was involved.
Family asks for privacy
Rivera’s family said she leaves behind two young daughters, ages 3 and 5.
“It’s tough for us to see all this evil stuff on social media of things that everybody says happened, and the mom knows the truth,” Jacqueline Gallo, the grandmother of Rivera’s two daughters, said.
“Let us grieve now in private. Let us protect these girls. Just give us our time now. That’s all we ask,” Gallo said.
Transportation department response
The Kansas Department of Transportation said there are no plans to cover or otherwise modify the gap in the roadway.

title: What we know about the Lewiston voting footage federal prosecutors are reviewing
text:
Election 2026
Visit the BDN election page for our latest coverage of local, state and national races.
Federal prosecutors are reviewing security footage of early voting at Lewiston City Hall but would not say whether they are investigating the interpreters a conservative outlet accused of coaching Somali-American voters.
A spokesperson for U.S. Attorney Andrew Benson confirmed only that the footage is under “review.” The Justice Department generally does not confirm or deny whether it is investigating. Lewiston City Clerk Kathy Montejo said Friday she was not aware of any investigation but did not respond to later messages seeking further comment.
The dispute comes four days before an election with the U.S. Senate race between Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson at the top of the ballot. Lewiston, Maine’s second-largest city, has some of the state’s most contentious local politics and is a major battleground in the 2nd Congressional District.
The accusations came from The Maine Wire, the media arm of the conservative Maine Policy Institute. Its report was based on City Hall security footage obtained through the state’s public records law. The Maine Wire said the footage covered early voting starting Oct. 13. In-person absentee voting ran statewide from early October through Thursday.
The Maine Wire said the video shows staffers from local immigrant-serving groups coaching voters and, in some segments, filling out ballots for them. Maine Wire editor Steve Robinson wrote in a follow-up Friday that he had reviewed about 20% of the footage.
The report rested largely on a statement from Benson, an appointee of President Donald Trump who previously served as a state prosecutor and lower-court judge.
“We review all evidence concerning complaints of voter intimidation and election interference, including the video from Lewiston’s early voting at City Hall,” Benson said, according to the newsletter. A Benson spokesperson declined to elaborate on the statement when contacted by the Bangor Daily News.
Only U.S. citizens can vote in Maine. Under federal law, a voter who needs help because of a disability or because they cannot read or write may be assisted by a person of their choice. A federal appeals court ruled in 2017 that this includes an interpreter.
Maine law mirrors that. A voter who cannot read or mark a ballot because of a disability, illiteracy or religious faith may ask another person to help read the ballot or mark it according to the voter’s wishes. The helper cannot be the voter’s employer or a union officer or agent. They may not tell the voter how to vote or otherwise influence the voter’s choices.
Trying to influence a voter who is marking a ballot is a Class E misdemeanor, carrying up to six months in jail and a $1,000 fine. Federal law also bars intimidating or interfering with voters.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows, a Democrat, told the Maine Morning Star last week that her office had not received a credible report of an interpreter engaging in illegal electioneering. She issued a Friday statement that did not say whether her office knew of an investigation.
“Every citizen has the right to vote free of intimidation or interference,” Bellows said. “A citizen for whom English is a second language has the right to have an interpreter present. We are proud of the checks and balances that safeguard our elections.”
Lewiston Mayor Carl Sheline, a Democrat in a five-way Tuesday race for his third term in the nonpartisan office, said the city’s Somali community “has been harassed nonstop by political provocateurs and agitators all throughout early voting.”
“It’s imperative that every eligible voter be able to make an informed decision and cast their ballot without intimidation or interference,” he said in a statement. “It’s worth noting that ballots are only printed in English and not all citizens can speak and read English.”
The Justice Department plans to send election monitors to polls in Lewiston, Portland and South Portland on Tuesday. They are the first federal observers sent to Maine since Bellows took office in 2021, the Maine Morning Star reported. Bellows told WMTW the department gave no reason for adding South Portland.
The deployment is part of a national effort by the Trump administration that includes more than 1,000 monitors. It follows Justice Department lawsuits seeking unredacted voter rolls in Maine and other states. A Trump-appointed judge dismissed the Maine suit in May.

title: Lily Robbins returns home to Searsmont after months-long hospitalization
text:
SEARSMONT, Maine (WABI) - A local first responder received a hero’s welcome Friday as family, friends, and emergency crews from across the state lined the streets to celebrate her return home.
Lily Robbins, a volunteer EMT with the Searsmont Fire Department, returned to town months after suffering critical injuries while battling the May 15 fire and explosion at Robbins Lumber.
Robbins had been undergoing treatment and rehabilitation at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston before making the long journey north. A statewide convoy of first responders escorted her through Maine, culminating in a celebration at her home station in Searsmont.
Along the route, supporters gathered with signs and waved as the procession passed. Searsmont Interim EMS Chief Amy Drinkwater said the outpouring began the moment they left Massachusetts and grew as they traveled north.
“Honestly, all the way from Boston all the way through, she had people waving, signs, and then we all, you know, got together at the Augusta Civic Center and she was just overwhelmed when she got there. She’s like, ‘Oh my god, look at all these people!’ But it was great. It was great to have so many departments here to welcome her,” Drinkwater said.
The May 15 blast at Robbins Lumber claimed the lives of three people and injured 10 others.

title: Patriots try to bounce back against young Dolphins
text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. — Most of the current players on the Miami Dolphins roster haven’t faced the New England Patriots very much.
But coach Jeff Hafley wants his young team to understand the significance of divisional matchups — especially its game Sunday against a Patriots team that has accomplished nearly everything Hafley hopes the Dolphins will some day.
“I’d be lying to you if I (said I) didn’t feel like I had to teach them about division play and the division,” Hafley said. “All these guys watched them play in the Super Bowl last year. I mean, we have 15 rookies. I hope they all watch the Super Bowl — who knows nowadays — but I’d imagine they all understand that team just went to the Super Bowl and they’re the reigning champs in our conference.”
Vrabel had praise for Hafley and the Dolphins, who are coming off their first win of the season after beating the New York Jets. It was the best game of the season for quarterback Malik Willis, who threw for 208 yards, two touchdowns and rushed for a score.
“They play extremely hard. I have a lot of respect for what Jeff’s done,” Vrabel said, “and probably a unique set of circumstances, which they’ve kind of admitted to. … I think that they’ve continued to improve, and I know that they’re probably — and they should be – excited to play at home in front of their crowd. We’ll have to go on the road inside the division here and continue to improve.”
Vrabel coached Willis in Tennessee during the Miami quarterback’s first two seasons in the NFL.
The Titans traded up in 2022 to draft Willis out of Liberty in the third round while Ryan Tannehill was still the starter. Willis made three starts as a rookie, never throwing for more than 99 yards. The following season, Tennessee drafted Will Levis, and Willis was eventually traded to Green Bay.
“I can’t say anything but great things about Coach Vrabel,” Willis said. “He taught me a lot about ball in general in this league, at this level. So I can’t be any type of way toward him. Obviously, he had to do what the best thing was for his team at that point, in his opinion. You can’t control other people’s opinion. All you can do is keep working and when your opportunity arises, take advantage of it.”
The Patriots haven’t been quite as dominant this season as they were last season, when they went 14-3 en route to a Super Bowl appearance.
They’re coming off a loss at Chicago that snapped a three-game winning streak, and Vrabel said this week there may be some things the team isn’t able to improve on this season.
“When I look at it from my perspective, it’s like, this is what we’ve seen from seven weeks,” Vrabel said Wednesday, “and we can yell and scream about it until we’re blue in the face, or we can coach it, and it’s maybe not going to change.”
Need to know
New England (4-3) at Miami (1-5)
When/where to watch: 4:25 p.m. Sunday, CBS
Latest odds: Patriots by 7 1/2
Against the spread: Patriots 4-3; Dolphins 2-3-1
Last week: Patriots lost to the Bears, 30-24; Dolphins beat the Jets, 28-25
Last meeting: Patriots beat Dolphins 38-10 on Jan. 4, 2026, in Foxborough, Massachusetts
Series record: Dolphins lead, 63-55
Matchup to watch
Dolphins rushing offense vs. Patriots run defense. Miami enters Sunday with the seventh-best rushing offense in the league, averaging 131.5 yards per game, but they’re going against a tough opponent in the Patriots, who have the eighth-best run defense in the NFL. New England is allowing just 95.3 yards per game but is coming off an outing in which it allowed the Bears to rush for 116 yards. The Dolphins have rushed for more than 100 yards in five straight games, which is the longest streak in the NFL. Running back Ollie Gordon has a rushing score in each of the past four games, and Willis has elevated the run game with his scrambling ability.
Stats and stuff
• Since 2000, the Patriots are 113-49 against AFC East opponents and 29-23 against the Dolphins.
• The Patriots scored more than 30 points in both wins against Miami last season. It was just the sixth time in the series that New England has done that.
• New England is expected to have its starting secondary of cornerbacks Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis III, and safeties Kevin Byard and Craig Woodson available for the first time since Week 1. Gonzalez has missed two games because of a shoulder injury, Davis four games because of a neck injury, and Woodson one game (shoulder). Byard is the lone member of the group to start all seven games.
• The Patriots downgraded receiver A.J. Brown (ankle/knee), running back TreVeyon Henderson (illness) and offensive tackle Marcus Bryant (ankle) to out for the game.
• Hunter Henry needs one more touchdown reception to move into sole possession of third place on the team’s all-time list for TDs among tight ends. He has 28.
• Miami’s defense has not allowed a rushing touchdown in three consecutive games, the longest such streak in the league, while ranking fifth in goal-to-go defense and ninth in third-down defense against the run.
• The Dolphins do not score a lot of points — their 16.3 points per game is 30th in the league — but they have scored on six drives that covered 70 or more yards, including three against the Jets last Sunday.
• Hafley coached Vrabel’s son, Tyler, for three years at Boston College.
• Left guard Kadyn Proctor and cornerback JuJu Brents are in the concussion protocol after reporting symptoms earlier this week. Neither player practiced Wednesday.

title: Consensus looks elusive at G20 talks in Atlanta after objections to Russia cancel group photo
text:
Consensus looks elusive at G20 talks after objections to Russia cancel group photo
Top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies appeared far apart on critical global security issues as they began meeting Friday in Atlanta, after European objections to Russia’s participation forced the U.S. hosts to cancel the traditional group photo.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio pulled the plug after several European officials threatened to boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such gatherings. But he still opened the talks with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”
Related video above: Energy experts predict high gas prices will stick around
He pointed to disruptions to global energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation and said many are posing “severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order.”
Yet there was no sign that the G20 diplomats could come to a consensus on many of the most contentious issues they face. Among them are the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, U.S. tariffs and Chinese machinations in the South China Sea. All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as uncertainty about trade.
No joint statement expected from the diplomats' meeting
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding — as is its opposition to Poland's membership in the G20.
Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration's not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will likely prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up Saturday, participants said.
That did not surprise Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, who was representing his country for the first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.
“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.
Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month's G20 leaders summit hosted by President Donald Trump in Florida a success.
Russia's presence at G20 gathering roils Europeans
Already poor prospects for the talks worsened when the Europeans balked at being photographed with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Rubio decided to scrap the picture because he thought the controversy would be a distraction, according to two U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.
Some G20 countries had already expressed concern that the U.S. invited Russia during its heightened attacks on Ukraine, especially after Trump pushed ties with Ukraine to new lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance.
However, the State Department announced Friday that it had approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot air defense interceptors for Ukraine.
Lavrov, when asked about the planned three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. next month, told Russian reporters that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s position regarding long-range strikes against Russia “doesn’t help preparation for the talks.”
Moscow will not allow a situation in which Ukraine poses a “military threat to legitimate security interests of the Russian Federation,” he said.
Lavrov also said Russia sees no point in inviting Poland to join the G20 meeting, adding that it “violates the principles of diplomacy” and the country “adds nothing” to the grouping.
Sikorski, whose country is a strong ally of neighboring Ukraine, earlier said, “I am not the only one who does not want to be photographed with Lavrov.”
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband explicitly called out Lavrov, saying that “if we are serious about our values and our interests, we must also work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine.”
“An assault not only on Ukraine but on us all — trampling international law, sovereignty and self-determination — core principles on which we all depend,” he said.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said “there is no normality with Russia” but “we must exchange the controversies at the table here,” the German news agency dpa reported. He added that “we also must not send falsely optimistic signals.”
Lavrov has traveled only infrequently to NATO member states since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and the resulting severe sanctions were imposed on Moscow, and it is unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin will accept Trump’s invitation to attend the G20 leaders summit at his Miami golf club in December.
G20 member South Africa was not invited
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year as U.S. officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland is seeking formal membership with U.S. support.
But missing from the invite list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top U.S. officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola.
Kunene welcomed support from other G20 members that had expressed reservations about the exclusion and said South Africa was ready to participate “on an equal footing with other members” when Britain takes over the presidency next year.
The Iran war hangs over the G20 event
The U.S. has said a top priority for the meeting is resolving differences over issues related to freedom of navigation, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the South China Sea. The topic will include discussions on Iran, Russia-Ukraine and China and its smaller neighbors.
But hanging over the meeting is the prospect of new U.S. military intervention in Iran, which has put the region, including G20 member Saudi Arabia, on edge. Rubio met on the sidelines with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, as well as Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, whose country has been a key mediator.
The Associated Press has reported that U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military strikes against Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections and the possibility that Iran will retaliate against them.

title: ICE agent charged with assault for hitting a fleeing man with his car will turn himself in on Monday
text:
A federal immigration officer charged with aggravated assault after he ran over a Mexican man with his car in Houston will turn himself in on Monday, according to his attorney.
Mario Alberto Morales, a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer, struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old construction worker, with his unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as he chased Parra Hernandez through a parking lot. A grand jury indicted Morales on Friday on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.
Morales is planning to turn himself in at a courthouse sometime on Monday, David Lindenmuth, his attorney, told The Associated Press. Lindenmuth previously told the AP that the incident was “clearly just an accident” and that local officials had “invented a crime out of thin air.”
Parra Hernandez broke his leg and is recovering at a rehabilitation facility while in federal custody, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told reporters on Friday.
ICE has said Parra Hernandez ran in front of Morales’ car.
Previously released surveillance camera video shows Morales’ vehicle drive over a median and strike Parra Hernandez as he runs away.
Teare played footage from Morales’ body camera on Friday that showed the agent making sharp turns with his steering wheel. He then stops and exits the vehicle and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is lying on the ground, screaming.
“I was coming in, and I hit him with the car,” Morales can be heard saying after another ICE agent arrives.
Parra Hernandez told deputies that he fled the traffic stop when Morales started pulling on a mask, and Morales “threw the car” at him, according to a Harris County Sheriff’s Office incident report reviewed by the AP. Morales told deputies that he did not brake before he hit Parra Hernandez, but that he did not intentionally strike him, according to the report.
ICE said after the incident that the target of the operation was a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who the agency said was seen getting into a car with Parra Hernandez. Mendoza-Cervantes’ daughter told the immigrants’ rights group FIEL that her father has been dead for nearly a decade.
Morales is among a small handful of federal agents who have been criminally charged for wounding people during the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration crackdown. ICE agent Christian Castro pleaded not guilty last month to charges that he lied to the FBI after he shot and wounded a Venezuelan man as immigration agents swept Minneapolis earlier this year.
Many other ICE shootings, including some that were fatal, have not ended in charges for the agents involved.
Morales, 34, has served as an ICE agent for a little over a year, according to Lindenmuth.
Teare said on Friday that authorities have a “significant amount of information” on Morales, and that, in his experience, law enforcement agencies would not hire someone with his background. He did not elaborate.
Morales was charged with a misdemeanor in 2013 for stealing four DVDs, according to Harris County Court records. Those charges were dismissed after he paid a $270 fine and struck a plea deal.
Morales unsuccessfully ran to represent Texas’ 34th congressional district in this year’s election cycle under the name “Bam Morales,” which Lindenmuth confirmed. Morales served in the U.S. Army’s 82nd Airborne Division and later as a corrections officer and law enforcement officer, he wrote in a Ballotpedia candidate survey. He wrote that his top priorities were veterans’ rights, economic issues and service guided by the Christian principles of “compassion, integrity, service, and accountability.” He listed illegal immigration as one of the country’s greatest challenges.
Morales also wrote in the survey that he was endorsed by an organization called “Make America Godlier Again.”
Morales appeared at a 2024 Christian conference held by televangelist Johnson Suleman. In video of the conference, Morales appears to act as a Spanish translator as Suleman serves free food and “extends his touch of love to migrants.”
“I want to pray for the immigrants,” Suleman said, as Morales translated those words into Spanish. “I bless you. May the lord grant your request and open your doors.”
___
Mayes-Osterman is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues.
