title: From salmonberry harvests to traditional tattoos, Native American culture is spotlighted in November
text:
LAS VEGAS (AP) — Fawn Douglas puts an urban spin on traditional basketmaking.
Instead of using desert plants, she tightly weaves heavy conduit wire to form the base of a basket she plans to display at the new Wai Gallery in Las Vegas. There, she and her partner, A.B. Wilkinson, showcase pieces from Indigenous artists and host free art programs, from collage projects to sidewalk chalk paintings.
Douglas, a Las Vegas Paiute Tribe citizen, says she sees how art can heal and bring people together.
“They’re off their phones. They’re having actual conversations together,” Douglas said.
The gallery and IndigenousAF storefront dismantle stereotypes, including that Native Americans and Alaska Natives are a monolith and all live on reservations, she said. It opened just ahead of National Native American Heritage Month, which celebrates the diverse histories and cultures of hundreds of tribal communities across the U.S. in November.
Native American art isn’t just geometric, Douglas said, and each piece has a narrative.
A painting behind her featured a silhouetted Joshua tree and a backlit mountain range with a brilliant night sky. It’s a desert twist on Vincent Van Gogh’s “Starry Night” — and it acted as a call to action for turning Gold Butte into a national monument in Nevada.
A black-and-white underwater photograph depicts a Hawaiian dancer, seemingly floating in space. It is called “Ha’ina ’ia mai,” which translates to “let the story be told.”
Here is a collection of short stories highlighting joy in Native American and Alaska Native communities:
Families scattered after typhoon return to the land and each other
When the salmonberries are ripe in Kipnuk, Alaska, the Paul family isn’t far behind.
They are one of several families who returned to practice subsistence gathering a year after Typhoon Halong struck their village, damaging 90% of its buildings, floating some houses miles away and leaving nearly all of the community’s residents displaced.
It’s been an especially good year for salmonberries because of heavy snow last winter, locals say.
From a boat, Burt Paul scanned the tundra for the orange berries — or naunraqs as they’re called in coastal Yup’ik — like orange carpet on a sea of green grass. They giggled as the dogs ferociously defended them against two musk oxen grazing on shore.
The Pauls typically camp out for several days and pick berries. But this summer was broken up into shorter trips when Burt Paul’s scattered family could return together.
The family never misses a year of berry picking, they said.
“Coming home, seeing everyone, the community — it’s heartwarming,” Caley Paul said.
When the day ended, the family had a five-gallon bucket filled to the brim. Not as much as most years but enough for Burt Paul to make his famous naunraq pie. Enough for everyone to have a taste.
— Samantha Watson, KYUK
Her upbringing led to a lifetime of advocacy for Native children
Foster care didn’t separate Rosa Soto Alvarez from her Pascua Yaqui community.
She and her siblings were placed with another family on the tribe’s reservation in Arizona, where their foster mother served up tortillas and fry bread with pots of chile con carne. They grew up surrounded by saguaros and the sounds of relatives speaking the Yaqui language. They took road trips to powwows.
Under the 1978 Indian Child Welfare Act, tribal children taken into foster care have the right to remain with Indigenous families.
That experience has guided Alvarez’s life work. At 50, she is a mother and grandmother who has cared for 25 foster children in her home. She leads the tribe’s ICWA Committee, coordinating statewide advocacy that supports the federal child welfare law and encourages states to adopt versions of it.
Nationwide, Native children are disproportionately represented in state foster care systems.
“I’m just a rez girl trying to make a difference,” she said. “There’s so many children out there who don’t have a voice, and I know I have to be that voice.”
— Nancy Marie Spears, The Imprint
Indigenous girls secure rights for a river
A group of Indigenous girls carried a vessel of river water to the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Council and walked out with rights for the river.
The council unanimously passed a resolution this year recognizing the rights of the water system that rises in the Great Smoky Mountains and flows into the Gulf of Mexico. To the Cherokee, these waterways are known as Longperson and are a living relative.
The NAIWA Daughters, girls ages 10 to 17, brought the resolution forward after receiving training on the rights of nature, hosting community dinners, conducting surveys and meeting with council members. The Earth Law Center says it’s the first all-female-led rights-of-nature effort in the U.S.
The resolution grants the waterway five rights, including the right to flow freely and to be free from pollution.
The council later passed another resolution to raise money to remove the decommissioned Ela Dam in North Carolina, which has blocked the sicklefin redhorse, a freshwater fish, for more than a century.
“We hold the responsibility of stewarding the headwaters, so every living being downstream has water for life,” said NAIWA Daughters co-founder and Chairwoman Jasmine Smith.
— Liz Kimbrough, Mongabay
Immersion program connects students with language and culture
Sugarbush is a springtime tradition in many Native communities.
Students in the Minneapolis-based Wicoie Nandagikendan early childhood program trekked through the snow this past winter to learn about tapping maple trees and processing the syrup at Porky’s Sugarbush Camp.
The children and their parents walked past colorful buckets hanging on trees to catch the sap. They helped stir syrup already boiling in a large black kettle and helped make sugar and cakes. One student placed tobacco at a maple tree during a ceremony.
For parents like Christian Swor, the program provided his son and family an opportunity to connect with Indigenous culture and language. The early childhood program immerses children in the Ojibwe and Dakota languages.
Other cultural activities in the curriculum include how to cook dishes with rabbit or duck and how to process wild rice.
“We do hit all the state standards, but it’s like hitting all those early childhood indicators, progress and more,” said Ojibwe classroom teacher Liz Zoongwegiizhigook Zinsli.
— Chandra Colvin, Report for America corps member, MPR News
A boxer finds a home at a Native American youth center
At 67, Kerry Butler still fits into his old Tulsa Indian Youth Center boxing jacket.
He joined the team for three years in the 1970s when he was 15. The center served a vital role for Native Americans after the federal government pushed them off their ancestral homelands and into major cities to assimilate them into white society.
Many Native youth had low self-esteem in those days, but a common gathering space and boxing helped change that, Butler said.
“When you got in front of a crowd of people, and they were cheering for you, and when you got into the ring, and people were clapping, ‘Awesome! Let’s go, Kerry! You can do it!’”
“It just rose up confidence inside that you never felt before,” Butler, who is Muscogee and Cherokee, added.
The youth center no longer exists. But a nonprofit called Tulsa Indian Community Center, Inc., recently formed with a vision to provide another gathering space for youth.
More than 60 tribes are represented in the Tulsa Public Schools district.
— Brittany Harlow, Crosswinds News
Muscogee artist navigates tattoo industry and cultural traditions
Hodokii Johnson leans in closely, as they tattoo three brown lines on each of Kristin Gentry’s fingers.
One is for the strength of Gentry’s mother. One is for Gentry. And one is for Gentry’s daughter.
When all the lines are darkened, the two say a prayer.
Johnson, a 24-year-old Muscogee Nation citizen and descendant of the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes, have been interested in body art since they were a teenager to cope with mental health struggles and now sees it with greater purpose.
They’ve worked with Inchunwa, a project dedicated to healing through traditional tattoos from the southeastern U.S., and recently attended a convention highlighting Indigenous tattoo practitioners in Oklahoma City.
Giving tattoos and ancestral markings is sacred work, they say, because of the permanence and deeper meaning.
“So much of the tattoo tradition that we had has since been weeded out through the efforts of colonization,” Johnson said. “Tattoos are seen as a taboo, unholy thing. When we talk about ancestral markings, it’s rather the opposite.”
— Sarah Liese, KOSU
___ This story is published through the Global Indigenous Reporting Network at The Associated Press.

title: Margaret Chase Smith didn’t have a bachelor’s degree, either
text:
Since 1913, U.S. senators have been directly elected. Only one Maine senator, after 1913, did not have a college degree. That senator was a total failure, right? Margaret Chase Smith, ex-telephone operator, only had a high school education. In 1964, she became the first woman nominated for president by a major party convention.
Give a hard-working Mainer a chance and you never know what may happen. Judge not, lest you be judged.
Just the facts, from a Maine-born political geek.
Kevan Jonassen
Suffolk, Virginia

title: Letter to the Editor: US, Maine, and World are at an historic crossroad
Maine lobstermen lock down a top Democrat’s support days before Jackson-Collins election
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Election 2026
Visit the BDN election page for our latest coverage of local, state and national races.
A top Senate Democrat whom U.S. Sen. Susan Collins accused this week of blocking a lobstering bill told Maine fishermen in Ellsworth on Saturday that she would help move it, according to the union leader who organized the meeting.
U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Commerce Committee, held the closed-door meeting at the Ellsworth Elks Lodge with former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democrat challenging Collins in Tuesday’s election.
The bill now appears to be on solid footing in the Senate, thanks in part to one-upmanship in the toss-up race between Collins and Jackson, which could decide control of the chamber. It broke out when word of the meeting leaked this week. On Thursday, U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, the commerce chairman, said his panel would take up the bill next month and credited Collins.
“Exactly what we’re asking for was bipartisanship for the industry, and I’m pretty sure we got that,” said Virginia Olsen, the political director of the Maine Lobstering Union Local 207, who organized the event billed as an opportunity for fishermen to speak to Cantwell.
The bill, championed by outgoing U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, a Democrat from Maine’s 2nd District, would extend a pause on new federal rules meant to protect endangered whales from 2028 through 2035. It will need Democratic votes to get through the Senate, and the lame-duck session is the last chance to pass it before a new Congress arrives in January.
The fight over credit has also gotten personal. On Friday, Collins told Fox News that Cantwell worked against the Maine delegation’s effort to stop Biden administration regulations in 2022 and has been blocking the extension this year.
Her office got more specific Saturday. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller said the pause was added to the last page of the 2022 government funding bill in the final hours of negotiations. Collins started out seeking 10 years but went down to eight and then six because Cantwell kept pushing back, Keller said.
“We’re glad she flipped her position today,” Keller said.
Neither Jackson’s campaign nor Cantwell’s office commented on the Saturday meeting. In a statement to Fox News, the Washington senator called criticisms from Collins “desperate” and “false accusations.”
“I support the Northeast Lobsterman Protection Act and extending regulatory relief for Maine lobstermen through 2035,” she said. “When the Senate returns next week, I will continue to do the hard work on this bill, instead of engaging in political finger pointing.”
Olsen said the machinists saw Cantwell as helpful in 2022. Dave Sullivan, the International Association of Machinists’ general vice president for the Eastern Territory, reached out to her for help with the pause then, she said. Sullivan and the IAM are close to Jackson. The union’s Maine State Council endorsed him in July and paid him $90,000 as a consultant until he won the Senate nomination in August.
The House passed the extension 219-196 in September, with 10 Democrats in support. Golden first introduced the bill, but Republican leaders moved an identical version from U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler, R-New York, who is in a toss-up race. Golden worked with former Gov. Paul LePage, the Republican running to replace him, to lock down Republican support.
Environmental groups oppose the extension, noting the right whale population is estimated at roughly 380. Industry groups point to federal data showing more births since the first pause.
Collins’ office said Republicans plan to move the extension as a standalone bill rather than attach it to a larger package, as the delegation did with the pause in 2022. That means it would need to clear the Senate’s 60-vote threshold or pass by unanimous consent.
Cantwell and Jackson spent Friday on the water with a lobsterman on a trip Olsen set up. She noted the Saturday meeting was planned before Cruz’s announcement and was kept quiet so it would not become a political event. Reporters were not allowed in.
Olsen said Jackson “barely spoke,” mostly about getting the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to survey the Gulf of Maine.
“I didn’t want it to be a campaign event,” Olsen said. “I wanted fishermen to be comfortable speaking their thoughts, and that’s just what it was.”

title: ‘I Voted’ sticker creator talks about how it started
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The “I Voted” sticker given to people who cast ballots began with one woman, Janet Boudreau, who designed it after seeing a local county hand out a different sticker on Election Day.
Boudreau said she has long supported voting, which she described as the right and duty of American citizens to share their voice.
“This is the one day that we have to amplify what we want our world to look like, and it just irritated me and my folks, too, when people would say, oh I forgot the election,” Boudreau said.
In 1987, Boudreau owned an election supply and voting equipment company. She noticed a county in Washington state had started handing out stickers on Election Day.
“It was black and white and had an X in a square. And that’s it. And I thought, this is not inspiring,” Boudreau said.
She said she then created her own design.
“I went home and got out a blue and red pen and decided on an ellipse with a waving flag,” Boudreau said.
The sticker started in a few counties and quickly spread across the country.
“By 1992, wow, it was nuts!” Boudreau said.
Election Day memorabilia has a long history that includes pins, buttons and ribbons - including those used during the women’s suffrage movement in the 1920s.
After taking off in the 1990s, the “I Voted” sticker has led to other versions, including state-specific images and future voter patches. Contests have also invited children to design their own stickers.
Boudreau said the goal behind the sticker is to inspire Americans to vote.
“What gets me the most about this is that it’s become this badge of honor,” Boudreau said.
She hopes the sticker continues to carry meaning as a promise and a call to action every election cycle.
“So get out and vote and then spread the word,” Boudreau said.

title: Gardiner volleyball beats MDI to win Class C title
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
BANGOR — The Gardiner volleyball team was back in the Class C state championship match against the team that raised the Gold Ball a year ago.
This time, the Tigers wouldn’t be denied.
Top-seeded Gardiner swept No. 3 seed Mount Desert Island, 3-0, to win its first state championship on Saturday afternoon at Husson University.
“I think what really drove us to beat them was our energy,” said Gardiner outside hitter Lexi Ouellette. “Last year, our energy was not very high when we played (MDI). Now, we’re so much more together and we communicate much better.”
Gardiner’s attack was balanced across the floor. Senior middle blocker Lila Anderson provided multiple aces and kills, while Ouellette blocked MDI attacks with precision.
“The youth and experience meshed together is really good,” Gardiner coach Bill Boardman said. “It creates some leadership. They don’t care what grade they’re in.”
Gardiner won the first two sets, 25-20 and 25-23, then started fast in the third set, jumping out to a 7-2 lead on its way to a 25-18 score.
“They played a tough game,” MDI coach Whitney Walls said. “It wasn’t (our) best, but sometimes that’s just the way it goes. I think that they fought hard, and they played with heart.”
For the Tigers, the triumph may have been more decisive than they expected, but that doesn’t make it any less sweet.
“I knew that we were going to bring it,” said Anderson. “I knew that it was going to be tough, but we did better than I ever imagined.”
UNSUNG HERO
Both on the court and off it, Joely Cote was one of Gardiner’s most valuable players. She was able to block multiple kill attempts while securing some kills for herself.
STAT LEADERS
• MDI: Janiece Anderson (eight kills, eight aces, three assists), Ella Watson (five kills, two aces, one assist), Cora VanDongen (one kill, four aces, one block), Lanaia McDaniels (four kills, two blocks)

title: Fire destroys Presque Isle building
text:
A Saturday morning fire has taken out a building in Presque Isle.
The blaze started in the early morning at 172 Main St., according to city spokesperson Kim Smith.
The three-story building housed a business and apartments.
There are no known injuries or fatalities, and it is not yet clear how many people were displaced, Smith said Saturday.
The building is likely a total loss. State fire marshal investigators are on the scene, she said.
At about noon, smoke billowed around the structure as fire crews worked. A Red Cross van was nearby.
The roof was largely gone and firefighters trained water down on the remaining building.
Mutual aid came from Easton, Caribou, Mapleton and Fort Fairfield, Smith said.

title: Maine football falls to Rhode Island after blocked PAT in overtime
text:
Rhode Island blocked a PAT in overtime to pull out a 14-13 victory over Maine on Saturday in Pawtucket, Rhode Island.
In overtime, Maine (1-8, 1-5 Colonial Athletic Confefence) got the ball first and settled for a 30-yard field goal after two incomplete passes from Caden Drezek, but the Rams (5-4, 2-3) were called for a personal foul on the kick. Maine took the points off the board for a first-and-goal from the 6, where Malik McNeely rushed for 5 yards before Nick Laughlin scored from 1 yard out. The point-after kick, however, was blocked by Patrick Converse to left Maine’s lead at 13-7.
Rhode Island came back when Alex McClelland connected with Marquis Buchanan on second down for a tying touchdown. Ty Groff kicked the winning PAT.
Rhode Island scored the only points of the first half when Tyson Grimm returned an interception 84 yards for a score less than two minutes before intermission.
The Black Bears tied the game 7-7 with 12:48 left in the fourth quarter as a 25-yard scoring run by Rashawn Marshall capped a five-play, 48 yard drive.
Drezek was 21-of-34 passing for 149 yards while Marshall had 139 yards on 25 carries.

title: Selectmen, Boothbay Region Land Trust discussing dog park proposal
text:
The town of Boothbay and Boothbay Region Land Trust are in agreement about creating a dog park at Cross River Preserve. Nick Ullo is BRLT's executive director. He explained the trust's dog park proposal Oct. 28 during the Boothbay selectmen's meeting.
Ullo explained the trust's intent for donating a 2.8-acre Cross River Preserve parcel for the dog park. "The town would develop the property for a dog park. We are very excited about this," he said. "We've heard from people in the community about the dog park who are excited about this, and so are our trustees."
Town and land trust officials will work out the details, in hopes of a May or June town vote in 2027.
Cross River Preserve was once tax-acquired property which Boothbay gifted to BRLT after a town vote. Ullo explained an agreement in 2014 was reached where the trust would build a 1,500 square foot nature center. The structure would also serve as their headquarters. Under the agreement, BRLT had 15 years to build a structure or the land would revert back to the town; 2029 is the agreement's deadline.
So far, no structure has been built. Ullo explained the trust later decided to build the nature center and headquarters at Oak Point Farm. The trust considered building a pavilion in lieu of the 1,500 square foot Cross River Preserve building, but that didn't materialize.
Ullo asked selectmen if the dog park would serve as the building requirement under the 2014 agreement, and selectmen were agreeable.
Town Manager Dan Bryer said all the details must be finalized in January in order to make the May 2027 town meeting warrant.
In other action, selectmen approved a Coastal Maine Botanical Gardens liquor license renewal for a temporary extension of the premises for a special event.
Selectmen meet next at 6 p.m. Wednesday, Nov. 11 in the community room.

title: A great Halloween weekend weather wise
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Halloween Saturday will be a great day for outdoor events and trick-or-treating even though it will be on the cooler side and Sunday will be yet another very pleasant fall day with highs near or into the 50s. It also may be a bit breezy to start the day on Saturday but winds die off as the day goes on. It will get chilly overnight into Sunday with lows dropping to the mid 20s but overall about as good a weekend as you could ask for this time of year.
Saturday: Clear skies but cooler, overall a pleasant Halloween
It will be a cooler day Saturday with highs only reaching near or just above 50. But will be filled with sunshine. Winds will lighten up as the day goes on and it should be generally a very nice day to be outside and taking in the fall weather and doing some trick-or-treating.
Saturday night: A cold and clear night
Temps will drop off quickly on Saturday night with clear skies so if you’ve got any late night Halloween events make sure to grab your jacket because it’ll get chilly fast. Temps will drop into the mid to low 20s for a large portion of the state and winds will be light. And don’t forget to reset your clocks!
Sunday: A slightly warmer day with clear skies
It will be a few degrees warmer than Saturday and clear skies. Most places get to the middle 50s with some colder areas still stuck in the 40s. It will feel comfortable though with full sun for most. Winds will be light.
Sunday night: Near freezing for most
It will be chilly once again but probably not as cold as the previous night. Most places will be clear and drop to only the middle 30s or so with some spots into the 20s.
Monday and beyond: Placid weather continues
Monday into Election Day on Tuesday will be calm and quiet with no major weather events on the horizon. A few showers may be possible late Tuesday night into Wednesday but they look light and scattered in nature. Late next week may bring a storm but it’s a long way off and details are still hard to pin down.
Saturday: Cooler but sunny. Highs near 50. Winds NW at 10-15 mph
Saturday night: Cold with lows in the middle 20s. Winds light.
Sunday: Warmer with highs in the 50s. Winds light.
Sunday night: Clear with lows in the middle 30s. Winds light.
Monday: Mainly sunny with highs in the 50s and 60s. Light wind.

title: Ambulance driver accused of abandoning patient, said he was ‘done driving for the day’ and called an Uber home
text:
CLEVELAND, Ohio (WOIO/Gray News) — An ambulance driver is accused of abandoning a patient he was transporting to the hospital earlier this week in Ohio.
The incident happened Wednesday evening in Cleveland.
The patient was being transported to the Cleveland Clinic with chest pain when the ambulance driver got lost, told her he was done driving for the day, and called an Uber to take him home.
The driver worked for Lynx EMS, a private ambulance company, and not for Cleveland EMS.
According to Cleveland Association of Rescue Employees (CARE) Local 1975, once the driver left the patient, a Cleveland EMS unit responded to the scene.
The paramedics then administered medical care and brought the woman to the hospital, a CARE spokesperson said in a statement.
“We stand by our EMTs, paramedics and dispatchers who strive to provide the best care to anyone who is in need of it,” the CARE spokesperson added.
In a statement to WOIO, a spokesperson for Lynx EMS wrote:
“Patient safety and quality care are of the utmost importance to us and responsibilities we take very seriously. Upon becoming aware of the situation, immediate steps were taken to address the matter and ensure the patient’s well-being and care needs were addressed.
We are continuing to review the circumstances surrounding this incident and will take appropriate action based on the findings of that review. As this involves personnel and patient related matters, we are unable to comment further.
We remain committed to providing high-quality care and maintaining the trust of our patients, their families, healthcare partners, and the communities we serve."

title: Mother of 2 dies after falling through 30-inch gap in bridge median
text:
KANSAS CITY, Kan. (KSHB) — A Kansas mother of two died after falling 40 feet from a raised trafficway bridge.
Police said surveillance video shows Monica Rivera, 24, walking across the lanes of traffic early in the morning Oct. 23 after exiting a car.
Police: No foul play involved
Rivera was seemingly unaware of a 30-inch gap in the median that allowed her to fall. Police said no foul play was involved.
Family asks for privacy
Rivera’s family said she leaves behind two young daughters, ages 3 and 5.
“It’s tough for us to see all this evil stuff on social media of things that everybody says happened, and the mom knows the truth,” Jacqueline Gallo, the grandmother of Rivera’s two daughters, said.
“Let us grieve now in private. Let us protect these girls. Just give us our time now. That’s all we ask,” Gallo said.
Transportation department response
The Kansas Department of Transportation said there are no plans to cover or otherwise modify the gap in the roadway.

title: How ranked-choice voting could affect Maine’s US Senate and House races
text:
Only two names will appear on ballots for U.S. Senate and U.S. House. But ranked-choice voting could still factor into the results of two of Maine’s three congressional races.
That’s because the Senate and 2nd Congressional District races have declared write-in candidates, so voters will be asked to rank their choices among three options.
Write-in candidates face long odds of winning, but they could delay the final results of each contest, since the winner of each race must win a majority of all of the ballots cast — including those listing a write-in as a first choice and ballots that are left blank.
If no candidate wins a majority in the first round, the race will head to an automatic ranked-choice runoff, which could take a week or more to complete.
Here’s how Maine’s ranked-choice voting process works and how it could affect Maine’s top races.
WHAT IS RANKED-CHOICE VOTING?
Ranked-choice voting, approved for statewide use by Maine voters in 2016, allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference in races featuring three or more contenders.
Voters can rank as many or as few candidates as they choose. Ranking just one candidate is allowed.
If no candidate ranks first on more than 50% of the total ballots cast in the first round, then the last-place finisher is eliminated, the second-choice votes of that candidate’s supporters are reallocated to the remaining candidates, and the results are retabulated. The process repeats until a winning candidate receives more than 50% support.
Ranked-choice voting cannot be used in the general election for state-level offices because of the state constitution. It can only be used in gubernatorial and legislative primaries, as well as federal and municipal races.
WHO IS ON THE BALLOT
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson will be on the ballot for the Senate race.
Former Republican Gov. Paul LePage and State Auditor Matthew Dunlap, a Democrat, will appear on the 2nd District ballot. And Democratic Rep. Chellie Pingree and Republican Ronald Russell will be on the 1st District ballot.
Maine’s governor’s race features three candidates: independent Rick Bennett, Republican Bobby Charles and Democrat Hannah Pingree. But again, ranked-choice voting will not be used in the governor’s race.
ARE THERE WRITE-IN CANDIDATES?
In two races, yes. The Senate race has six declared write-in candidates, while the 2nd District race has one, independent Gregory Ward, of Limestone. No write-in candidates have been declared in the 1st District race.
The Senate write-in candidates are: Democrats Sigrid Ann Olson, of Cape Elizabeth, and Ashley Webb, of Farmington; independents Brent Andrews, of York, Gina Oswald, of Strong, and Michael Turcotte, of Burnham; and Joseph Steinberger of Rockland, who claims to be part of the “Faith in Humanity Party,” which is not an official party.
Write-in candidates had until Aug. 25 to declare with the state.
Any write-in votes for a candidate who did not formally declare with the state will not be counted and that selection will be considered blank.
HAS A TWO-PERSON RACE EVER TRIGGERED A RUNOFF IN MAINE?
Yes. While it’s more common with three or more candidates listed on the ballot, a runoff for a two-person race is not unprecedented here. That happens when neither major party candidate obtains a majority in the first round of voting.
In 2024, the 2nd District race between incumbent Rep. Jared Golden, D-Lewiston, and state Rep. Austin Theriault, R-Fort Kent, went to a runoff after 3% of voters did not select either candidate.
After the first round of voting, Golden emerged with 48.65% of the vote, while Theriault had 48.11%, neither of which was a majority. The Democrat held a 2,159-vote lead out of nearly 400,000 votes cast on Nov. 5 that year.
In that case, it took a week for the 2nd District ballots and memory sticks from vote tabulators to be collected and sent to Augusta for the runoff. Officials estimated the process would take three to five days to finish.
The runoff began on Nov. 12 and finished on Nov. 15, and Golden was declared the winner with 50.35% of the vote. He was reaffirmed as the winner after a subsequent recount that ended Dec. 4.
PROSPECTS FOR THIS YEAR
A similar situation could unfold this year. If it happens in the Senate race, it would be the first statewide runoff in a general election since the method was adopted in 2016.
In 2020, Collins earned 51% of the vote, despite four candidates being on the ballot. Sen. Angus King, an independent, earned majorities in the first round of voting in three-way races in 2018 and 2024.
In this year’s Senate contest, most polls show a very tight race, with Jackson, the Democrat, holding a slight lead — usually within the margin of error — against Collins.
A few polls have shown either candidate getting more than 50% of the vote. But polls reflect a snapshot in time, not a prediction of an election outcome.
Of the 26 polls tracked by The New York Times since Jackson entered the race in July, only seven put him at 50% or higher.
If that pattern holds, and enough voters choose to write-in a candidate or leave their ballot blank, the race very well could go to a runoff.
Don’t expect to know the winner of Maine’s Senate race within a week of Election Day if that happens. In the spring, it took Maine election officials nearly 10 days to determine that Hannah Pingree had won the Democratic primary for governor after a ranked-choice runoff.

title: Restaurant closure leaves a culinary and community void in the Midcoast
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Peter Imber lives in Camden.
It’s not often that a restaurant closure makes the newspaper. Many close and are hardly noticed. Not this one closure in Rockland recently, which didn’t need press coverage to make news in the Midcoast.
The odds of a new restaurant succeeding in America are not great — a quarter fail within the first year and half fail in the first five. Although that’s actually not higher than the success rate of most other new businesses, for a restaurant to succeed for nearly 20 years with its original owners is rare.
Home Kitchen Cafe in Rockland called it quits after 18 years not because it no longer attracted customers or was losing money. It had plenty of loyal patrons; having to wait before getting a table or a seat at the counter was nearly always a given. No, Home Kitchen closed because in the owners’ own words:
“This is not a post we ever thought we would make, but in today’s world, maintaining our level of quality has become increasingly challenging. Like many in our industry, we’ve faced a growing struggle to find and keep the skilled, dedicated team needed to consistently deliver the experience our customers expect and deserve. Rather than compromise what Home Kitchen Cafe stands for, we feel it’s the right time to step away.” — James Hatch and Susan Schiro.
I’ve never frequented a neighborhood bar like Frasier, Cliff and Norm did on the sitcom “Cheers,” but there was seldom a week when I didn’t make the eight-mile drive from Camden to meet friends and have breakfast or lunch at Home Kitchen. In fact, I was enough of a regular visitor that although, unlike “Cheers,” not everybody knew my name, the waitstaff did. And as long as I can remember — and that’s years — the waitstaff never changed.
In the two weeks after the announcement that the place was closing, the lines at Home Kitchen were nonstop from before it opened in the morning until it closed in the afternoon. It wasn’t hyperbole to call the place unique and special. It was. The food was good, and I mean really good, but there was more to it than that.
I feel fortunate to have the lifestyle we do in Maine but it can be deceptive if you refuse to look around. Right now, the autumn leaves have reached their peak. Income inequality among us, however, is in full bloom regardless of the season.
Was Home Kitchen an oasis where all of us at least ate in the same building? I’d like to think so. Certainly, political divisions were concealed there and perhaps that’s nothing novel for a public space. The ambiance at Home Kitchen, however, was different. Everybody was happy.
Here’s what happened to me there a few months ago that I’d claim was different. Home Kitchen also had its own bakery, just down the street from the cafe. When I discovered it sold turkey pies, an offering not on the restaurant menu, I bought one. But when I scored it before putting it in the oven at home, I was surprised that I had been given a fruit pie instead.
I returned to the bakery the next day and asked to exchange it but there were no turkey pies available and no one there at that moment who knew how to handle a refund to a credit card. I went to the restaurant, pie in tow, and was immediately reimbursed. I thought that was the end of the story.
A few weeks later, I was having lunch when one of the waitstaff came to my table and handed me a bag with a turkey pie. I protested to her that it wasn’t necessary and I wanted to pay for it but she remembered what had happened and refused my offer. Home Kitchen made a fine turkey pie.
The Home Kitchen Cafe menu was large and varied. I had my favorites: the turkey Reuben, a Vietnamese banh mi, the Cubano, fish tacos, pancakes, build your omelets. Can I console myself with the possibility that now it might be easier for me to lose a few pounds?
My absolute favorite thing to order was the huevos rancheros and it was this that chef and owner James considered Home Kitchen’s signature dish. I ate half and brought the rest home and waited a few days to part with it.
We have plenty of other places to eat where we live but Home Kitchen Cafe’s loss leaves a void that fond memories can’t fill.
What I know about myself and food is that I am a food person more than a restaurant person. The Michelin stars and the James Beard awards definitely have their place. But in the past in California before I moved to Maine, I drove a couple hours from Los Angeles for a great crabmeat sandwich at Point Loma Seafoods in San Diego. And I kept returning to Caffé Sport in San Francisco’s North Beach despite the waiters badgering me every time to order something other than the shrimp and mostaccioli that I always came there to eat.
Yes, I’m just a food person. But Home Kitchen Cafe was more than that for many of us. Not every business that closes is noticed. Not every restaurant that closes is missed. And not every business that was a restaurant is beloved. Home Kitchen Cafe was.
Adiós, huevos rancheros, and gracias.

title: Shooting at Spirit Halloween store in California leaves pregnant woman dead and 6 wounded
text:
FAIRFIELD, Calif. (AP) - A targeted shooting inside a Spirit Halloween store in Northern California left a pregnant woman dead and six other people wounded, police said.
Gunfire rang out at about 8:30 p.m. Friday inside the store, which sells Halloween costumes and decor, at the Solano Town Center in Fairfield, the city police department said Saturday in a statement on Facebook.
The shooting “stemmed from a targeted incident involving one suspect,” police said.
The woman who died was identified by police as Constance Hages, 31, and family members told authorities she was pregnant.
Three male victims ages 16, 19 and 32 were in critical condition, and a 23-year-old man was hospitalized in critical but stable condition.
Two other men, ages 19 and 43, were treated for gunshot wounds and released from the hospital.
No arrests have been made. Authorities said they were reviewing video and other evidence “to identify the individual responsible for this heinous act of violence.”
The department said no additional information would be released at this time.
“We recognize the concern and uncertainty this incident has created throughout our community, particularly with the many Halloween events and celebrations planned for today,” the department said. “We understand that an incident of this nature is frightening and deeply unsettling. We encourage everyone to remain vigilant, look out for one another, and report any suspicious activity.”
Solano Town Center, which has 130 stores and restaurants, remained open but said it was canceling its planned trick-or-treating event scheduled for later in the day “in light of last night’s event.”
“We appreciate your patience and understanding during this time,” the mall said in a statement.
The FBI’s Sacramento office said it was assisting Fairfield police in the investigation.
Fairfield, a city of some 120,000 residents, is about 37 miles (60 kilometers) southwest of Sacramento and halfway between there and San Francisco.

title: ‘Broomstick’ brings the season of the witch to the Bangor Opera House
text:
The season of the witch has arrived at the Bangor Opera House and oh what a delight it is.
Penobscot Theatre Company’s production of the one-woman show “Broomstick” is spooky and creepy but also mesmerizing.
A.J. Mooney reveals the witch’s humanity while divulging secrets about how she came to be the old lady living alone in a cottage in Appalachia that several children passed through. It is a memorable tour de force and multi-layered performance unlike Mooney’s previous turns on the Opera House stage.
Mooney has been a Penobscot Theatre company member for more than 20 years. She has starred in “Misery,” “Birthday Candles,” “August: Osage County,” the musical “The Full Monty,” “Trapped! A Lobster Tale,” and many more.
“Broomstick” was written by John Biguenet, a playwright and novelist based in New Orleans. The 90-minute one-act production is written in verse and was first performed in 2013 in New Jersey.
The play is written as a conversation between the Witch and a visitor whom she cared for as a child. There are cackling confessions about a tragic love affair, stories of when and how she developed her powers and how she’s used them over the years. It is not for children or the faint of heart.
Director Ben Layman uses every inch of the Opera House stage. Mooney is upstage, downstage, in doorways and a fireplace, on the floor and atop a table. She is almost never still, which gives the show a frenetic feel and matches the character’s emotional roller coaster ride into the past and back to the present.
Layman and Mooney, who have worked together many times, mine the script for every cackle, laugh, surprise and pathos. There is some ambiguity here too, as it’s just possible the Witch might be stretching the truth a mite.
The technical work by the design team — Michael DiMauro (lighting), Anna Kate Mason (costumes), Jess Ploszaj (set and props) and Ryan McGowan (sound) — is dazzlingly eye popping. Ploszaj, the company’s production manager, turned the “On Golden Pond” camp set into the witch’s cottage and filled it with dried herbs and flowers, a few children’s toys and a lot of stuff acquired over a lifetime. Theatergoers might recognize rooms in their own homes on stage.
While all the technical work is excellent, DiMauro’s complex lighting design is stunning. In the opening scene, the candles in Witch’s home light up as she walks by them. The Witch often is bathed in light that matches her moods and the kind of story she is telling: yellows for the sunshine and happiness or her youth and blues and reds for the tragedies she’s endured.
“Broomstick” is a fascinating 90 minutes of fun and gets the audience rethinking its opinion of witches from childhood. Gather your coven and get to the Opera House.
Penobscot Theatre Company’s production of “Broomstick” will be performed through Nov. 8 at the Bangor Opera House, 131 Main St. For information, visit penobscottheatre.org or call 207-942-3333.

title: Good riddance to the political mailers
text:
I have kept the political mailers received at my house for the past two weeks. The total is at least 39.
I say “at least” because it turns out my wife might have recycled a few that she didn’t realize I was collecting for the purposes of this column. Thirty-nine political mailers in 14 days (plus a plastic baggie of pamphlets from the Androscoggin County Republican Committee, which I am not counting because it was dumped on my doorstep rather than arriving in my mailbox).
Of the 39 mailers, six were in favor of Democrats. One was a “make sure you’re registered to vote” paper from the Democratic Senate Campaign Committee that didn’t mention any issues or candidates. Thirty-two were in favor of Republican candidates. Only one was from the Maine Republican Party and a total of seven mailers were authorized by a candidate (mostly Paul LePage.)
On the Democratic side, four were directly from the Maine Democratic Party and two were from PACs. I don’t know why the Maine Republican Party isn’t sending out their own mailers. Maybe they’re secretly broke? Or, more likely, they’d rather have billionaire-backed dark money do their dirty work for them.
Elon Musk’s personal super PAC, America PAC, sent five mailers. SLF PAC, which has received over $158 million from Musk (and that’s just what I could find with a quick Google search) sent eight. There’s other PACs and committees as well, too many for one column.
Many of the mailers clearly used AI; some might have been regular photo editing by human hand but there was one where clearly someone prompted an image generator with something along the lines of “scary blue wave with famous Democrats” and it created images of Chuck Schumer and Elizabeth Warren looking like sea gods. Troy Jackson, the choice of Poseidon! On the other side, Troy Jackson, Elizabeth Warren and Chuck Schumer are edited to all be standing on a beach in the rain. I’m genuinely unsure what this ad is trying to communicate.
Also, and I’m afraid I don’t know how else to say this, but several of the AI-influenced attack ads accidentally made Troy Jackson look sexy. I think whoever at SLF PAC designed them was going for an “evil rich guy” theme but they just made him look like he is auditioning to be the next James Bond, successfully. Jackson in real-life suits is nowhere near as svelte as these mailers make him out to be.
There was a great deal of implied racism in the Republican ads. Five of these ads featured Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a congresswoman from New York, who has nothing to do with Maine but is a Latino woman and therefore, I guess, terrifying.
One even said, “You can’t stop them if you don’t vote,” featuring a picture of Troy Jackson alongside pictures of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Zohran Mamdani — the mayor of New York City, which doesn’t have anything to do with a Senate race in Maine (although at least, as a Bowdoin grad, Mamdani was once a Maine resident) and Kamala Harris.
The inclusion of Harris is particularly egregious because she doesn’t even hold an elected position right now. “America PAC” clearly just wanted to include a Black woman for purposes of getting the base fired up with hatred.
None of the attack ads featured Rep. Chellie Pingree, who also supports the Green New Deal and Medicare for All and, unlike Mayor Mamdani and Rep. Ocasio-Cortez, is a Maine politician. Is it because she’s white and the conservative “get out the vote” operation needs to rely on a base sense of racist fear to drive turnout?
There was one ad that really summed up the whole election for me and, honestly, the whole country’s political situation. It’s from America PAC, and it says “Troy Jackson and his radical socialist allies want to change Maine forever. Susan Collins is fighting to keep Maine, Maine.”
There’s no details about how Jackson wants to change Maine, or what exactly “keeping Maine, Maine” means.
That’s the point: the reader can fill in the blanks with whatever they want, whatever scares them the most. (This being an Elon Musk-funded ad, I suspect that “keep Maine Maine” means “keep Maine white” and no, I’m not talking about a snowy winter).
Personally I think it would be great if we could change Maine forever by, for example, passing universal healthcare so nobody has to worry about going bankrupt from a cancer diagnosis, or maybe investing in moving the state away from depending on foreign-sourced heating oil. That would be a great change.
But this flyer just boils everything down to “change” vs. “stay the same” even though it’s plain as day that the system now just isn’t working. And I get it. I’m autistic, I struggle with change to a clinically diagnosable degree. Change can be scary. But it’s inevitable. And change can be good! It’s not necessarily something to be scared of, not that you can tell from Republican political mailing, which is like 70% scaring old people that illegal immigrants are coming to get them somehow.
I cannot wait for this election to be over, for many reasons but at this point I am mostly just excited to stop getting all these gross mailers. They’re a total waste of money, time and trees.

title: See who’s raised the most money in the Bangor City Council race
text:
Visit the BDN election page for our latest coverage of local, state and national races.
Bangor City Council candidates have raised nearly $40,000 in total, and one candidate, Terry Dinkins, has raised nearly $15,000 alone, according to campaign finance reports.
That money is one part of a significant influx of cash to the Bangor City Council race. Last year, each candidate raised a few thousand dollars at most, and all nine contenders raised less than $15,000 collectively. The three candidates who have been endorsed by a conservative PAC that’s racked up nearly $30,000 this election cycle are also dominating individual fundraising.
On average, the candidates have raised about $3,500 each, compared with about $1,600 last year, according to campaign finance reports obtained by the Bangor Daily News through a public records request.
But there’s a wide disparity between the highest-raising candidates and the bottom of the pack.
After Dinkins, Anthony Cote has raised nearly $8,000, and Joseph Pratt has raised more than $5,000.
Joe Leonard, the only incumbent councilor running, hasn’t raised any money at all for his campaign. Katherine Devine has raised just over $100, and John King has about $430.
Fundraising doesn’t always correlate with winning the council election. Last year, Daniel Carson won a seat as the highest-raising candidate with about $4,300, but Angela Walker was in the middle of the fundraising pack and Susan Faloon was in the bottom half. The candidate who raised the second most, Steven Farren, came in seventh place at the polls.
About 40% of the money raised by candidates in 2025 came from the candidates themselves or their spouses and domestic partners. This year, that’s only the case for about 16% of the funds in the race.
Only one political committee has given directly to candidates: the Greater Bangor Democratic Committee, which contributed $50 each to Adam Baker and John King.
The other groups working to influence the race, including the Concerned Citizens of Bangor PAC on the right and Food and Medicine on the left, are making independent expenditures, meaning they don’t contribute or coordinate directly with the candidates they support. Wealthy tech entrepreneur and Cape Elizabeth resident Jonathan Bush is also running ads ahead of the election, although they don’t name any particular candidates and are not subject to campaign finance reporting requirements.
Three candidates have campaign balances with a majority coming from their own funds: Katherine Devine, Dawson Nevells and Andrei Yermakov.
Devine is also the only candidate who hasn’t spent any money on her campaign and has not put up signs around the city. Leonard only spent money on an event and seems to be re-using signs from his previous campaigns.
Most of the money spent by candidates this cycle has gone toward campaign literature such as signs and palm cards.
Dinkins is the only candidate running TV ads and has spent about $5,700 to do so on Spectrum TV.
The rest of the candidate expenditures are scattered among categories like hardware for putting up large signs, postage and apparel. Click through the chart below to see all of the expenditures made in this reporting period, which ended Oct. 20.

title: Trump administration's social media posts ahead of elections criticized for being inflammatory
text:
The Trump administration’s online accounts are circulating images of a pumpkin carved with a sombrero design and a fake Halloween-themed background around a Black man apparently accused of food assistance fraud, in social media posts slammed by critics as inflammatory rhetoric.
Only days before the midterm elections, the posts coincide with the government’s sweeping campaign to show its aggressive immigration enforcement, and highlight efforts to crack down on fraud to save taxpayers money when rising healthcare costs and other economic stressors have made affordability a top voter concern.
Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins posted Saturday on the social platform X a photo of the Black man standing in front of stacks of what appear to be U.S. currency with the headline, SNAP FRAUDSTER, an apparent reference to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, formerly known as food stamps.
He is holding aloft what appears to be a bill set aflame.
“Some costumes come with a price tag. This one comes with a prison sentence,” it says to the backdrop of fake Spirit Halloween costume packaging.
Another photo posted by the White House on X on Thursday showed a pumpkin with the shape of a sombrero carved across it and the words “Spooky szn is here.”
The post by Rollins, who was nominated by Trump to serve as the U.S. Secretary of Agriculture in November 2024, appears to be taken from an Instagram post from September 2025 by an account under the name Shawty Dred.
Earlier this month, Mercedes Reshard New, identified by the Justice Department as a social media personality also known as “Shawty Dred,” was arrested on federal charges for fraudulently obtaining more than $4 million in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits in Georgia.
It’s not the first time the White House has been accused of posting inflammatory images on official government social media accounts.
Just over a year ago during the government shutdown, the White House revived a deepfake video posted by Trump of House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries in a fake mustache and sombrero to accuse the Democrats of acting on behalf of illegal immigrants instead of U.S. citizens. Jeffries described the meme as bigoted. They played it on repeat in the White House briefing room, though Vice President JD Vance promised that the “sombrero memes will stop” when Democrats agreed to end the shutdown.
The NAACP did not respond to an email seeking comment, nor did the White House or Rollins.
The Trump administration in recent weeks has ratcheted up its anti-immigrant rhetoric and accusations of fraud, including against U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar whose Washington, D.C., home was searched by federal agents earlier this month. Federal authorities are investigating potential fraud in her family’s immigration paperwork. Omar, who was born in Somalia, is a naturalized U.S. citizen.
It also has taken a series of punitive steps linked to allegations of fraud in mostly Democratic-led states, including California and Minnesota whose governors accused the federal government of targeting their states for political reasons.
Federal prosecutors said in a news release Oct. 21 that the influencer, New, controlled more than 350 fraudulent SNAP accounts under stolen identities between January 2020 and July 2026. He allegedly applied for his company, Shawty Dred LLC, to become an authorized SNAP retailer and used EBT debit cards to extract about $4 million from the accounts.
New’s Instagram account, which has more than two million followers, has flaunted his extravagant lifestyle, federal prosecutors said. Posts depict him flying on private jets, posing with Rolls-Royce vehicles in front of his “super mansion,” and handling massive stacks of cash.
“Instead of this money feeding families in need, New, the social media personality known as ‘Shawty Dred,’ allegedly used the cash to bankroll a life of luxury,” Special Agent in Charge of FBI Atlanta Marlo Graham said in the release.
New was indicted by a federal grand jury Oct. 7 on dozens of counts of mail fraud and aggravated identity theft, and one count each of SNAP fraud and illegal transactions with access devices. He was arrested Oct. 13 and remains in federal custody.
According to Fulton County jail records, New has been arrested multiple times on suspicion of crimes including identity theft, insurance fraud, financial transaction card fraud, forgery and simple assault.
A federal defender listed in court records as representing New, Joseph Austin, did not return a phone message.

title: Maine must insist on its independence
text:
Maine is a bastion of independent thinkers and doers. Always has been, always will be. During this election, a “Star Wars” cantina of megadonors, CEOs and dark money bundlers is pumping cash into Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign. Ninety-three percent of her contributions are from out-of-state. These “donors” want to tell Mainers how to vote.
Do Down East lobstermen need a New Jersey billionaire’s advice on hauling a line? Do Augusta teachers need a Silicon Valley tech bro’s lesson plan? Do Portland nurses need directives from New York financiers?
We can read the ballot. We know what to do.
I’m voting for the candidate who answers to Maine, not Manhattan. I’m voting for Troy Jackson.
Jim Morrison
Vinalhaven

title: Blocked extra point in OT proves costly as UMaine football loses 8th-straight
text:
The University of Maine’s football team had plenty of opportunities to snap its seven-game losing streak during Saturday’s Coastal Athletic Association game against rival Rhode Island at Centreville Bank Stadium in Pawtucket, Rhode Island.
UMaine took a 13-7 lead in overtime on Nick Laughlin’s one-yard touchdown run.
But Sam Tremblay had his extra point kick blocked by URI’s Patrick Conserve. It proved costly as Alex McClelland threw a game-tying 25-yard touchdown pass to 2025 All-American wide receiver Marquis Buchanan, and Ty Groff decided it by kicking the extra point as URI triumphed 14-13.
Defending CAA champ URI improved to 5-4 overall and 2-3 in the CAA while UMaine fell to 1-8 and 1-5, respectively. It was URI’s fifth-straight win over UMaine.
The eight-game losing streak is the longest by a UMaine team in a single season since the 1967 team went 0-8.
On UMaine’s overtime possession, a personal foul penalty on URI gave UMaine the ball at the URI six-yard line, taking Tremblay’s 30-yard field goal off the board.
A five-yard run on a reverse by Malik McNeely set UMaine up at the 1-yard line, and Laughlin scored on the next play.
But Tremblay failed to convert the extra point, the second time he has done so in his last three tries.
URI began its OT possession at the UMaine-25 and didn’t gain a yard on a first down run by McClelland.
But the quarterback hooked up with Buchanan in the end zone on the second down play, and Groff ended it with his kick.
Buchanan’s reception was his ninth of the game for 107 yards, and he set the school’s career record for receiving yards with it. He now has 3,954 receiving yards, 10 more than former record-holder Brian Forster.
McClelland only completed 11 of 19 passes on the day for 110 yards. Nobody else had more than one catch.
UMaine had plenty of chances to win the game in regulation thanks to a superb performance from its defense, which limited URI to 212 total yards and nine first downs and forced two fumbles, both of which the Black Bears recovered. They also had three sacks.
UMaine had a 35:32-24:28 edge in time of possession, a 352-212 edge in total yards and a 22-9 edge in first downs.
The UMaine defense only allowed one touchdown, the one in overtime, because the first URI touchdown came on an 84-yard interception return by Tyson Grimm of a Caden Drezek pass with 32 seconds left in a first half that was dominated by UMaine.
UMaine had three drives that moved the ball inside the URI 40-yard line but couldn’t convert any of them into points.
Tremblay missed a 34-yard field goal, his second consecutive miss after nailing his first 10 this season.
UMaine had six possessions that started in URI territory in the second half but only converted once when Rashawn Marshall scampered 25 yards for a game-tying TD with 12:48 left in the game.
UMaine had a glorious opportunity to win it late when the Black Bears gained possession at the URI-40 following a punt with 1:49 remaining in regulation.
But Laughlin gained only one yard on first down, Drezek threw an incompletion and then completed a throw to Laughlin but only for three yards, creating a fourth-and-six situation.
UMaine took a delay of game penalty and punted and the game went to overtime.
Brayden Richardson was URI’s leading rusher with 92 yards on 19 carries. Linebacker Rohan Davy spearheaded the Ram defense with a game-high 19 tackles. Sam Ofurie, another linebacker, had 10.
Drezek completed 21 of 34 passes for 149 yards and Eddie Buehler completed three of seven for 19. Marshall rushed for a game-high 139 yards on 25 carries and also caught three passes for 17 more yards.
Laughlin gained 62 yards on 12 carries.
Keyon Concepcion had five catches for 62 yards, Evan Wallace had four for 19 yards and Ty’ee Stephens had four for 11 yards.
Linebackers Sam Oppenheimer and Noah Carpenter led UMaine in tackles with eight and seven, respectively.
Maine had two trips into the red zone but didn’t produce any points on those two drives.
UMaine will have next weekend off before going to Albany for a noon game on Nov. 14. URI will travel to take on New Hampshire at 1 p.m. Saturday.

title: Thornton boys cross country edges Portland by a point for 1st state title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
AUGUSTA — In an era where razor-thin margins of victory are a theme at the Maine cross country state championships, what happened between Thornton Academy and Portland on Saturday might top them all.
The Thornton boys topped Portland by a single point, registering 79 points to the Bulldogs’ 80, to win the Class A title at Cony High School. It’s the first state championship in program history for the Golden Trojans, who were runners-up to Portland in the South regional a week ago.
“(The wait) was crazy,” Thornton senior Ryan Bolduc said about the delay before the final score was available. “We were all standing around after the end and trying to calculate it in our heads because we knew it was close, and someone’s mom read out that we won. It’s an incredible, surreal feeling.”
Yarmouth (Class B) and Winthrop (Class C) claimed the other boys team championships. Hampden Academy (A), Freeport (B) and Maine Coast Waldorf took home the girls titles.
Scarborough’s Atticus Merriam won Class A boys in 16 minutes, 6.78 seconds, beating Falmouth’s Mateo Diaz (16:19.79) and Bangor’s Sam Bergmark (16:26.84). Bolduc (16:36.88) took fourth, and Thornton teammate Noah Loveys-Messenger (seventh, 16:57.72) joined him in the top 10.
Ambrose Clarke (11th, 17:18.61), Reid Hughes (14th, 17:32.01), Emile Olins (17th, 17:36.47) and Everett Smith (17:36.51) put Portland in the title mix. Thornton, though, had just enough, as Jonathan Perry (12th, 17:21.54), Mason Thurlow (30th, 17:55.23) and William Tripp (31st, 17:55.36) secured a title by the slimmest of margins.
“We knew it was going to be a battle,” said Thornton coach Josh Wynne. “All of this started back in mid-June, and they’ve been locked in ever since then for this day. We’ve had this motto all year of working together as a wolf pack, and that’s what they did today: They worked together.”
Portland’s Nora Schmidt (18:00.58) won the Class A girls race, beating out Falmouth’s 
Georgia Moon (18:05.05), who edged Schmidt by 1.12 seconds last Saturday in the South regional. Addison Elliott (18:33.39) finished third for Hampden, which claimed just its second girls state title (2003).
Lincoln Academy’s Karen Higgins won the Class B girls race in 18:58:41, well ahead of Caribou’s Emma Graves (19:28.70). After MDI’s Kulani Granholm took third in 19:33.46, Ella Olshetski placed fourth in 19:46.15 to mark Freeport’s first finisher.
That started an avalanche of Freeport runners. Maddy York (19:53.83) and Stella Kryzak (19:56.53) finished sixth and seventh, and Maddy Gilbert took 12th (20:23.00). Molly O’Brien was 47th in 22:44.76 to secure the title for the Falcons (67 points) over MDI (81).
“That last 0.1 (miles), I can’t remember it much,” Gilbert said. “The course, we know it’s hard, but we worked on hills a lot this season. We knew the hay was in the barn, and we just had to run … We knew we had to fight for it (with MDI), but we knew that if we ran with confidence, had fun and just ran together as a team, we would get it.”
Caribou’s Pierce Gorneault won the Class B boys race in 16:26.85. Yarmouth’s pack followed, as Jackie Chalmers (16:36.41), Bowen Mitchell (16:47.22), Eli Chalmers (16:53.70) and Jesse Canfield (17:04.20) rounded out the top five to give the Clippers a repeat title.
“It was incredible; they worked really well together,” said Yarmouth coach Sarah Carrigan. “They practice trading off all the time in practice, and they all get a chance to lead in practice. Then, on race day, we just see who has it on the day.”
Dirigo’s William Morris defended his Class C boys crown in 16:18.47. Winthrop’s Alfie Cognata (16:51.20), who was runner-up to Morris last year, took second place again, beating out Waynflete’s Tadhg Lake (16:57.26) in a tight battle.
Winthrop’s Sawyer Wess (seventh, 17:19.44) and Sam St. Germain (eighth, 17:20.54) also claimed top-10 finishes. It was the second state championship for the Ramblers, our current Varsity Maine Boys Team of the Week, whose other Class C title came in 2007.
“We came in with a plan, and we wanted to break the course down into a few spots we were going to focus on,” said Winthrop coach Ed Van Tassel. “The kids worked well together all year, and it really just all came together for us. I couldn’t be prouder of them.”
Maranacook’s Reagan Mattson continued her phenomenal freshman campaign by winning the Class C girls race in 19:52.73. Maine Coast Waldorf (58 points) claimed the girls team championship, beating out North Yarmouth Academy (81 points).

title: Gorham volleyball tops Scarborough in 5 sets to win 4th straight Class A title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SOUTH PORTLAND — In the Class A volleyball final’s tensest moment, Gorham coach Emma Tirrell looked toward the Rams’ student section and implored an already fevered group to get even louder. They obliged, and Tirrell returned to the bench, laughing.
One point later, laughter was replaced by jubilation. Gorham won its fourth straight volleyball title, overcoming a first-set defeat en route to taking down Scarborough, 3-2, at Southern Maine Community College.
It’s another Gold Ball for the Rams. And this one couldn’t have been harder earned.
“These seniors have never lost a playoff game, and this would have been their first loss,” Tirrell said. “It was extremely special for them to round this out. I don’t know how many players can say that they won four state championships, ever. And it was wicked special, because most of our roster is seniors.”
Gorham, which became the first Class A volleyball team to win four straight titles since Greely from 2003-08, dropped the first set 25-21, then won the next two, 25-18 and 25-16. But the Rams were pushed to the all-or-nothing fifth set when Scarborough pulled out a 25-22 win in the fourth.
In an all-too-familiar theme, the Rams raised their game with the pressure on. They took a 10-7 lead, then won five of the last six points after the Red Storm evened the score at 10-10.
“It’s phenomenal. I’m so proud of all my teammates,” said senior setter Liana Edwards, who finished with 36 assists and eight kills. “It’s crazy to go to four state championships in a row, all throughout high school. I think it’s such an accomplishment.
“Each time we played Scarborough, we went to five sets. Obviously the game could go either way, but I think we just proved again that we’re the top team.”
With the four-peat in jeopardy, Gorham got a kill from Luna Button (nine kills) and Scarborough sent a return into the net, putting the Rams ahead 12-10. A Calli Juhring kill brought the Red Storm within a point, but a long Scarborough return and Abbie Stevens’ 27th kill of the match brought up match point.
Scarborough called timeout. Tirrell pumped up the fans.
“If Gorham is up 14-11 in the fifth set, I trust 10 out of 10 times that we put that game away,” she said.
And the Rams did, in fitting fashion. Edwards, the two-time Varsity Maine and Gatorade Player of the Year, hit a serve toward the back of the court that hit off Scarborough hands and fell to the floor for the winning point.
“Two years ago, we played at SMCC and I was serving on (match) point, too,” said Edwards. “What a coincidence. It’s an amazing feeling. I have no voice.”
The Rams met an opponent that was up to the task. Scarborough got 20 kills from Caleb Atwood, and their duo at the net of Juhring (14 kills) and Lexi Cowie (12 kills) proved formidable, even with starting hitter Elena Pijunovic out after getting injured in the semifinal win over Cheverus.
“For not even our starting lineup to take them that deep into the fifth set, it’s just a testament to our team,” Scarborough coach Nicole Petherbridge said. “Our mentality was not ‘What happens if we lose,’ it was ‘How fun will it be to win.’ When we play with that mentality, we’re unstoppable. I think you saw that in the fourth set.”
Gorham, however, didn’t cave after being pushed to the brink.
“We’re known as the ‘fifth set queens.’ We like to go all the way,” said senior libero Adyson Hutchins, whose defense, along with serves from Kasey Plaud (six aces), helped carry Gorham through. “It’s great that we can overcome it. We have the practice. … Our coach always tells us to keep our heads up, and keep believing in each other.”

title: Tennessee escapee crossed state line hours before local police were notified, DA says
text:
Tennessee prison escapee crossed state lines before prison officials alerted external law enforcement, district attorney says
A convicted murderer who escaped a Tennessee prison last weekend had already crossed state lines before prison officials alerted external law enforcement agencies, according to District Attorney Danny Goodman Jr.
Jacob Morley had been in Marion, Illinois, by 4:40 a.m. Monday, but local law enforcement was not notified until 6:15 a.m., following multiple cell counts late Sunday, Goodman said Friday.
Related video above | Tennessee murder victim's sister fears for safety amid manhunt
“The biggest concern I have, obviously, is just the large gap between the time that someone was notified,” he said. “If they had known as quickly as the department of corrections knew…that would have given two hours for local police to be patrolling, and good chance they catch him before he gets out of the county.”
Now, authorities in multiple states are scrambling to find Morley, who is “considered dangerous and could be anywhere,” the Tennessee Department of Correction warned in a social media post Friday afternoon. The department asked truck drivers and travelers who were in Marion Monday morning to review dash camera footage for suspicious activity.
“We ask the public to remain vigilant, check on family members and neighbors, and be alert for suspicious activity on your properties, including vacant homes, vacation properties, and outbuildings.”
Morley, 28, escaped late Sunday from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, in the northwestern corner of Tennessee, officials said.
Before fleeing the state, Morley stole a 2008 white Ford F-350 early Monday, investigators said. The truck was found abandoned Tuesday in Marion, Illinois – about a 130-mile drive north of the prison, the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said.
The stolen truck apparently sat in southern Illinois for more than a day before police found it, investigators said. Surveillance video shows the truck was apparently abandoned in Illinois around 4:40 a.m. Monday, Marion police Lt. Justin Dwyer told CNN. He said police found the truck around 10 a.m. Tuesday.
Video evidence so far indicates Morley headed toward a highway after leaving the truck, Dwyer said.
Marion police have reviewed a handful of grainy surveillance videos, saying some details match Morley’s description but haven’t been able to confirm whether he is still in Marion, according to Dwyer.
“We have continually searched neighborhoods, knocked on doors and followed every lead and tip that we receive. Although there is no indication he is still in Marion, we will continue to assume he is and will be on the lookout,” Dwyer said.
“All of our officers and detectives are well versed in Morley’s descriptors, photographs, etc., and will diligently canvass the area until we are confident he isn’t here or has been captured.”
Morley is the second inmate to escape this month from the custody of the Tennessee Department of Correction, whose commissioner resigned after the botched execution last month of Christa Pike. Pike is now back in a maximum-security prison. Gov. Bill Lee announced the appointment of Christopher Hansen as interim commissioner of the department on Friday.
Morley is now on the TBI’s “Most Wanted” list, with a combined reward of $17,500 offered by the Tennessee governor’s office, the TBI and the US Marshals Service for information leading to his arrest.
Convicted killer vanishes in the dark
Morley was sentenced to life in prison after he was convicted of first-degree murder, aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, evading arrest and vandalism.
A correctional officer conducted a routine cell count at 9:30 p.m. Sunday, according to Goodman, the district attorney. When an officer knocked on Morley’s cell and asked how many inmates were inside, an inmate falsely claimed two were present, but Morley was not in the cell, Goodman said.
CNN has reached out to the Tennessee Department of Correction for comment.
He escaped through a fence at the prison in Tiptonville late Sunday, and staff confirmed he was missing around 11:30 p.m., the Tennessee Department of Correction said. Prison staff alerted an internal investigator around 2 a.m., but state agencies and the DA’s office weren’t notified until 5:30 a.m., according to Goodman.
Security camera footage later revealed Morley “breached the perimeter fence” and fled wearing his prison uniform, the department said. Goodman said he cut through the security fences and hid among pallets and a trash cart behind the main kitchen. Goodman added he doesn’t know what tool he used to cut through the fence or how he obtained it.
He then stole the truck early Monday in Lake County, where Tiptonville is the county seat, the TBI said.
“Everybody is locking their car doors now,” local attorney Bridget Lawler said Wednesday. “My husband checked all of our doors before he went to bed.”
In Marion, a small Illinois city of about 17,600 people, one resident told CNN: “It’s a scary time.”
Marion police said they notified the public through local media outlets. But one resident said she didn’t get an alert from local authorities.
“No one that I have talked to has mentioned seeing it, either,” Lachelle Hartline told CNN. “We only got information through Facebook."
Victim’s family worries what the fugitive might do next
Morley was convicted in the killing of Cody Birchfield, who was initially reported missing in February 2022, the Carter County Sheriff’s Office said. Birchfield’s body was found weeks after he went missing, in a box under Morley’s house, The Associated Press reported.
Birchfield’s older sister said her brother was always there for his family. “It didn’t matter when, where, or what you needed,” Carrie Norman told CNN affiliate WCYB.
After learning her brother’s killer had escaped, “You feel sick to your stomach,” Norman said. “It’s all those feelings come rushing back.”
A cousin of Birchfield’s, who asked not to be identified for safety reasons, told CNN Morley’s life sentence gave the family “a small sense of closure and the reassurance that justice had been served.” But learning of his escape has reopened their “deepest wounds.”
The cousin said the family’s primary concerns are public safety and keeping attention on Morley’s escape, urging anyone with information to tell authorities.
But the victim’s family also wants to make sure Birchfield is never forgotten.
“Above all, we want Cody to be remembered not for the tragedy of his death, but for the warmth, kindness, and decency of his life,” the cousin said.
Another cousin of Birchfield’s, who also asked to speak anonymously for safety reasons, told CNN they’re worried about the safety of Birchfield’s father and sister, who still live in the same area.
“If that man can do that to my cousin,” the family member said, “what’s he going to do to the next individual?”

title: ‘Feels like he’s still on leave’: Families mourning after crash that killed 3 Navy sailors
text:
PENSACOLA, Fla. (WWSB/Gray News) - Three service members assigned to Naval Air Station Pensacola died in an Oct. 24 crash in Florida, the Navy confirmed.
What happened
The vehicle was traveling westbound when it hit a barrier at M Street and caught fire, Pensacola police said.
All three sailors were pronounced dead at the scene.
Sailors identified
The Navy said two of the sailors killed were assigned to the Naval Air Technical Training Center. The third was assigned to Naval Aviation Schools Command.
Cmdr. David Gardner, a spokesperson for Naval Education and Training Command at Naval Air Station Pensacola, identified the service members as:
- Aviation Ordnanceman Airman Apprentice Dracon Bagley
- Aviation Ordnanceman Recruit Francois Longdayeyambete
- Airman Apprentice David Deanda
Bagley, of Michigan, enlisted in the Navy on May 14.
Longdayeyambete, of Massachusetts, enlisted on July 9.
“He’s the best one that anyone could ever ask for. He always had my back every time my mom would get mad at me. He always told me right from wrong,” Longdayeyambete’s brother Joseph said.
Dane Laboissonniere, Longdayeyambete’s school football coach, said his former player always wanted to be an aeronautical engineer.
Deanda, of California, enlisted in the Navy on June 4.
“It just feels like he’s still on leave. So, he ain’t coming home, but, we think like, ‘Oh, he’s still out there,’” Deanda’s father said.
Navy statement
The Navy also issued a statement.
“The Navy is mourning the loss of our shipmates and extends our deepest condolences to the sailors’ families, friends and fellow sailors during this difficult time,” the statement said.
Navy chaplains are providing grief counseling and support.
Investigation
The circumstances leading up to the crash are still under investigation.
