title: ‘I Voted’ sticker creator talks about how it started
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The “I Voted” sticker given to people who cast ballots began with one woman, Janet Boudreau, who designed it after seeing a local county hand out a different sticker on Election Day.
Boudreau said she has long supported voting, which she described as the right and duty of American citizens to share their voice.
“This is the one day that we have to amplify what we want our world to look like, and it just irritated me and my folks, too, when people would say, oh I forgot the election,” Boudreau said.
In 1987, Boudreau owned an election supply and voting equipment company. She noticed a county in Washington state had started handing out stickers on Election Day.
“It was black and white and had an X in a square. And that’s it. And I thought, this is not inspiring,” Boudreau said.
She said she then created her own design.
“I went home and got out a blue and red pen and decided on an ellipse with a waving flag,” Boudreau said.
The sticker started in a few counties and quickly spread across the country.
“By 1992, wow, it was nuts!” Boudreau said.
Election Day memorabilia has a long history that includes pins, buttons and ribbons - including those used during the women’s suffrage movement in the 1920s.
After taking off in the 1990s, the “I Voted” sticker has led to other versions, including state-specific images and future voter patches. Contests have also invited children to design their own stickers.
Boudreau said the goal behind the sticker is to inspire Americans to vote.
“What gets me the most about this is that it’s become this badge of honor,” Boudreau said.
She hopes the sticker continues to carry meaning as a promise and a call to action every election cycle.
“So get out and vote and then spread the word,” Boudreau said.

title: High schools Saturday: Cheverus field hockey keeps streak alive with OT win
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Gracie Copper scored her second goal of the game on a penalty corner 55 seconds into overtime, giving three-time defending state champion Cheverus a 3-2 win over Sanford/Kennebunk in a Class A South field hockey semifinal Saturday in Portland.
Sanford/Kennebunk (10-6) forced overtime when Reese Beaudoin slapped in a penalty corner insertion from Zoey McCann after regulation time expired. But the Stags quickly answered as they extended their unbeaten streak to 70 games and their winning streak to 33.
The Stags advanced to the sixth consecutive regional final. They’ll face third-seeded Thornton Academy on Wednesday at Scarborough High.
Cheverus (16-0), the No. 1 team in the Varsity Maine poll, scored all three of its goals off corners. Sydney Brunelle opened the scoring early in the second quarter, and Copper made it 2-0 early in the third.
Brooke Brunelle assisted on both of Copper’s goals.
Ella Tederous cut into the deficit midway through the third quarter, assisted by Miranda Payeur.
THORNTON ACADEMY 2, BIDDEFORD 0: Shyla McVeigh scored off a penalty corner with no time remaining in the first half, Avery Root added a fourth-quarter goal, and the third-seeded Golden Trojans (13-3) upset the second-seeded Tigers (13-3) in a Class A South semifinal in Biddeford.
The loss was Biddeford’s first against an opponent other than Cheverus since 2023. Biddeford was ranked third in the most recent Varsity Maine Top 10, while Thornton was eighth.
SKOWHEGAN 2, CAMDEN HILLS 1: Charlotte Haynie and Avery Farnham scored first-half goals for the second-seeded River Hawks (15-1) in a Class A North semifinal victory over the third-seeded Windjammers (12-4) in Skowhegan.
Haynie gave Skowhegan a 1-0 advantage with 2:19 remaining in the first quarter. Farnham added to the lead in the second quarter, with Kaitlyn Dufour picking up the assist.
Alana Smith scored for Camden Hills in the fourth, assisted by Margaret Holland-McCase.
Skowhegan goalie Michelle Williams made three saves for the win.
The River Hawks will seek a second straight regional title on Wednesday when they face top-seeded Mt. Ararat at Messalonskee High in Oakland.
MT. ARARAT 2, MESSALONSKEE 0: Top-seeded Mt. Ararat scored two goals just 26 seconds apart in the third quarter to beat No. 5 Messalonskee in a Class A North semifinal in Topsham.
Addison Chubbuck scored with 9:47 left in the third. Cali LeClair quickly made it 2-0.
YARMOUTH 7, LAKE REGION 1: Vivienne Corriveau scored four of her five goals in the first half as the top-seeded Clippers (15-1) cruised to a Class B South semifinal win over the fifth-seeded Lakers (9-7) in Yarmouth.
Corriveau put in two goals in each of the first two quarters and made it 5-0 in the third as Yarmouth set up a fourth straight regional final against second-seeded Freeport.
Celia Smith and Delia Rich added fourth-quarter goals.
Abigail Travis scored for Lake Region.
FREEPORT 2, GREELY 1: Lydia Porter scored in the first and third round of a penalty corner tiebreaker to give the second-seeded Falcons (13-3) a Class B South semifinal win over the third-seeded Rangers (12-4) in Freeport.
Greely forced overtime when Maya Tracey scored on a penalty corner after regulation time expired.
After two scoreless overtimes, Porter and Greely’s Grace Tyll exchanged goals on the first set of penalty corners. Neither team scored on its second attempt, but Porter’s goal in the third round was the winner.
Freeport, the reigning regional champion, led for most of the game after a first-quarter goal by Megan Ritz.
Freeport goalie Lydia Costa made seven saves, while Cameron Esposito of Greely stopped 13 shots.
NOKOMIS 5, OLD TOWN 1: Annie Nyce scored four times to lead the top-seeded Warriors (15-1) to a berth in the Class B North final with a win over the fourth-seeded Coyotes (11-4) in Newport.
Maeve Rush also scored for Nokomis. Meredith Cyr scored for Old Town.
LEAVITT 3, GARDINER 1: The second-seeded Hornets (15-1) came alive in the second half as they advanced to the Class B North final by defeating sixth-seeded Gardiner (10-5) in Turner.
Brylee Emmons broke a scoreless deadlock when she ripped a shot with 8:26 remaining in the third quarter. Adeline Hastings tipped in an Ainsley Barry shot late in the third to make it 2-0.
Izzy Stone put the Tigers on the board with 9:20 remaining, jamming the ball into the cage off a penalty corner.
Barry restored Leavitt’s two-goal advantage with 5:32 left, redirecting an Emmons shot.
Leavitt will face top-seeded Nokomis in the regional final Wednesday at Messalonkskee High in Oakland.
WINTHROP 4, BOOTHBAY 1: Addie Daigle paced the top-seeded Ramblers (15-1) with two goals in a Class C South semifinal win against the fourth-seeded Seahawks (10-5) in Winthrop.
The Ramblers will face second-seeded Spruce Mountain (14-2) in the regional final at Scarborough High on Wednesday.
Daigle’s goals came in the second and fourth quarters. Sophie Shuman scored in the first quarter, and Grace Folsom added a goal in the third.
Folsom, Natalie Irwin and Evelyn Mortimer were each credited with an assist. Cyara Harriman stopped five shots.
Meabh Hennessy scored for Boothbay in the fourth quarter. Seahawks goalie Abigail Locke-Smith made nine saves.
BOYS SOCCER
YARMOUTH 7, FREEPORT 0: Lucas Hayner, Tate MacVane and Luke Brown all scored twice in the first half, leading the top-seeded Clippers (14-1-1) over the fourth-seeded Falcons (10-4-2) in a Class B South semifinal in Yarmouth.
The defending state champions took control early, as Hayner and MacVane scored just 34 seconds apart to give the Clippers a 2-0 lead less than four minutes into the contest.
Each of them scored again in a three-minute span midway through the first half. Brown then put in two headers in the final four minutes of the half to make it 6-0.
Hayner added a third goal in the second half.
Yarmouth will play No. 7 seed Cape Elizabeth for the regional title on Wednesday at Falmouth High.
GIRLS SOCCER
OLD ORCHARD BEACH 1, TELSTAR 0: Emelia Michaud scored 10 minutes into the second half to lift the second-seeded Seagulls (8-7) over the third-seeded Rebels (6-9) in a Class D South semifinal in Old Orchard Beach.
Old Orchard Beach will face No. 1 Monmouth Academy in the regional final Wednesday at Cony High in Augusta.
Amelia Gervais stopped three shots for the Seagulls, while Telstar’s Mya Buck made 10 saves.
CAPE ELIZABETH 3, FREEPORT 0: Addi Miller, Matilda Connolly and Pippi Hooper each scored a goal as the top-seeded Capers (14-1-1) beat the fourth-seeded Falcons (11-5) in a Class B South semifinal in Freeport.
Haisel McGeachey contributed two assists and Kelsie Law made three saves for the defending state champion Capers, who set up a rematch with Yarmouth in the regional final Wednesday at Falmouth High.
Freeport keeper Karleigh Costello made 15 saves.
YARMOUTH 6, GREELY 0: Lilah Pernal poured in four goals and added an assist, propelling the top-seeded Clippers (14-2) to a Class B South semifinal win over the sixth-seeded Rangers (8-6-2) in Yarmouth.
Emma Sullivan and Kennedy Hamilton were the other goal scorers for Yarmouth, which avenged a loss to Greely in its regular-season finale.

title: Teen survives fall through pier as king tides batter Florida beaches
text:
Teen survives fall through pier as king tides batter Florida beaches
A Florida teenager is recovering after reportedly falling through the pier at Sebastian Inlet State Park and being swept away by waves.
“Next thing I know, I’m just falling through the floor,” Landen Williams said. “It was insane.”
Video above: Hail in Fort Pierce during severe storms in South Florida
Hearst sister station WESH spoke with the 16-year-old on Wednesday with his mother’s permission.
“I guess a wave knocked up the grate and I didn’t see it, and next thing you know, I’m falling,” Williams said. “Probably 15 to 20 feet.”
Williams credits the king tide with keeping him from crashing into the rocks, but said the experience was still scary.
“I kind of just went with the current and I ended up in that little tide pool over there,” Williams said.
Elsewhere, the combination of strong winds and the highest tidal cycle of the year forced the closing of a fishing pier Tuesday.
The conditions also caused notable beach erosion at Ponce de Leon Beach, Melbourne Beach and Satellite Beach.
“The combination of very high tides and strong winds have driven waves up and over the beaches, and in some cases into the dunes,” Brevard County Communications Director Don Walker said in an email. “The county has prepared for events like this by investing in our beaches over the years, placing sand and dune vegetation. The beaches are adjusting to the storm conditions as expected, and doing the intended job of protecting upland property and infrastructure.”
In Satellite Beach, some beach access is blocked off with wood and yellow caution tape. Ocean rescue officials are urging people to stay out of the water.
“Repair options for the South Beaches are being considered, but a final recommendation will wait until after the weather calms in a few days,” Walker said in an email to WESH. “For our three federal (Army Corps) project areas, the North Reach, Mid Reach and South Reach, the response plan will be coordinated through the Army Corps. The Corps is aware of our circumstances and is working to determine the best steps.
“In the most narrow Mid Reach, we were already encouraging the Corps to plan a renourishment as early as December 2027. This ‘best-case’ schedule is, however, dependent on passage of a FY 2027 federal budget.”
As for Williams, he said that if you’re ever caught in a rip current, you should swim with it.
“I just knew I had to stay calm in that current and everything else,” Williams said.

title: No. 4 Indiana holds off Minnesota in overtime thriller
text:
No. 4 Indiana holds off unranked Minnesota in overtime
Indiana coach Curt Cignetti always believed in backup quarterback Grant Wilson.
When the seventh-year player got his chance Saturday, he delivered.
Video above: Curt Cignetti on future of college football
Wilson took over for the injured Josh Hoover in the second half and threw a 25-yard touchdown pass on the first play of overtime to help No. 4 Indiana rally for a 23-16 victory over Minnesota. The defense closed out the win by sacking Minnesota quarterback Drake Lindsey on fourth down to end it.
“This is entertainment, so I thought we'd bring some entertainment to this game,” Cignetti joked. “Minnesota played great and we just made some plays, but this team just finds a way (to win).”
Indiana (8-1, 5-1 Big Ten) needed overtime for the second straight week to avoid a damaging second loss as it tries to repeat as national champions. Last week, the Hoosiers won 13-6 at Michigan.
This one appeared to be over when the Golden Gophers (5-3, 3-2) took a 16-13 lead with 19 seconds left on Luke Drzewiecki's career-long 60-yard field goal. But Becker's 33-yard catch on the next play from scrimmage set up Paddy McAteer for a career-long 60-yarder to tie the score as time expired.
It marked the second season in Big Ten history that multiple field goals of 60 or more yards were made — and it happened in the same game.
For Minnesota, it was a crushing blow after leading most of the game on the road and on national television. Instead, the Gophers fell to 0-13 against defending national champs, and they still have beaten Top 25 opponents in back-to-back weeks since 1956.
“They made some big-time plays, and we did everything we could to put ourselves in position to win,” Gophers coach P.J. Fleck said. “But our kids never blink, never back down. We expected to win this game. That's a hurt locker room in there."
Indiana pulled struggling starting quarterback Josh Hoover at halftime after he took a big shot on his second interception of the season, and two late replay reviews overturned potential game-winning situations — one erased a go-ahead TD pass, the other took away an interception that would have put Indiana deep in Minnesota territory with 2:59 left in regulation.
Wilson was 9 of 17 for 156 yards and one score after Hoover went 8 of 19 for 119 yards with one TD and the interception in the first half. Becker caught eight passes for 149 yards and the decisive score.
Quarterback Drake Lindsey led Minnesota by going 20 of 37 for 120 yards and one TD. Javon Tracy had seven receptions for 40 yards.

title: Months-long road closure in Portland's Payson Park to end, new measures being added
text:
Months-long road closure in Portland's Payson Park to end, new measures being added
A section of road through Portland's Payson Park will soon reopen for the first time since June.
The city closed part of Catafalque Drive between the baseball field parking lot and Baxter Boulevard next to the playground in June as part of a pilot project designed to test safety measures to improve access for users in the park.
The section of road will reopen on Nov. 16, and traffic will return to normal through the park.
On Nov. 3, crews will install six new speed bumps in Payson Park. Two will be installed on Catafalque Drive, two on Inlet Road and two more will be added to Arboretum Road.
Arboretum Road and Inlet Road will be closed for part of the day to allow crews to install the bumps.
The changes for the summer were the result of concerns raised by people who live in the area, visitors to the park and the groups that use it about drivers going too fast through the park, where speed limits are 15 miles per hour.
Numerous events are held in Payson Park, including concerts, youth sports, and fundraiser walks and runs for a variety of causes.
A speed study in the park in March found that 97 percent of vehicles exceeded the posted speed limit on Arboretum Road, with the 85th percentile of speed being 28 mph. The study found that 58 percent of vehicles on Catafalque Drive were going over the speed limit.
Crews have already added new speed bumps and wider bike lanes.

title: Capturing a piece of Biddeford history, one item at a time: Cultural group plans time capsule
text:
Picture this: It’s 2076, and downtown Biddeford looks a lot different than it did in 2026. People aren’t walking around with smartphones — they’re using projections to talk with friends and family.
Forget strawberry matcha and iced lattes with cold foam. Teenagers are sipping on hyper-personalized wellness drinks designed to deliver the exact nutrients, vitamins and minerals their bodies need.
And as a 77 year-old woman (who looks and acts like she’s 40, thanks to synthetic age reversal) walks past City Hall, its historic bricks won’t be evident at first. Instead, the building will be covered in hydroponic greenery to help accommodate an ever-changing coastal climate.
Who knows if that’s really what Biddeford will look like in 50 years — it probably isn’t — but whatever does happen, a new time capsule project organized by the Biddeford Cultural and Heritage Center will allow residents of the future to look back on what life was like in 2026.
“I graduated in 1976, and things have changed so much even since then,” center President Diane Cyr said. “We didn’t have cellphones, we didn’t have computers. Things can change so much in 50 years.”
The project is a way to capture what Biddeford is like right now, Cyr said: the people who call the city home, its leadership and the events that shaped the community.
REMEMBERING AND LOOKING AHEAD
The idea was conceived long before 2026, when the cultural center was beginning to think of how to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the United States. By the time the capsule is reopened, the United States will be 300 years old, and Biddeford will be over 400 years old (it was first settled in the early 1600s).
“We just want people to understand where they come from and what it was like 50 years ago,” Cyr said.
University of New England student Damien Jones is volunteering along with the cultural center to help make the time capsule a reality.
Jones has been working with the center as part of a class called Management of Nonprofit Organizations. During that time, he has been assisting Cyr with various tasks and conducted street interviews to learn what it’s like to live in Biddeford.
The time capsule project caught his eye, he said, because he believes preserving history can help future generations learn from or even emulate the past to further advance humanity.
“Learning how Biddeford operated and what it looked like 50 years ago can help residents either reconnect with the good parts of Biddeford’s roots or learn from our mistakes, so they don’t repeat them,” Jones said.
WHAT’S GOING INSIDE
What goes in the capsule is important, Cyr said — the items that are chosen will represent the Biddeford of today. Some have already been chosen: an essay from a Biddeford High School student, a proclamation from Mayor Liam LaFountain, a walking map of the current downtown and menus from popular restaurants like Pizza by Alex.
Jones also hopes to include an art project created by a resident and something that represents the city’s minority populations, “to show how diverse the community is,” he said.
The capsule might also include objects related to the killing of Biddeford resident Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was fatally shot by a federal immigration officer in July.
Rather than being buried in the ground like traditional time capsules, this one will be displayed in a case at City Hall, serving as a reminder of the future that is being created every day.
Submissions are also still open to the public, Cyr said, and ideas can be sent to [email protected].
A closing ceremony to celebrate the capsule’s sealing will be held at The Lincoln Hotel on Jan. 7.
“(The time capsule) will be a valuable learning tool for the future,” Cyr said. “It gives residents a little bit of their history.”

title: Support Ron Russell in Congressional District 1
text:
We need a representative in Congressional District 1 who will focus on the needs of the people of Maine. We do that by voting for Ron Russell. Chellie Pingree has been congresswoman since 2009. It’s time to retire her. She’s not working for us.
Pingree’s most important job is to be “against Trump.” We’ve had enough of her not being “for Mainers.”
Ron was born and raised in Maine, and has a big family here. He’s a West Point graduate and a retired Army colonel. He founded a business; he knows how to take care of his employees. Ron is who we need “for Mainers.” Ron says “Hard working families and seniors are left behind by jet-setting politicians who ignore their reality.” Mainers need their reality to be brought to Washington, D.C.
This election is about being “for Mainers,” not about “being against Trump.”
Ron Russell is “for Mainers.” Vote for Ron to represent Maine.
Paul Kowacki
Walpole

1 dead, 6 injured in shooting at California Spirit Halloween
text:
31-year-old pregnant woman shot, killed at California Spirit Halloween
A 31-year-old woman was identified as the person killed in Friday's mass shooting at a Spirit Halloween store at the Solano Town Center in Fairfield, California.
The woman, Constance Hages, was pregnant at the time of her death, family told police.
Fairfield police on Saturday also shared more details about the six others wounded in the shooting, who ranged in age from 16 to 43 years old.
They included a 16-year-old boy, a 19-year-old man, a 32-year-old man, and a 23-year-old man who all remained hospitalized in critical but stable condition.
Two other victims, a 19-year-old man and a 43-year-old man, have been released from the hospital after being treated for gunshot wounds.
No one has been detained in connection with the shooting, which police responded to at 8:30 p.m.
As of Saturday morning, police said they believe the shooting stemmed from a targeted incident involving one suspect inside Spirit Halloween.
Detectives are still reviewing video footage and other evidence to identify the person responsible, the department said.
A witness told Denzen Cortez of Hearst sister station KCRA that his wife, who was inside the Spirit Halloween store, heard gunshots and people were running.
"I think she told [me] that there was like five, six, seven shots when people were running," the witness said.
Another witness, Miena Davis, said she heard a series of popping sounds shortly after entering the store. A second round followed, and shoppers began running.
“Everything froze and was like, ‘What was that?’” Davis said. “And then another round of the same sound went off and then a bunch of shoppers started running.”
Davis said people broke open a gate leading back into the mall, allowing them to escape. She left her car in the parking lot overnight as she ran to safety.
“It was immediate panic,” Davis said. “You heard a mom crying out for their child. And it just was so surreal.”
Solano Town Center announced it has canceled its planned Mall-O-Ween trick-or-treating event in light of the shooting. However, the mall will be open Saturday from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.
FBI Sacramento said it was deploying its Evidence Response Team to help Fairfield police with the investigation.
Among the other law enforcement agencies that responded were Suisun City police and the California Highway Patrol.
Anyone who has information can contact the Fairfield Police Department at 707-428-7600 or email 1030mall@fairfield.ca.gov.

title: Hugh Jackman pays tribute to Patrick Stewart
text:
'Tremendous friend': Hugh Jackman pays tribute to late ‘X-Men’ costar Patrick Stewart
Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed English actor known for his roles in "Star Trek" and "X-Men," has died. He was 86.
Video above: Patrick Stewart at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival
Tributes poured in from fellow actors and celebrities, but one Instagram post garnered nearly 3 million likes, more than 8,800 comments and 150,000 reposts.
"We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days," his "X-Men" co-star Hugh Jackman said on Instagram, featuring two photos of the pair embracing.
Jackman's breakout role was playing Wolverine in Bryan Singer's "X-Men" — a superhero film based on the Marvel Comics. Stewart was cast as Professor Charles Xavier, founder and mentor of the superhero team.
Stewart played the role in nine feature films ("X-Men," "X2," "X-Men: The Last Stand," "X-Men Origins: Wolverine," "The Wolverine," "X-Men: Days of Future Past," "Logan," "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness," and "Avengers: Doomsday") and voiced the role in several video games ("X-Men Legends," "X-Men Legends II," and "X-Men: Next ")
Stewart died Wednesday at his Los Angeles home following a brief battle with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, a statement on the actor's Instagram page reads.
The 2017 film "Logan" dives deeper into the relationship between Wolverine and Xavier, which was emblematic of the deep friendship between Jackman and Stewart.

title: ‘Feels like he’s still on leave’: Families mourning after crash that killed 3 Navy sailors
text:
PENSACOLA, Fla. (WWSB/Gray News) - Three service members assigned to Naval Air Station Pensacola died in an Oct. 24 crash in Florida, the Navy confirmed.
What happened
The vehicle was traveling westbound when it hit a barrier at M Street and caught fire, Pensacola police said.
All three sailors were pronounced dead at the scene.
Sailors identified
The Navy said two of the sailors killed were assigned to the Naval Air Technical Training Center. The third was assigned to Naval Aviation Schools Command.
Cmdr. David Gardner, a spokesperson for Naval Education and Training Command at Naval Air Station Pensacola, identified the service members as:
- Aviation Ordnanceman Airman Apprentice Dracon Bagley
- Aviation Ordnanceman Recruit Francois Longdayeyambete
- Airman Apprentice David Deanda
Bagley, of Michigan, enlisted in the Navy on May 14.
Longdayeyambete, of Massachusetts, enlisted on July 9.
“He’s the best one that anyone could ever ask for. He always had my back every time my mom would get mad at me. He always told me right from wrong,” Longdayeyambete’s brother Joseph said.
Dane Laboissonniere, Longdayeyambete’s school football coach, said his former player always wanted to be an aeronautical engineer.
Deanda, of California, enlisted in the Navy on June 4.
“It just feels like he’s still on leave. So, he ain’t coming home, but, we think like, ‘Oh, he’s still out there,’” Deanda’s father said.
Navy statement
The Navy also issued a statement.
“The Navy is mourning the loss of our shipmates and extends our deepest condolences to the sailors’ families, friends and fellow sailors during this difficult time,” the statement said.
Navy chaplains are providing grief counseling and support.
Investigation
The circumstances leading up to the crash are still under investigation.

title: Maine is better when we work together
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
David Libby is president and CEO of Town & Country Federal Credit Union, one of Maine’s largest credit unions with nearly 40,000 members.
Maine has always been a place where people understand the power of working together.
We are an independent bunch. We take pride in doing things ourselves and making our own way. But some of Maine’s greatest successes have come when we recognize that doing something together can accomplish far more than doing it alone.
That is the spirit of the cooperative movement, and it is one of Maine’s greatest strengths.
October is National Co-op Month, providing an opportunity to recognize the many cooperatives that contribute to the economic and social fabric of our state — and to celebrate the people who make them possible.
Cooperatives are built around a simple idea: people coming together to meet a shared need, with ownership, decision-making and benefits staying close to the people and communities they serve.
You don’t have to look far to see that spirit in Maine.
We have community-owned food cooperatives connecting consumers with local farmers and producers. Our fishing communities have long relied on cooperatives to help independent fishermen gain greater purchasing and marketing power. There are agricultural cooperatives, worker-owned businesses, housing cooperatives and, of course, credit unions. Maine even has resident-owned manufactured housing communities where neighbors collectively own and manage the land beneath their homes.
These organizations operate in very different industries, but they share a common philosophy: We are stronger together.
The economic impact of that philosophy is significant.
When a cooperative buys from a local farmer, producer or business, those dollars can stay within the local economy. When residents own their housing, more control and wealth can remain in the community. When workers have an ownership stake, they have a greater opportunity to participate in the success of the business where they work.
And when people join a credit union, they become members and owners of a financial cooperative whose success is directly connected to their financial well-being and the communities it serves.
That is local economic development at its most fundamental level.
But the impact of cooperatives goes well beyond dollars and cents.
Cooperatives create connection.
A food co-op can be a gathering place for neighbors, a market for local farmers and a way for consumers to support the local economy. A housing cooperative can give residents a stronger voice in their homes and create a deeper sense of community. A credit union can provide financial services while building relationships and reinvesting in the communities its members call home.
At Town & Country, we describe our approach as “Local Helping Local.” For us, that reflects a belief that a financial institution should be more than a place to conduct transactions. We have an opportunity — and a responsibility — to help strengthen the people, businesses and communities that make Maine such a special place to live and work.
That is really what the cooperative movement is about.
It puts people at the center of the equation. It gives people a voice and a stake in the organizations they rely upon. And it creates opportunities to build wealth and strengthen communities from the ground up.
Perhaps most importantly, cooperatives remind us that community is not something that simply happens. It is something we build together.
Maine has a tremendous cooperative tradition, but our greatest opportunity is to continue building upon that tradition. As we confront challenges such as affordable housing, food insecurity, workforce development, and keeping more wealth in Maine communities, cooperation can be part of the solution.
We don’t have to reinvent the idea. We simply have to remember what Mainers have understood for generations. We’re better when we work together.
This National Co-op Month, let’s celebrate the organizations that embody that belief — and the people who continue to prove that when Mainers cooperate, we don’t just build stronger businesses.
We build stronger communities, stronger local economies, and a stronger Maine.

title: ‘Bravest person I know’: School shooting victim leaves hospital after 262 days
text:
‘Bravest person I know’: School shooting victim leaves hospital after 262 days
A 13-year-old girl who was critically wounded in the deadly February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, Canada, has been released from hospital after 262 days, her father said Thursday.
“There was never a day I stopped believing we would get here. The road ahead is still long, but this is a milestone no one thought we would reach,” David Gebala wrote in an emotional social media post addressed to his daughter Maya, calling her “the bravest person I know.”
Related video above | Safety experts weigh in on additional measures schools could take to prevent or delay a shooter from gaining entry
Maya was among more than two dozen people wounded in the mass shooting at a secondary school in the small mining town in northern British Columbia, which left eight people dead, including six children, in the country’s deadliest school shooting in decades.
She was shot three times and airlifted to British Columbia Children’s Hospital in Vancouver, where doctors initially told her family she was unlikely to make it through the night, according to Gebala.
“You refused to accept the words we heard 262 days ago when you came out of the OR. Look at you, my girl. You blew every expectation out of the water,” Gebala wrote in the post to Facebook, which included a video of Maya smiling in her wheelchair.
Since February, Maya has undergone five surgeries, including receiving a prosthetic skull, Gebala said in the post, which listed challenging and hopeful milestones over the past 262 days.
“251 days ago, you opened your eye, moved it, and shifted your leg only to be rushed back for emergency surgery that morning,” he wrote. “179 days ago, your prosthetic skull was placed. Your fifth surgery, and the one that finally stuck.”
“145 days ago, you smiled for the first time (intentionally) while we played thumb war,” Gebala went on. “61 days ago, I heard your voice again.”
“Now it’s time to leave these hospital walls behind and keep moving forward, Maya Bear,” Gebala wrote, thanking the nurses, doctors and therapists “who walked every step of this with us.”
Gebala has frequently offered updates on Maya’s long recovery in posts to Facebook, including a recent excursion to see the rock band Foo Fighters and celebrate her 13th birthday.
Maya, who was in the school library when the massacre unfolded on February 10, was shot three times, including in the head, which shattered parts of her skull and left her with catastrophic brain injuries, according to a criminal complaint filed by her family against OpenAI.
The lawsuit, filed by Maya’s mother Cia Edmonds on her behalf, is one of dozens filed against OpenAI in both US and Canadian courts on behalf of victims, survivors and witnesses accusing the tech company of negligence after it emerged that the shooter, 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, had used ChatGPT to plan the attack. The province of British Columbia is also suing OpenAI.
OpenAI has pushed back against claims that it does not take safety seriously. In response to the lawsuits from the victims’ families, a company spokesperson told CNN in April that it has a “zero-tolerance policy for using our tools to assist in committing violence.” The company has said it deactivated an original account created by the shooter in June 2025 for violent activities, but Van Rootselaar made a second account to keep using the chatbot.
The company’s CEO Sam Altman has previously apologized to the community of Tumbler Ridge for failing to notify authorities to the shooter’s disturbing online conversations with the AI chatbot even after staff flagged the account internally.
Earlier this month, US authorities arrested a 30-year-old from Washington state who allegedly offered advice and sent money to Van Rootselaar ahead of the shooting.
CNN previously reported Van Rootselaar posted about guns and hunting and her apparent mental health struggles online in the lead-up to the massacre.

title: Man posing as Amazon delivery driver accused of stealing multiple packages from neighborhood
text:
LAKE OSWEGO, Ore. (KPTV/Gray News) - A Portland man has been arrested after police say he stole packages while posing as an Amazon delivery driver.
According to the Lake Oswego Police Department, 51-year-old Ramiro Despaigne Rodriguez was arrested on Oct. 21 after packages were reported stolen from at least eight homes in the Lake Oswego area.
Police said the suspect was caught on surveillance video driving a car marked with a “delivery driver” sticker and wearing an Amazon vest.
Rodriguez was arrested and booked into the Clackamas County Jail, where he faces first-degree theft charges.
Investigators believe there may be more victims connected to this case.

title: 20-year-old man dressed as zombie accused of stabbing 2 people at a coffee shop, police say
text:
AUSTIN, Texas (KEYE) - A man dressed in zombie makeup and clothing that looked like a Halloween costume is accused of stabbing two people Wednesday night at a coffee shop in southeast Austin, according to police.
The stabbing happened at Buzz Mill Coffee around 9 p.m. Wednesday.
According to the Austin Police Department, 20-year-old Shanor Temple Grace then left in a pickup truck. APD said he hit an unoccupied Tesla Cybercab.
Officers arrested Grace a short time later as he walked on a nearby trail, APD said. He is facing two counts of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.
Both victims were taken to a hospital. One had life-threatening injuries, and the other had non-life-threatening injuries. Both are now in stable condition.
Detectives are working to determine whether Grace knew the victims. Police have not said what led to the disturbance.
The stabbing comes as APD is urging people to take precautions around Halloween.
Asked whether police see criminals use Halloween costumes to commit crimes, Cmdr. Christopher Juusola of Austin police said:
“No, that’s not something that we normally observe downtown. And again, I think that one’s just related to it’s Halloween time. People are going to costume parties, and that’s what caused that to occur.”

title: Virginia and DC sue over Trump's arch, adding to legal challenges as government wants work to begin
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The legal challenges to President Donald Trump’s proposed memorial arch are mounting, with the District of Columbia and Virginia suing in federal court Saturday as the administration says construction could begin as early as next week.
There are now three lawsuits calling for a halt to potential work on a monument that would rise 250 feet (76 meters) on a patch of grass off the bridge that spans the Potomac River, connecting the city with Arlington National Cemetery. That would make the arch 100 feet taller (30 meters) than the Statue of Liberty is from its base to the top of the torch.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan is already considering issuing an order to halt the project until the original lawsuit against the Trump administration by three Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian is resolved. She held a hearing Friday but did not immediately act, though she said she would move expeditiously.
In the latest lawsuit, two attorneys general, Brian Schwalb of Washington and Jay Jones of Virginia, argue that “as soon as Defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm on both the District and Virginia. The Arch site sits at the center of a major traffic artery between the District and Virginia, in the monumental core of the capital, on an island that straddles the Potomac River. During the three-year period of construction, the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges. ‘’
As the original plaintiffs have, they also are seeking a temporary restraining order that would slow the administration’s plans to move ahead imminently with construction.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The lawsuit raises concerns about how the traffic interruption would impact emergency responses in a region where joint operations are the norm, including the January 2025 midair collision between a military helicopter and airliner that killed 67.
The Republican administration, in a recent court filing, said it had plans to seek final approval of the project, a Trump-favorite, at Thursday’s meeting of the Capital National Planning Commission and possibly begin construction the same day, despite the then-two active lawsuits pending.
On Friday, the government submitted a 106-page plan for the arch that envisions a massive structure more than 12 stories high that includes a huge bronze statue of Lady Liberty with wings and carrying a torch with an eternal flame. The structure would include an observation deck with views to the east and west, an “occupied roof” and two mezzanines.
Inside the arch are rooms for program space, offices, a staff lounge, circular staircases, multiple elevators and a “fire command center.” The project proposes significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic on nearby roads. Administration officials have said the arch also will have a national security function.

title: Man and two dogs die in Belfast fire
text:
State officials are investigating the cause of a fire that killed one person and two dogs in Belfast on Friday afternoon.
Firefighters initially responded around 2:40 p.m. to a report of a fire at 142 Back Searsport Road. When they arrived at the mobile home, crews were challenged by “heavy fire conditions,” according to the Maine Department of Public Safety.
As they worked to suppress the fire, first responders discovered a body inside the home.
“The deceased individual was transported to the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Augusta, where an examination will be conducted to confirm the individual’s identity and determine the cause of death,” Maine State Police Major Aaron Turcotte said in a statement.
Two dogs were also found dead inside.
The Office of State Fire Marshal is investigating the fire’s cause and origin. They have “narrowed the area of origin to a rear porch that contained a laundry area,” Turcotte said, but a precise cause remains undetermined.

title: Putting a section of the Appalachian Trail to bed for the season
text:
Rain drums on the truck roof in the pre-dawn grey. Comfortably ensconced in downy warmth inside the pickup’s bed, I roll over and continue my slumber. There’s no rush on this early October morning. Several hours later, an open eye spies the sun filtering through the spruce and fir. I crawl out of the bag into my work clothes, puffy jacket and beanie, slide off the tailgate and set about making a cup of coffee and gathering up the trail tools.
The Appalachian Trail is just a few minutes down a gravel logging road from my campsite. I park the truck off to the side just beyond the bridge over Sandy Stream, shoulder my pack full of safety gear, snacks and water, grab my chainsaw, and head for the footpath. It’s not lost on me as I cross the stream that Benedict Arnold and his men passed through this very spot on their long, arduous march to Quebec in the autumn of 1775.
As a volunteer for the Maine Appalachian Trail Club (there are hundreds of us, thankfully), I’ve been maintaining this section since 2004. Maintainers are expected to visit their respective sections a number of times each year to keep the pathway open, clearing trees and brush from the trail, maintaining infrastructure such as water bars and bog bridges, and where applicable, caring for signs, blazes, shelters, campsites and privies.
My section of the AT leads through mossy spruce and fir before crossing a creek. The trail then climbs over a hillock topped by a grove of mature hemlocks before meandering along to cross a tote road. After a perennially wet stretch, the trail reaches East Carry Pond. Here, it turns sharply left and follows the west shore to a pocket sand beach before continuing on its beautiful way to the pond’s northwest corner and the end of the section.
I walk without hurry over the familiar ground, not another soul around this late in the year. I come upon a yellow birch across the trail that has also pushed a tangle of branches into the treadway. I buck up the mess, toss the pieces aside and move on to the next scenario, a moose maple that’s only a step-over, but I take it out just the same. Here and there, I sweep my saw horizontally through clumps of shrubs; it’s faster than clipping stems individually.
When I first took over this section, it hadn’t been regularly maintained for a while. On that first weekend trip, I removed 180 blowdowns, with lots of help from a strong crew of swampers, who also worked feverishly at chopping back the wild shrubbery that had not only encroached on the trail but, in places, completely obscured it. It took a few years to get the stretch in proper order, but the end result was highly satisfying.
I proceed carefully on the slippery bog bridges, individual sections and strings of log planks stretching for 100 feet or more. All told, there are about 1,200 feet of bog bridges on the section, all newly installed in the last 15 years. It was a monumental task made possible only with the help of many hard working, bug slapping volunteers. The last of the logs was finally spiked in place last summer. Whew.
The last half-mile of my saw-in-hand saunter along East Carry Pond is glorious, one of the finest stretches anywhere of the entire 2,200 miles of the AT. The sandy beach, the huckleberries, the clear water, the fragrant spruce, the views of far off summits, the remote feel of the place, it’s all magnificent.
At section’s end, I plop down on a rock, gobble up a candy bar and consider my good fortune for the opportunity to care for this beloved pathway. I then wander back the way I came, and at the truck, take a deep breath. The trail has been “put to bed” for another season, and it feels good. I drive out through the colorful foliage with another satisfying thought on my mind: the all-day breakfast at Griswold’s in Solon.
If you’d like to become an MATC volunteer (there are a wide variety of roles you can play), visit www.matc.org and you’ll find all the information you need. Many hands make light work, and the club would love to have your help. Thank you!
Carey Kish of Mount Desert Island is a Triple Crown hiker, freelance writer, and author of three hiking guides. Connect with Carey on Facebook and Instagram and at [email protected].

title: Heavy rains expected to bring flooding risk to already saturated parts of the US Southwest
text:
Heavy rains starting Saturday evening were expected to bring a threat of flash flooding to already saturated areas of the U.S. Southwest through Monday, according to the National Weather Service.
As much as 4 inches (10 centimeters) of rain could fall across the region, where a number of weather systems have brought a deadly autumn of soaking rains. In the Phoenix area on Friday evening, emergency crews rescued people from several vehicles on flooded streets.
“It’s not going to take much rainfall to be impactful at all in some of these locations just because of how saturated they are,” said Allison Santorelli, a meteorologist with the Weather Prediction Center in College Park, Maryland.
The National Weather Service has issued flood watches for nearly all of Arizona and parts of southern Utah, southwestern Colorado, and western New Mexico, in addition to part of southern Nevada. Those watches include the Four Corners region, a sparsely populated area where Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah meet that has been hit especially hard by recent rains.
Santorelli said this weekend’s rain was expected to bring both flash flooding and small-stream river flooding.
The Phoenix Fire Department said in a post on X that it rescued people from four vehicles on flooded streets on Friday night, while a fire captain in nearby Scottsdale said on Facebook crews were rescuing a person in one vehicle on a flooded street when another vehicle carrying two people drove into the same waters and had to be rescued.
Scottsdale fire Capt. Dave Folio said in a video posted on Facebook that just 2 inches (5 centimeters) of water can “sweep your vehicle off its wheels,” and that the vehicles were in 3 to 4 feet (0.9 to 1.2 meters) of water.
In Bullhead City, Arizona, located on the state’s border with California, heavy rains on Friday left water, rocks and debris on streets across the city and closed parks, the city said in Facebook posts.

title: Kyle Chrisley pleads guilty to charges stemming from 2025 arrest, reports say
text:
(Gray News) - Kyle Chrisley, son of reality television star Todd Chrisley, has pleaded guilty to resisting arrest in an incident from December 2025.
Chrisley was arrested on charges including assault on a police officer, disorderly conduct, domestic assault, public intoxication and resisting arrest. According to Us Magazine, the remaining charges were dismissed.
He was arrested Dec. 20 after his wife called police, reportedly saying he was “belligerent.” When police arrived, Chrisley reportedly punched multiple officers.

title: Democratic congressional candidate served with felony warrant at campaign event
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A Democratic candidate running for North Carolina’s Congressional District 14 was served with a felony warrant at a campaign event earlier this month.
According to the Polk County Sheriff’s Office, deputies served 49-year-old Lakesha Womack with a felony warrant on Oct. 11.
Authorities said the warrant was from 2020, charging her with failure to return a hired motor vehicle valued at more than $4,000.
The arrest warrant stated that Womack rented a 2019 Toyota Corolla from Budget Car Rental in October 2019 and did not return it by the agreed-upon date.
The car was reportedly worth $20,000.
The criminal summons was originally issued in January 2020 but was not served until this month. It was not immediately clear why the warrant was not served earlier.
Womack is running for Congressional District 14, which includes Gastonia, Shelby, Morgantown, and parts of far south Charlotte. She is challenging Republican incumbent Rep. Tim Moore.
Womack’s campaign did not directly address the felony warrant when asked about the situation, but did address the alleged attack ads from Moore’s campaign.
“Over the past few weeks, allegations involving me have drawn significant media attention and attack ads from Friends of Tim Moore. Candidates for public office should be held accountable and voters deserve transparency,” a statement read in part.
“Throughout this campaign, I have emphasized accountability and affordability. I believe every candidate and elected official should be evaluated by consistent standards, including their record of public service, their decisions in office, and their responsiveness to the people they represent,” the statement continued.
The midterm general election will be held on Nov. 3.

title: Reality TV show contestant said he drinks raw milk. Research shows that’s risky
text:
Netflix’s ‘Love is Blind’ contestant said he drinks raw milk. Research shows that’s risky
It’s not often that romance reality show drama turns to public health matters.
But when Netflix’s hit matchmaking series “Love is Blind” introduced John Shannon, an account manager, to Sarah Williams, a public health professional, it was only a matter of time before Shannon’s habit of drinking raw cow’s milk would send shockwaves through the conversation.
“Is that safe?” one of Williams’ friends asked after Shannon disclosed he consumes unpasteurized milk from a farm.
“No,” Williams said.
Public health officials have long warned against drinking raw milk and championed milk pasteurization as a modern public health triumph.
But Williams told her friends, “I’m looking past the raw milk.”
High profile figures have promoted raw milk in recent years, including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., soccer star Erling Haaland and actor and wellness mogul Gwyneth Paltrow, who says she has raw cream in her daily coffee.
Since the episode was released, Shannon said on social media that he no longer drinks raw milk after moving away from the farm that supplied it. But science shows there are other important reasons to steer clear of unpasteurized dairy.
What is raw milk?
It’s a term used to refer to cow’s milk in its most basic form, when it is taken straight from the animal and rapidly chilled.
Raw milk can be creamier and taste different or slightly sweeter than traditional milk. As raw milk ages, it gets more sour. Raw milk fat also separates from the rest of the liquid, forming cream at the top.
Unlike the cow’s milk most people buy at the grocery store, raw milk is unpasteurized and non-homogenized.
What is milk pasteurization and homogenization?
Milk pasteurization is the process of heating something up to kill harmful pathogens. In most cases, cow’s milk is heated to at least 161 degrees Fahrenheit for at least 15 seconds before it is quickly cooled again. Pasteurization also extends milk’s shelf life by killing bacteria that can cause it to spoil.
Homogenization keeps milk from separating and forming a layer of cream at the top. For milk, the process involves forcing milk through small openings under high pressure, which breaks fat globules into extremely small particles and evenly distributes them throughout the fluid.
Homogenization gives typical store-bought milk its smooth, consistent texture and appearance.
What kinds of pathogens does pasteurization kill?
The dangerous, illness-causing organisms and bacteria it kills include listeria, salmonella and E. coli. It also kills the bacteria that causes tuberculosis and the virus that causes bird flu. Cows that appear healthy can shed these pathogens in their feces, making it easy for milk to become cross-contaminated during the milking process.
Research shows raw milk is far more likely than pasteurized milk to be linked to illness and hospitalizations from foodborne pathogens.
Have there been documented cases of raw-milk related illness outbreaks?
Yes. In the U.S. from 1993 to 2006, researchers examined 121 dairy-related disease outbreaks that caused about 4,400 illnesses, 239 hospitalizations and three deaths. Seventy three of those outbreaks, or 60%, were caused by raw milk, a 2012 Centers for Disease Control and Prevention study found. The raw milk outbreaks accounted for 1,571 illnesses (36%), 202 hospitalizations (85%) and two deaths.
“Raw milk product outbreaks led to much more severe illnesses, and disproportionately affected people under age 20,” according to the CDC. For raw milk-related outbreaks where ages were known, about 60% of patients were younger than age 20, while 23% of patients in outbreaks from pasteurized products were under age 20.
“This study shows that raw milk has great risks, especially for children, who experience more severe illnesses if they get sick,” study co-author Dr. Barbara Mahon said in a press release. “Parents who have lived through the experience of watching their child fight for their life after drinking raw milk now say that it’s just not worth the risk.”
A 2017 study found people who consume raw milk products are 839 times more likely to experience illness and 45 times more likely to be hospitalized. It said dairy consumption-related outbreaks cause about 760 illnesses and 22 hospitalizations each year on average, and unpasteurized dairy products cause 95% of those illnesses.
What are the laws on selling raw milk?
Raw milk isn’t available for purchase everywhere. It is illegal to sell raw milk across state lines, so large commercial dairy operations don’t often sell it, but laws vary.
In some states such as California, Washington, Arizona, Nevada and Pennsylvania, in-state retail sale of raw milk is allowed. In others — including Massachusetts, where “Love is Blind” filmed this season — dairy farms can sell unpasteurized milk directly to consumers.
Public health authorities from the CDC, the Food and Drug Administration, the American Academy of Pediatrics, other health groups and various state and local officials have for decades said consuming raw or unpasteurized dairy can be dangerous — especially for young children, elderly and immunocompromised people. Unpasteurized dairy is also especially risky during pregnancy: Listeria can cause miscarriage, stillbirth and illness or death of a newborn.
Still, survey data shows that about 4% of U.S. adults reported drinking raw milk in the past year and about 1.6% reported frequent raw milk consumption. Studies have also found that unpasteurized dairy-related illness outbreaks are more frequent in states where it’s legal to sell unpasteurized dairy.
Does heating milk to kill bacteria reduce its nutritional value?
No.
“There are some minor changes, but nutritionally, pasteurized milk is really, really close to raw milk,” Gabriel Keith Harris, a food science professor at NC State University, said in 2025.
A 2011 analysis found that pasteurizing milk reduced the concentration of vitamins B12, C, B9 and E, but milk isn’t considered a strong source of those vitamins in North American diets to begin with. Dairy products are, however, an important source of vitamin A and pasteurization appeared to increase milk’s vitamin A concentration. Studies have shown mixed results about pasteurization’s impact on vitamin B2, but pasteurized milk is still a good dietary source of the vitamin. Pasteurized milk is also often fortified with vitamin D.
Does raw milk have benefits for digestion?
No. Despite raw milk proponents’ claims that it’s a good source of enzymes or beneficial bacteria called probiotics that support digestion, it does not contain probiotics at all. In a 2015 study, University of Wisconsin-Madison food science researcher John Lucey called claims to the contrary “myths.” Enzymes found in raw milk have no proven role in digestion.
Bifidobacteria, a bacteria raw milk advocates sometimes cite as a “good,” is present in human and cow GI tracts, and its presence in raw milk “indicates fecal contamination and poor farm hygiene,” the FDA said.
Ultimately, said David Mills, a food science and technology professor at the University of California at Davis, the risk-benefit analysis of drinking raw milk is a “no-brainer.”
“We have lack of proof of a benefit, and we have overt proof of a higher rate of infection of the humans consuming it,” he said. With that in mind, he said, people should seriously consider: Is it worth the risk?
For public health and food science experts, the answer is clear: No.

title: Ambulance driver accused of abandoning patient, said he was ‘done driving for the day’ and called an Uber home
text:
CLEVELAND, Ohio (WOIO/Gray News) — An ambulance driver is accused of abandoning a patient he was transporting to the hospital earlier this week in Ohio.
The incident happened Wednesday evening in Cleveland.
The patient was being transported to the Cleveland Clinic with chest pain when the ambulance driver got lost, told her he was done driving for the day, and called an Uber to take him home.
The driver worked for Lynx EMS, a private ambulance company, and not for Cleveland EMS.
According to Cleveland Association of Rescue Employees (CARE) Local 1975, once the driver left the patient, a Cleveland EMS unit responded to the scene.
The paramedics then administered medical care and brought the woman to the hospital, a CARE spokesperson said in a statement.
“We stand by our EMTs, paramedics and dispatchers who strive to provide the best care to anyone who is in need of it,” the CARE spokesperson added.
In a statement to WOIO, a spokesperson for Lynx EMS wrote:
“Patient safety and quality care are of the utmost importance to us and responsibilities we take very seriously. Upon becoming aware of the situation, immediate steps were taken to address the matter and ensure the patient’s well-being and care needs were addressed.
We are continuing to review the circumstances surrounding this incident and will take appropriate action based on the findings of that review. As this involves personnel and patient related matters, we are unable to comment further.
We remain committed to providing high-quality care and maintaining the trust of our patients, their families, healthcare partners, and the communities we serve."

title: Searsmont welcomes home Robbins family member months after deadly lumber mill explosion
text:
As she prepared to come home from Massachusetts General Hospital after five and a half months there, Lily Robbins asked if she could drive the ambulance herself. Her supervisor at Searsmont EMS, where Robbins is a volunteer, laughed.
“I told her it was too soon!” recalled Amy Drinkwater, the interim EMS chief.
Robbins and several others were seriously injured in a fire and explosion at Robbins Lumber mill on May 15. They were all either first responders or members of the Robbins family, and Lily Robbins is both. Three people have died, including Lily’s father, Alden Robbins.
On Friday, though, Drinkwater’s recollection reflected the celebratory mood: Lily Robbins was finally coming home to Searsmont. Drinkwater, who has visited her at the hospital recently, said Robbins has been eager to get back and to do medical work again.
She left Mass General on Friday midday. A caravan of seven trucks from the Searsmont Fire station went to pick her up, joined along the way by first responder vehicles from dozens of agencies, including many that had been in Searsmont on May 15.
Arriving back on Friday for a reception, trucks rang their bells and honked horns, and a crowd of locals, friends and extended family members cheered and waved.
Robbins walked slowly into the fire station, greeting people. One hand was wrapped in a bandage; burn marks showed on the other and on her face. Robbins looked at the little kids holding up “welcome home” signs.
“Thank you all so much,” she said. Later, she added thanks for everyone who has sent cards, letters or gifts.
“I’ve read every single word of every single card I got, and it made me smile,” she said.
She went into a deep embrace with three of her closest friends from college who are all paramedics — Taylor Church, Blake Tripp and Lila Bell. With tears streaming down their faces, they said it doesn’t feel real to have Robbins home at last.
Church said she’s been texting nonstop with Robbins, and they already have plans to get together at Church’s house.
The day was meant to feel like a big hug for Robbins and her family, said Jodi Staples, a fellow EMS volunteer who was driving one of the ambulances in the procession on Friday. Supporters started bringing homemade cookies and signs to the fire station earlier in the morning. Deb Pickering came from Belfast wearing a Searsmont Strong T-shirt.
“We want to let her know we’ve been thinking about her all this time,” Pickering said.
Members of the Robbins extended family came with signs, too.
“We have prayed so hard for her,” Lily’s great aunt Suzanne Philbrook said with tears in her eyes. “We’re so grateful God spared her life.”
On May 15, a silo full of wood shavings at Robbins Lumber caught fire, exploded and rocketed off the ground about an hour after the initial fire. Dozens of volunteer firefighters and EMS personnel had arrived at the mill. Morrill volunteer firefighter Andrew Cross died the same day, and Searsmont Assistant Fire Chief Wayne Woodbury died in June, shortly before Alden Robbins.
Other people injured in the explosion were on hand Friday to help welcome Lily Robbins home, including Thomas Wolf, a Searsmont Fire volunteer and an employee of Robbins Lumber. He walked into the fire station on Friday morning to take his place in the procession.
“Hospitals are great but there’s nothing more satisfying than being at home,” he said. “I can’t wait for Lily to get home and be in that environment.”
Wolf’s most severe injuries were to his head; he also has visible scarring from burns on his hands, though he said he can now hold a pencil to write. He has returned to work at Robbins and intends to volunteer with the fire service again.
The explosion has motivated more people in town to volunteer, as well. Searsmont Selectman Chris Staples said he thinks eight people have joined the fire and EMS, doubling the roster.
He decided to volunteer himself and plans to take his fire truck driving test on Sunday.
Robbins’ homecoming reception is healing for the town, said Clerk Angela Cilley. When Cilley posted about it on Facebook hundreds of people cheered the news and Lily Robbins responded, saying, “I’m so grateful for this community.”
“It’s something joyful for the town after so much uncertainty and loss,” Cilley said on Friday. “I think people want to see her face to make sure it’s real.”
The family founded Robbins Lumber in 1881 and still operates it, which is a point of pride in the community. The town and the company are closely intertwined. Searsmont is raising relief funds by selling stickers, hats and shirts with an image of Robbins Lumber alongside fire department and EMS logos. Kids from the area often take field trips and tours of the lumberyard.
Lily Robbins, 23, graduated from the University of Maine a week before the explosion and plans to apply to medical school, her great aunt Jane Newcomb said Friday.
The Midcoast Villager reported Robbins needed several blood transfusions during her treatment at Mass General. A GoFundMe organized by the restaurant where she worked in Camden to support her recovery has raised more than $81,000.
Investigations into the fire and explosion are ongoing. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration has a mid-November deadline to release its findings. In August, a separate agency, the National Institute of Occupational Safety and Health, called for better labeling and identification of hazards at silos and more training to deal with them.
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Rachel Estabrook can be reached at restabrook@metln.org.

title: Police corporal killed in ‘freak’ motorcycle crash remembered by wife, father
text:
AUTAUGA COUNTY, Ala. (WSFA/Gray News) - An Alabama woman says she just had two and a half weeks with her husband before he was taken away from her in a motorcycle crash.
“I’m waiting for him to walk through the doors,” newlywed bride Chloe Greiner-Davis said.
Greiner-Davis’s husband, Dakota Davis, was a corporal with the Prattville Police Department.
The 25-year-old was killed after a wreck on his motorcycle, something Davis’s wife and father say was a freak accident with no one to blame.
According to loved ones, motorcycles were a hobby for Davis and something he had a passion for since he was a kid.
“I was so upset that he got a motorcycle, but I knew it was his calling,” Greiner-Davis said. “My biggest thing was you could be the best driver on this planet, but other people just don’t know how to drive.”
Davis was described as a family man who was intentional with his words and found real purpose in his job as a police officer protecting and serving the public.
“A man of few words, and he meant what he said. Deep into the heart. He didn’t say it unless he meant it,” his father, Paul Davis, said. “Very outgoing young man, but a man of few words. You know, he loved his family, loved playing sports.”
The emotions remain raw as the family prepares for a funeral on his favorite holiday: Halloween.
Paul Davis shared a heartfelt message for this son through tears:
“He is loved, and he is missed.”
For Greiner-Davis, the message to her husband is simple:
“I just want him to know that I love him. So much. I just love him so much.”
Greiner-Davis said she has been left to navigate mortgage payments and moving expenses without the love of her life, all while continuing to work toward her master’s in elementary education.
Thankfully, the community has already stepped up, raising thousands of dollars in support.
