title: A third weekend of protests in France as youth-led rallies sweep Europe
text:
A third weekend of protests in France as youth-led rallies sweep Europe
Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.
About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy.
Related video above: Student protests rock France
France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers' turnout estimates are much higher.
Authorities in France reported about 300 arrests nationwide so far — down from 800 at the same point in last week's protests.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches the previous two Saturdays.
At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, thousands gathered behind a line of students who led the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France's largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed on side streets.
The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle.
The marchers' grievances are diverse.
Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.
Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats."
The crowd streamed along the Boulevards des Maréchaux, the ring of avenues that skirts the edge of Paris, in a march that was joyful for hours. Techno music blasted from speakers, a painter at work along the route drew cheers from the crowd, and some marchers went trick-or-treating. A police helicopter hovered overhead as the sun set slowly over the city.
Later, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, where the march ended. Protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police. Officers responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. The blasts echoed through the streets, and smoke filled the air as dusk fell.
Many peaceful marchers turned back, coughing, their eyes streaming with tears, and left the march, some scattering into the nearby Bois de Vincennes, one of the largest parks in Paris.
Police impose curfew and other measures
The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.
While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.
Macron said that Saturday's marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday.
Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.
Protests took place in Germany, Portugal and the Netherlands
In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.
In Berlin, young protesters also gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.
"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.
Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.
"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage; nothing is being done about it. We have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.
Later on Saturday, police ended a protest march early in the western city of Cologne after protesters used pyrotechnics, threw stones at them and covered their faces despite a ban. Police also used water cannons to disperse demonstrators. In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds in Hamburg. In Frankfurt, protesters pummeled police with stones, injuring several officers, one of them severely, police said.
Elsewhere in Europe, people also protested against the housing crisis and for a better future.
Thousands of protesters, including families with small children, converged in downtown Lisbon to peacefully protest Portugal's housing crisis, holding up placards reading "Houses or Fire" and "We are not Afraid." Others in the crowd held aloft small cardboard houses while a few dressed up for Halloween.
In The Hague, Netherlands, there was a strong police presence in and around the downtown shopping area on Saturday afternoon after online appeals for protests and fears of rioting and looting. However, there was little sign of protests and no major disturbances by midafternoon. Police frisked some groups of black-clad youngsters and checked their identities, local media reported. Many stores in the city were boarded up as a precaution.
Kirsten Grieshaber reported from Berlin. Angela Charlton and Thomas Adamson in Paris; Kerstin Sopke and Geir Moulson in Berlin; Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands; and Helena Alves in Lisbon, Portugal, contributed to this report.

title: ICE raids could cost Maine billions in lost economic output
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Immigrant employment in Maine helps sustain nearly 74,000 jobs statewide and nearly $15 billion in total economic output, according to the Maine Office of New Americans. (Adobe Stock) By Kathryn Carley Listen to this story HERE Federal immigration enforcement surged in Maine this year, and a new report showed the removal of immigrant workers could cost the state up to […]
Immigrant employment in Maine helps sustain nearly 74,000 jobs statewide and nearly $15 billion in total economic output, according to the Maine Office of New Americans. (Adobe Stock)
By Kathryn Carley
Listen to this story HERE
Federal immigration enforcement surged in Maine this year, and a new report showed the removal of immigrant workers could cost the state up to $3 billion in annual economic output.
The report highlighted the contributions of more than 30,000 foreign-born workers in the state, particularly in the manufacturing, construction, agricultural and healthcare industries.
Julia Trujillo Luengo, director of the Maine Office of New Americans, said the arrest of even one employee can have a chilling effect on a workplace, keeping other workers home or dissuading new applicants.
“We’re gravely concerned as a state if this continues. It’s going to have devastating consequences, irreparable consequences for our state as a whole,” Luengo asserted.
Close to 500 people in Maine were arrested by federal immigration agents through early August, according to the Deportation Data Project, and of those, 98% had no criminal conviction.
More than 40% of ICE arrests took place in January, when federal agents launched what they called “Operation Catch of the Day.” Shortly thereafter, the Maine State Chamber of Commerce and its regional offices sent a letter to the state’s congressional delegation requesting greater oversight of enforcement actions. They noted businesses across nearly every sector were triaging operations just to remain open.
Luengo added employers are still struggling with the uncertainty of ICE raids and the inability to plan.
“Certainly what Maine doesn’t need is any artificial methods coming in removing workers from our labor force when we already have a tight labor market,” Luengo emphasized.
The report cited previous research showing immigrants in Maine are generally younger and participate in the workforce at a significantly higher rate than those born in the U.S.
Maine has the oldest population in the U.S., and the share of people aged 65 or older is projected to grow to nearly 30% by 2050. Luengo pointed out immigrants fill a significant number of healthcare jobs, and when they are removed from the workforce, there is no one to replace them.

title: ‘I choked that dog out’: Rescue operator charged with felony animal torture
text:
BUTLER, Ind. (WPTA/Gray News) - An Indiana woman who operated an animal rescue is facing criminal charges.
Butler authorities say Kayla Dillenburg, 30, strangled a dog she pulled from an Indianapolis shelter, profited from donor pledges meant for its care, and admitted to the killing on a recorded phone call.
Dillenburg, who operated Welcome Home Canine Rescue out of her residence, has been charged with torture or mutilation of a vertebrate animal, a felony, and fraud.
Court documents stated Dillenburg pulled 21 dogs from Indianapolis Animal Care Services over a 10-day period in late April.
Investigators allege she targeted animals carrying high financial pledges raised by social media donors trying to save shelter pets from euthanasia.
According to an affidavit of probable cause filed by DeKalb County Sheriff’s Office Animal Control Officer Erika Hedge, the investigation began in May after an IACS volunteer rescue coordinator raised concerns that dogs transferred to Dillenburg had gone missing and her rescue’s social media accounts were taken offline.
Authorities said the criminal charges center on a dog named Motley. According to court documents, he was scheduled for rescue and had $925 in public pledges.
Investigators said Dillenburg picked Motley up from Indianapolis on April 28, but records showed Motley died and was dropped off for cremation that same day.
Court documents stated Dillenburg told an Indianapolis donor that Motley was alive and had an approved adoption lined up.
However, investigators concluded Dillenburg deceived the donor into paying for care after the animal was already dead.
Court documents stated Dillenburg claimed Motley died at her home of pneumonia and denied euthanizing him.
Investigators contacted a former friend of Dillenburg. That friend told deputies that Dillenburg approached her in April with a scheme to make money by pulling dogs with high pledges from Indianapolis.
Investigators obtained a recorded phone call between Dillenburg and the friend in which they say she admitted that she “choked that dog out” after claiming he went after her child.
Officer Hedge outlined the basis for the felony and misdemeanor charges:
“I believe Kayla Dillenburg has knowingly, intentionally, and recklessly tortured and/or mutilated a dog in her care because, by her own admission, as stated in a recorded conversation, she strangled Motley to death.
Kayla told the public that Motley died from pneumonia, but there was no record of Kayla providing him medical care or a diagnosis ... I believe Kayla has knowingly and intentionally committed fraud by obtaining dogs from Indianapolis Animal Care and Control for the sole purpose of making a profit off their pledges.”
While the criminal affidavit directly addresses Motley’s death, animal welfare advocates and volunteers still have questions about the other animals Dillenburg allegedly acquired.
Court records confirm that IACS received paperwork for only four of the 21 dogs.
Dillenburg told police that a mother dog and her puppies were placed with a rescue in Michigan, but investigators noted she never produced paperwork or proof to verify the claim.
Officer Hedge said she could not comment on the status of the remaining animals because the investigation remains active and ongoing.
Hedge added that she has received numerous calls from additional people coming forward with information as news of the charges continued.
Court records showed Dillenburg appeared before a judge on Friday. She entered a plea of not guilty, and a public defender was appointed to represent her.
Dillenburg was released on her own recognizance and scheduled to appear in court again in January 2027.

title: It’s always an extra sweet Halloween in Yarmouth
text:
I want to share a story about a lifelong friend whose heart is as big as her love for Halloween. My kindergarten buddy, Karen, is now 65 years old, and still possesses the pure, magical wonder of a child when October rolls around.
Over the past several years, Karen has transformed her garage into a spectacular, community-wide haunted house. She’s a teacher at heart, and it truly shows in the immense detail, thought and care she puts into every square inch of the display. From whimsical, festive sights for the youngest trick-or-treaters to genuinely spooky thrills for the older crowd, she designs unforgettable scenery and activities that offer something for absolutely everyone. She pours her entire heart and soul into this project every single year just to bring joy to the neighborhood.
But the real magic of Karen’s haunted house is its purpose. While admission is free, she collects donations from visitors and personally delivers them to the local food pantry in Yarmouth to help neighbors in need. Sixty years after we first met in kindergarten, Karen is still teaching all of us the true meaning of community spirit, creativity and generosity.
If people see a spectacular haunted garage in Yarmouth this week, please stop by, marvel at the scenery and drop off a donation. I thank Karen for making her community a brighter, more magical place.
Edie Ungar-Shafron
Shaker Heights, Ohio

title: This election is about who can do more for Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, is seeking her sixth term in the United States Senate.
Every six years, Maine posts a job opening for a United States senator. I’m applying to keep the job, and you are the hiring committee. On Tuesday, you make the hire.
A good committee looks for sound judgment, integrity and a record of working across party lines. It wants a leader who can negotiate agreements that last and who knows when to give a little and when to hold firm.
Then it checks references. Here are mine.
Denise, a retired Aroostook County schoolteacher who now collects the full Social Security she earned because of a law I worked to pass. Gerry, a Knox County lobsterman, and the nearly 5,000 others still hauling traps because I wrote the law that shielded them from federal rules that threatened the whole industry. Jean, who owns a hotel in York County that survived the pandemic thanks to the Paycheck Protection Program I wrote, which saved more than 250,000 jobs.
Mark in Androscoggin County, whose son has Type 1 diabetes and counts on the research I fight to fund to stay healthy. The emergency room teams in Bridgton, Rumford and Millinocket, where funding I secured is building and expanding the ERs families depend on. And ask Maine’s firefighters and police officers both of whose unions have endorsed me.
As chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, I have brought home nearly $1.5 billion for 672 projects in all 16 counties over the past five years, including $10 million to modernize Maine Veterans’ Homes and improve care for those who served. I fought for Bath-built ships and for jobs at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Kittery and Pratt & Whitney in North Berwick.
I am working to lower prescription drug costs for our seniors and to build more housing so your kids can build their lives here. I won’t stop.
I have always worked across the aisle. In 2009, I was one of three Republicans who joined President Obama to pass the recovery package that helped end the Great Recession. I led the effort to repeal Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell and to pass the Respect for Marriage Act. I voted to save the Affordable Care Act. Last year, I opposed this president’s signature budget bill over its Medicaid cuts and still secured $190 million this year alone to support Maine’s rural hospitals.
I don’t work for any president. I work for you. When this administration cut off funding for Maine Sea Grant, which serves our coastal towns, I called the commerce secretary and got it restored. When tariffs threatened Maine businesses that depend on Canadian trade, I pressed the White House and secured exemptions.
My opponent, Troy Jackson, says he is going to Washington to fight. I believe America is crying out for compromise and less chaos.
In Augusta, Jackson pushed costly programs, from solar subsidies that raised electric bills to spending that leaves the next governor a projected $1.3 billion budget gap. Governors of both parties vetoed more than 100 of his bills.
Fellow Democrats have questioned his temper. He says he has no regrets for telling me to “shut up” in our final debate. Shouting may win “likes” on social media, but it doesn’t pass bills in a closely divided Senate. That takes sound judgment, strong relationships and a willingness to find common ground with people you disagree with.
Outside groups have spent millions to mislead you about my record and my integrity. But you know me. You’ve seen me visiting small businesses, schools and in the grocery store. You trust me to work hard and do what is right, something I learned growing up in the County. I have never missed a roll call vote, more than 10,000 in a row.
Check my references. Compare our records. I offer results and the independent leadership to keep them coming. Maine needs a senator who puts Maine first and knows how to get things done.
On Tuesday, you make the hire and I ask for your vote.

title: Mariners’ winning streak snapped by Trois-Rivières
text:
Brooklyn Kalmikov scored twice and set up another goal against his former team, leading the Trois-Rivières Lions to a 4-2 win over the Maine Mariners in an ECHL game Saturday afternoon in Trois-Rivières Lions, Quebec.
Jack Works put the Mariners in front just 2:51 into the game, but Kalmikov tied it later in the first period. The Lions then got goals from Nathael Roy and Jacob Dion just 1:07 apart in the second period to make it 3-1.
Kalmikov, who ranks second on the Mariners’ career-scoring list, got his fifth goal of the season into an empty net with 2:59 remaining. Wyllum Deveaux then scored for Maine with 2:15 left.
The loss snapped a three-game losing streak for the Mariners, who will continue their road trip with three games in North Carolina against the Greensboro Gargoyles.

title: Obituary: Ruth “Tiny” Hoffman
text:
CAMBRIDGE, Mass. – Ruth “Tiny” Hoffman died Oct. 15, 2026, just shy of her 99th birthday at home in Cambridge surrounded by family as she had hoped.
Raised in Rochester, NY, she married Fenno Hoffman in 1947 whom she met in Small Point, Maine, a much-loved place their families spent summers for generations. They moved to Cambridge in 1957 where they raised their four children. From 1967-69 she flourished living in Rome, where Fenno taught through RISD.
After a second marriage to Jim Drier living in Staten Island, NY, and Bath and Brunswick, Maine, where she enjoyed the company of friends and local restaurants and time at the Spirit Pond cabin, she kept the friends and returned to Cambridge in 2003.
Some of her life interests beyond her family: 20 years in the hospice movement; Carl Jung (dreams, the shadow, the importance of intuition and the feeling life) through the Jung Centers in Cambridge and Brunswick, Maine; the natural world with the beach, the birds, the light on the Herons; making new friends and keeping old ones, including a beloved “death partner.”
Ruth took part in the civil rights movement; shared the influences of her privileged class background on the Phil Donahue show in support of the Haymarket People’s Fund; supported the women’s and GLBTQ movements through her children and stood on the on-going side of justice. In the last years, she asked daily about the war.
As she developed dementia, the family held a “living funeral” for her in 2022 to hear from friends and relatives. “I’ve had a good life. I’ve known a lot of interesting people.”
Her spirit is carried on by her children, their partners and grandchildren- John and Kate (Stevens) of Charlemont, Mass., Cathy and Betty (Burkes) of Cambridge, Mass. and god-son Aaron Cartterfield of Bath, Annie and John (Lapham) of Arlington, Mass. and son Adrian of LA, and Sarah and son Josh of Cambridge.
A celebration of her life will take place Saturday, Nov. 14, 2 p.m., at the Mount Auburn Cemetery Story chapel in Cambridge. Live stream at https://vimeo.com/event/6297829/fd31657424
In lieu of flowers,
vote Blue in her honor

title: Hancock County town expands EMS to 24/7 coverage
text:
A small Hancock County town is expanding its EMS to provide residents with coverage 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
Gouldsboro residents voted Thursday night to approve a supplemental budget that allows the town to expand its EMS coverage, Town Manager Joshua McIntyre said.
About 70% of the 122 registered voters approved the nearly $265,000 bump, which means EMS on the Schoodic Peninsula will move to 24/7 coverage through two-person crews, McIntyre said. Winter Harbor is also covered by that EMS and will need to approve a roughly $42,000 jump.
Gouldsboro is one of the few small Maine towns expanding its EMS services. Most are grappling with continually rising costs for running their own service, or simply have ceased funding their own department and contract with neighboring EMS providers instead.
Before the vote, the town shared with residents a Bangor Daily News investigation that found rural EMS is at the brink of collapse and residents are at risk of an ambulance not arriving when one is needed. Gouldsboro also shared a BDN report on Dennys River Volunteer Ambulance closing in Down East Maine as its 80 year old owners retire, as well as a copy of a 2023 report about the cost of rural health from the University of Southern Maine.
The overall budget will come in around $900,000 with the expanded hours. The area has about 450 calls a year, but there is no way to predict what time of day those calls will happen, McIntyre said.
“There was a lot of consideration that went into this, and it’s not done lightly, and it’s not done without the realization that this is a significant chunk of the budget and the burden on the taxpayers of Gouldsboro and then Winter Harbor,” McIntyre said.
There have been times where Gouldsboro hasn’t been able to respond to calls and relied on other services to help. That is always uncertain and part of what prompted the town to expand its EMS.
When an EMS call comes in overnight, first responders are at home and must go to the station to pick up the ambulance and then go to the call, McIntyre said. Some of the night shift workers left the service over the summer, he said.
“It just put a lot of stress on the system, which was one of the primary motivators to try to increase the budget in order to be able to hire former full-time employees and ensure paid hourly coverage around the clock,” McIntyre said.
There is an open EMT position, which Gouldsboro will fill before it starts hiring the additional staff, McIntyre said. The town also needs to hire a permanent EMS director. The interim has split his time between EMS and the fire department, which has been a lot of work, he said.
“Now we’ve got to get the hard work of getting things in place,” McIntyre said.

title: County Soccer Teams Advance as Cross Country State Titles Go on the Line
text:
County Teams Reach Soccer Regional Finals, More Soccer and Cross Country State Championships Take Center Stage Saturday
It was another big Friday for Aroostook County high school sports, and there's still plenty more to come before the weekend is over.
Fort Kent's girls, both Wisdom soccer teams, Madawaska and Fort Fairfield's boys all earned trips to the Northern Maine regional championships Friday. There were convincing shutouts, a dramatic penalty-kick finish, and another chapter added to a familiar Class D rivalry.
And Saturday won't be any quieter.
Both Presque Isle soccer teams are still fighting for spots in the regional finals, three County girls teams have Class D semifinal games, and Fort Kent's boys are heading to George Stevens Academy.
Meanwhile, some of the County's best distance runners are in Augusta for the Class B and Class C State Cross Country Championships, with Houlton/GHCA looking to defend its Class C boys state title.
Here's a look at Friday's results and everything coming up Saturday.
Friday's Girls Soccer Semifinals
Class C North: Fort Kent Breaks Open Scoreless Game Against Houlton
(1) Fort Kent 5, (4) Houlton 0
For the first 50 minutes Friday, there wasn't much separating Fort Kent and Houlton.
The two County teams battled through a scoreless first half, and the game remained tied until Reece Doucette stepped up for a penalty kick in the 50th minute.
Doucette converted to give the top-seeded Lady Warriors the lead, and from there, Fort Kent took control.
Doucette finished with two goals, Hannah Plourde added two more, and Avery Werntgen also found the back of the net.
The 5-0 victory sends Fort Kent back to the Class C North regional championship.
The Lady Warriors will face second-seeded Orono, which advanced past sixth-seeded Winslow in a penalty-kick decision following a scoreless game.
It's a matchup between the top two seeds in Class C North, with a trip to the state championship on the line.
Eight-Person Girls: Wisdom Hands Sumner Its First Loss
(2) Wisdom 5, (3) Sumner 0
Wisdom's girls are headed back to the eight-person North regional championship after a convincing 5-0 win over previously unbeaten Sumner.
The Lady Pioneers put together another impressive offensive performance, with Ellie Cyr leading the way with two goals.
Madi Cyr, Libby Cote and Hannah Martin each added a goal.
Wisdom has now scored 11 goals in its two tournament games while allowing just one.
The Lady Pioneers will face top-seeded Dexter in the Northern Maine championship after Dexter shut out Shead 2-0 in its semifinal.
Friday's Boys Soccer Semifinals
Class D North: Madawaska Returns to the Regional Championship
(1) Madawaska 2, (4) Hodgdon 0
Madawaska's boys are headed back to the Class D North championship after shutting out Hodgdon 2-0 Friday evening.
Owen Gagnon and Aiden Gagnon provided the scoring for the top-seeded Owls.
The victory sends Madawaska into the regional championship for another meeting with a very familiar opponent.
For the third consecutive season, the Owls will face Fort Fairfield with the Class D North title on the line.
Class D North: Fort Fairfield Earns Another Shot at Madawaska
(3) Fort Fairfield 3, (2) Central Aroostook 1
Fort Fairfield made sure the Tigers would get another opportunity to face Madawaska, defeating second-seeded Central Aroostook 3-1 in Friday's semifinal.
The third-seeded Tigers went on the road and earned the victory, advancing to the Class D North regional championship for the third straight meeting with the Owls.
It's become one of the area's most familiar postseason matchups, and this year's championship will once again feature two County teams competing for the Northern Maine title.
Eight-Person Boys: Wisdom Survives Dramatic Finish at Calais
(3) Wisdom 2, (2) Calais 1 (Penalty Kicks)
Wisdom's boys are also headed to a regional championship after a dramatic semifinal against Calais.
James Desjardins scored the Pioneers' goal in regulation, and the game eventually went to penalty kicks to determine who would advance.
Preston Lavoie, Sam Paradis, Zeek Cyr and Cayden Hargrove were among Wisdom's successful penalty-kick takers.
Goalkeeper Bentley Nadeau delivered the decisive moment, stopping Calais' final attempt to secure the victory.
The third-seeded Pioneers will now face fourth-seeded Penobscot Christian in the eight-person North championship.
Penobscot Christian advanced with a 3-0 victory over ninth-seeded Houlton, ending the Shires' memorable postseason run after their overtime upset of top-seeded Mattanawcook earlier in the week.
Saturday's State Cross Country Championships: County Runners Head to Augusta
While soccer teams continue their postseason runs across Northern Maine, Saturday is championship day for the state's top distance runners.
The Maine State Cross Country Championships are taking place at Cony High School in Augusta, with Aroostook County athletes competing in both Class B and Class C.
There are team championships to chase, individual titles on the line, and some County runners looking to finish outstanding seasons with one more strong performance.
Class B: Presque Isle and Caribou Bring Strong Girls Teams to States
Presque Isle and Caribou both enter the Class B state meet after strong performances at the Northern Maine regional championships.
Presque Isle finished second in the girls regional team standings, while Caribou placed third.
Caribou's Emma Graves will be one of the County runners to watch after winning the Northern Maine Class B individual championship.
Presque Isle's Lillian Johnson and Aleah Rideout have also turned in strong performances this season and will look to help the Wildcats against the best Class B competition in Maine.
The state meet gives both programs another opportunity to see how they stack up against teams from across Maine.
The Class B boys race gets underway at 11 a.m., followed by the girls at 11:40 a.m.
Class C: Houlton/GHCA Boys Look to Defend State Championship
One of the biggest County storylines in Augusta belongs to the Houlton/GHCA boys.
The Shires are the defending Class C state champions, and they're heading into Saturday with plenty of momentum after winning their second consecutive Northern Maine regional title.
Houlton/GHCA scored just 30 points at regionals, with four runners finishing among the top five.
Malachi Witmer, Brayden Drake, Wyatt Quint and Logan Witmer helped lead the way, giving Houlton another opportunity to compete for a state championship.
But Saturday brings a different challenge, with the top teams from both Northern and Southern Maine competing for the title.
The Shires will be looking to put together another strong team performance and bring another championship back to Houlton.
Class C Girls: County Individuals Earn Their Spots at States
Aroostook County will also have several runners competing individually in the Class C girls state championship.
Charlotte Estabrook and Isabella McCarthy of Houlton both qualified with strong regional performances.
Eleanora Streeter of Washburn and Sadie Wigmore of MSSM also earned places at the state meet.
Although Houlton's girls did not qualify as a team, these runners will have an opportunity to represent their schools individually against the top Class C competition.
The Class C boys race begins at 12:20 p.m., followed by the girls at 1 p.m.
Saturday's State Cross Country Schedule
Cony High School, Augusta
- 11 a.m. — Class B Boys
- 11:40 a.m. — Class B Girls
- 12:20 p.m. — Class C Boys
- 1 p.m. — Class C Girls
All times are subject to change.
Saturday's County Soccer Semifinals
There's still plenty of soccer left to play, too, with several County teams looking to join Friday's winners in the regional championship games.
Girls Soccer
Class B North
(7) Cony at (3) Presque Isle — 1 p.m.
Presque Isle is coming off a 3-1 quarterfinal victory over Skowhegan, with Peyton Boinske scoring twice and Carrlyn Buck adding another.
The Lady Wildcats will host seventh-seeded Cony, which upset second-seeded Gardiner 2-1 to advance.
Class D North
(3) Central Aroostook at (2) Fort Fairfield — Noon
Another all-County matchup will decide a regional championship berth.
Fort Fairfield advanced with a 4-0 shutout of Washburn, while Central Aroostook held off Van Buren 3-2.
(5) Madawaska at (1) Penobscot Valley — 1 p.m.
Madawaska will try to keep its postseason run going after defeating Ashland 2-1 in overtime Wednesday.
The fifth-seeded Owls now face top-seeded Penobscot Valley on the road.
Boys Soccer
Class B North
(4) Presque Isle at (1) John Bapst — Noon
Presque Isle's boys are one victory away from the Class B North championship after defeating Erskine Academy 4-1 in the quarterfinals.
The Wildcats head to top-seeded John Bapst, which survived a close 2-1 quarterfinal against Caribou.
Class C North
(3) Fort Kent at (2) George Stevens Academy — 2 p.m.
Fort Kent's boys will try to join the girls team in the regional championships.
The Warriors advanced with a 2-0 victory over Washington Academy, with Dom Cyr and Finn Marquis scoring.
Now Fort Kent travels to George Stevens Academy for a semifinal matchup in Blue Hill.

title: Residents evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky reach Ukraine after localized ceasefire
text:
Residents evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky reach Ukraine after localized ceasefire
Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky crossed into Ukrainian-held territory Saturday in a major rescue operation carried out under the most significant truce since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine 4½ years ago.
The civilians traveled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus, following a deal brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump. Ukrainian authorities imposed restrictions on disclosing the number of evacuees or the border crossing location. The measures are to safeguard those who chose to remain in Oleshky as well as to protect future humanitarian missions, the organizers said.
The ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, which began at 3 a.m. Tuesday, is expected to continue through Sunday evening. The estimated 2,000 remaining residents of Oleshky were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.
Those who chose to return to Ukraine were taken to the Russian city of Anapa, then flown to Homel in Belarus, from where they proceeded back home.
Daughters wait to see their fathers again
Relatives waited on Saturday at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them. Volunteers from organizations, including the Red Cross, Doctors Without Borders and the World Central Kitchen, were also there.
Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father over 2½ years ago when she, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory while he stayed behind, was among those waiting.
“We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said.
Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month.
He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbors but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family’s home and animals fell through.
“We realized that, well, there was no (other) way, and he walked us to the road and that was it — that was the last time” they saw him, Pavlyn said.
She said that since then, he had feared making the arduous journey out, particularly without Russian documents.
Russia’s ombudswoman and lead representative on the mission, Yana Lantratova, said buses also transported Oleshky residents who wanted to live in Russia. Russian media outlets on Saturday showed civilians arriving at a temporary accommodation site in Simferopol on the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
Russia and Ukraine have not specified how many people chose to leave the city, but the U.S. first lady posted on social media Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.
Apart from Melania Trump, Pope Leo XIV — the first American pontiff — also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to allow aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
The US approves Patriot missile sales for Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday welcomed U.S. approval of Ukraine’s purchase of 500 PAC-3 Patriot interceptors but urged partners to supply the weapons from existing stocks to protect the country this winter, warning the newly authorized U.S. sale could take years to deliver.
“Right now, the Russians are attacking our energy infrastructure every single day. In just these past two weeks of October, there have already been more than 30 Russian strikes on critical parts of our power grid,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
The Trump administration said Friday that it had approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot air defense interceptors, after Kyiv had accused the Pentagon of delaying deliveries of the vital munition needed to stop Russian ballistic missiles.
The U.S. State Department said 500 Patriot missiles would be purchased for Ukraine with donations from Canada, Germany and Norway through a U.S. program and that no American funds were involved.
A Ukrainian drone attack kills 2 in Russia
Meanwhile, a Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia’s western Bryansk region, local Gov. Yegor Kovalchuk said Saturday. Another five people were wounded, he said.
Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region’s capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.
Zelenskyy said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.
The attacks targeted combined heat and power plants in Kyiv and Sumy regions, four electricity substations and a gas distribution facility in the Dnipro region and railway infrastructure in Dnipro and Kharkiv, he said, adding that repair crews were working to restore power.
Zelenskyy urged partners to impose further sanctions on Russia and provide new support packages to Ukraine.
“The world sees Russia targeting civilian infrastructure every day. Everyone who does not want to see this Russian escalation spread further into Europe must help Ukraine,” he said in an online post.

title: Late for class: 8th grader says bus ride to school routinely takes up to 3 hours
text:
NEW YORK (Spectrum News NY1) — A New York City eighth grader is routinely late for school because his bus ride takes about three hours.
The bus also picks up children who attend a different school.
Michael Mileto gets up at 5:30 a.m. and catches the school bus at 6:20 a.m. He has been late to school on a regular basis, arriving after the first bell at 8:15 a.m.
“It’s ridiculous,” Michael said.
Commute longer than last year
Michael has a speech-language disability. He attends a private school on the Upper East Side at the city’s expense because his needs could not be met in a local public school.
The city’s Education Department is responsible for busing him from his home in Brighton Beach.
This year, the ride has routinely taken two and a half or three hours. Once, Michael did not arrive until 10 a.m.
Last year, Michael was picked up around 6:45 a.m. and arrived at school on time at 8:15 a.m.
This year, his bus also carries children who attend a different school in Manhattan. That has required Michael to be picked up earlier and dropped off later.
“Now, all of a sudden, they just decide to make my school late,” Michael said.
Missed class time
Michael’s mother, Annie Mileto, said he is missing class time.
“He’s missing math, literacy, main subjects, things, and I’m worried. Of course, school makes up for it, sits with him and makes sure he gets it right, but he’s not doing it with his other students. You’re missing out on all of that,” Annie Mileto said.
Michael said the late arrivals affect his lessons.
“I miss lessons, and then I had to rush and get catched up,” he said.
The ride home has also run long. Michael said there was one day he did not arrive home until 6 p.m.
“I always feel tired and drowsy. I just want to go to bed, but I have to do my homework,” Michael said.
Other students affected
At the start of the school year, around 2,000 children on 300 bus routes did not have a driver. The city provided students with prepaid rideshare options, bought new buses and worked to get more drivers online at bus companies that have contracts with the city.
Randi Levine, policy director at Advocates for Children, said her organization is hearing from families who still do not have bus service. She said the organization is also hearing from families, like Michael’s, whose buses are more crowded and arriving later.
“There are times when it is most efficient to have children on the same bus, going to two different nearby schools, and we’ve seen that in past years. But what we’re seeing this year, in some cases, is that routes that were probably meant to be separate are being combined,” Levine said.
City reviewing route
A spokeswoman for the city’s public schools said the department takes concerns about long routes seriously. She said the department is reviewing Michael’s route, including GPS data and any delays that may have been caused by stops along the way, to see what happened and whether it can be improved.
Michael said he hopes something changes soon.
“I know its not their fault, but I think they should do better,” he said.

title: Trump lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday letter is dismissed with prejudice
text:
Trump lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday letter is dismissed with prejudice
The ruling said the lawsuit was 'grasping at straws'
Trump lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday letter is dismissed with prejudice
The ruling said the lawsuit was 'grasping at straws'
A federal judge on Saturday threw out President Donald Trump's multibillion-dollar lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to wealthy financier Jeffrey Epstein.
Related video above: DOJ releases final batch of Epstein files: what is and isn't included (1/30/26)
U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice.
The ruling said the lawsuit was "grasping at straws" as it attempted to "manufacture" flaws in the Journal's investigative reporting.
When a case is thrown out "with prejudice," it cannot be refiled again, and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.
The lawsuit was over a story the Journal published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter that the paper said bore Trump's name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday.
The letter bearing Trump's name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, "Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret," according to the newspaper.
Trump denied writing it and called the story "false, malicious, and defamatory."
The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami, accused the paper and its reporters of having "knowingly and recklessly" published "numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements," which, it alleged, caused "overwhelming financial and reputational harm" to the president.

title: ‘Grasping at straws’: Judge dismisses Trump’s $10B lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
text:
(AP) - Saying the president was “grasping at straws,” a federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to Jeffrey Epstein.
U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law. The ruling said the lawsuit had attempted to “manufacture” flaws in the Journal’s investigative reporting.
When a case is thrown out “with prejudice,” it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible.
The dismissal is a blow to Trump and his administration, which have both pursued adversarial relationships with news organizations during his second term. In addition to the Journal, he is embroiled in lawsuits involving the BBC, The Associated Press and — most recently — CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which are suing him for restored access after he banished them from the White House in mid-September.
Trump has denounced media outlets that write things to which he objects and frequently calls them “fake news” and insults their journalists.
Trump called the reporting ‘malicious’
The lawsuit against the Journal was over a story it published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the paper said bore Trump’s name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein’s 50th birthday.
The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Trump.
The letter bearing Trump’s name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, “Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret,” according to the newspaper.
Trump denied writing it and called the story “false, malicious, and defamatory.”
The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami, accused the paper and its reporters of having “knowingly and recklessly” published “numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements,” which, it alleged, caused “overwhelming financial and reputational harm” to the president.
Epstein died by suicide in a New York jail cell in August 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges.
The lawsuit was dismissed once, then refiled
Gayles previously dismissed the suit in April, saying Trump had failed to make the argument that the article was published with the intent to be malicious. But he gave the president a chance to file an amended complaint, which he did in May.
In Saturday’s ruling, the judge cited the Supreme Court’s landmark 1964 ruling in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. That decision made it harder for public figures to win libel lawsuits because it requires proof that a media outlet knowingly published something false or showed a reckless disregard for the truth.
“The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice,” Gayles wrote. “Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false.”
The judge also noted that the Journal’s story did not ignore or minimize Trump’s denial, “Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it.”
Gayles also said several other allegations in the lawsuit did not have merit.

title: In Maine’s Senate race, it’s heating oil vs. electricity
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, nonpartisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
Over the course of two weeks in October, Maine’s incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger, former state Senate President Troy Jackson, met for four debates. Each debate focused heavily on energy affordability, and each exchange followed roughly the same script: When Jackson brought up the high costs of heating a home with oil, Collins volleyed back by talking about the high costs of powering it with electricity, and vice versa.
With Jackson trying to link Collins to the Iran War that has caused heating oil prices to skyrocket, and Collins in turn blaming state policies enacted under Jackson’s Senate majority leadership for rising electricity rates, experts say it’s unclear whether either gained a major advantage on this issue during the debates.
“We don’t have a whole lot of indication the debates have moved anyone,” said Mark Brewer, chair of the Political Science Department at the University of Maine.
In addition to trading blame for a phenomenon that, at least on the power side, analysts say has multiple overlapping causes, the candidates revealed a stark contrast in their proposals for getting costs under control.
Collins emphasized more U.S. drilling and imports of fossil fuels, while Jackson said he would prioritize large clean energy projects and ongoing electrification. The implications for fighting climate change are significant.
The race, deemed crucial to Senate control, has been most recently rated a “toss-up” by The New York Times. Jackson leads by two points in most polls, reflecting a statistical tie.
Heating Fuel and the Iran War
Mainers already contending with a host of affordability challenges were walloped with a new one when they went to fill their heating fuel tanks ahead of winter: The cost of heating fuel is up over 80% from just a year ago, which will put the average cost of heating a home with fuel this winter, as about half of Maine does, at over $4,000.
The high cost of fuel and gasoline has been directly linked to blockages of the Strait of Hormuz following the U.S.-Israel initiation of war with Iran in February. It’s a war Collins initially backed before opposing it beginning in late April and one that has claimed the lives of dozens of Americans and likely thousands of Iranian civilians.
Jackson unrelentingly linked Collins to the war during the debates, pointing to her five votes against resolutions to bring troops home in the first months of the war. Collins explained these votes in the debates by saying the 1973 War Powers Resolution recognizes the president’s wide discretion during the first 60 days of overseas conflicts, which is largely true, but ignores that the same law leaves Congress the avenue Democrats tried to use to end hostilities.
Collins also pointed to her nine votes since April in favor of ending the war and criticized President Donald Trump in the third debate. “The president did not have a good plan. He should have anticipated the closure of the Strait of Hormuz,” she said.
Collins emphasized how she has tried to blunt rising costs for consumers: pushing for the early distribution of financial support for low-income Mainers to buy heating fuel and the release of national reserves. The low-income heating assistance program is one that Trump has tried to end.
Trump’s signature 2025 budget law ended consumer tax credits for electric vehicles and heat pumps that could have helped more households afford to transition off fossil fuels. Heat pumps continue to offer a much more affordable way to heat a home in Maine than oil, propane or kerosene, despite rising electricity costs.
Collins helped advance that “One Big Beautiful Bill” on a procedural vote before voting against it. Collins’ campaign did not return multiple requests for comment.
Jackson also blamed high electricity prices on the war in Iran, even though the increases predate the war by several years. Jackson’s campaign did not respond to questions on this point.
Electricity Costs and State Policies
If the war’s not primarily behind high power bills, what is?
“If you look at the policies that have driven up the cost of living in Maine, you have to look at Augusta,” Collins argued. She pointed specifically to a program that requires utilities to buy power from rooftop and community solar arrays at guaranteed prices.
That program is a piece of the puzzle—but a relatively small one, according to Maine’s Office of the Public Advocate, an official appointed to represent the interests of ratepayers.
State Republicans have criticized the program, known as net energy billing, in recent years, saying it cuts power costs for largely well-to-do households who can afford to install solar panels, while increasing them for everyone else. Maine Democrats have defended it as making it easier for anyone who wants to save money by going solar.
Collins specifically pointed to Jackson’s leadership when the program was expanded greatly in 2019 and his vote against eliminating the program entirely in 2023, a move the Public Advocate said would save the average household $275 per year.
Instead, the Legislature modified the program by ending new applications for larger projects and effectively reducing the compensation for some existing ones. Jackson defended this compromise.
“It did cost more than it should have, but we reformed it twice,” he said in one debate.
According to an analysis prepared for the state Public Utilities Commission, the program cost Maine’s ratepayers $193 million on net in 2025.
Maine’s current public advocate, Heather Sanborn, found those costs explain about 14% of the increase in electric bills since 2020—a number dwarfed by the impacts of rising electricity supply costs (45%) and costs to build electric poles and wires and repair them after storms (27%).
Sanborn, who voted for the 2019 law as a state senator, explained in an interview that the recent reforms should limit the costs of net energy billing going forward, though not eliminate them.
“The goal of the reforms was to cap any further increases in stranded costs,” she said, using the catch-all category that includes net energy billing. “But we can’t really forecast exactly whether they will decline or stay flat in any given year, because it’s very dependent on the wholesale market.”
What’s driving the high supply costs? Sanborn blamed two things: the method by which the state procures electricity and high prices for natural gas, which powers about half of electric generation in New England. She acknowledged the latter factor was largely due to constrained gas pipelines into New England, as well as geopolitical conflicts like the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
“When the natural gas system in the U.S. gets a cold, New England gets the flu,” Sanborn said.
Those pipeline constraints are largely the result of decisions over the past two decades by state courts and Democratic state leaders — albeit in New York and Massachusetts, not Maine.
Jackson did not acknowledge these causes, other than the invasion of Ukraine. Collins, for her part, said she supported expanding pipelines into New England, as well as major federal permitting reforms that would realistically be necessary to do so.
Jackson has not said whether he would support permitting reforms now being debated in Congress.
Fundamental Differences
Both candidates said America needs to become energy independent but differed on how to get there.
Jackson promoted renewable energy projects as the best solution. “We can actually get off of this boom and bust cycle (of fossil fuel prices) and lower our energy costs,” he said in the final debate, spotlighting a large proposed onshore wind project and transmission line from northern Maine he has championed as one means of doing so.
Collins, in contrast, criticized the Biden administration for revoking permits for the heavy crude-carrying Keystone XL pipeline and expressed support for more drilling in the Gulf of Mexico, as well as the aforementioned gas pipelines.
“Reducing greenhouse gases does make a lot of sense, but we’ve got to have an all-of-the-above approach to energy,” she said.
But expanding drilling and preventing the worst impacts of climate change don’t go together.
“If we still want to aim for a 2 degrees (Celsius) change in global mean temperature … then we certainly need to start changing our energy sources as soon as possible and moving towards net zero as soon as possible,” said Karen McKinnon, a climate scientist at UCLA. “I would not say that expanding oil and gas drilling and using more fossil fuels is compatible with that goal.”

title: Boothbay football crushes Telstar, 44-17, in playoff game
text:
Boothbay football scored a big win, 44-17, Oct. 30 versus Telstar of Bethel at Sherman Field in the 8-man football Southern Conference playoffs. Telstar led 9-8 at halftime as the Rebels scored on a touchdown pass as time expired.
But the second half belonged to Boothbay. Midway throught the third quarter, the Seahawks took the lead for good as Peyton Barter scored on a 60-yard middle screen. Boothbay led 14-9 in outscoring the Rebels, 36-8, in the second. half.
Boothbay advances to the Southern Conference championship game next weekend. Boothbay plays the winner of Old Orchard Beach and Maranacook. No. 2 Boothbay improves to 6-2. No. 3 Telstar drops to 3-6.
